sources.title: US National Security Agency's classified internal network reportedly goes offline - BBC
passages: A highly classified network used by the US National Security Agency (NSA) for internal communications went offline on Tuesday for an unspecified period of time, according to US media reports.

"While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues," an NSA spokesperson said in a statement to the BBC.

Multiple sources told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, that the agency was seeking to avoid having large numbers of employees log on to their computers simultaneously while the network was experiencing problems on Tuesday.
The outage reportedly affected the NSANet network, which is how officials send and receive top secret or classified information.
Chase Bank - the largest banking institution in the US - said a "software bug" in its hardware systems may have affected other banks and that it was not a cyber security incident.

Last week, a massive Microsoft outage impacted schools, healthcare systems, businesses, courts and governments around the world - including the US and Canada - while a network failure grounded all US flights.

"NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events." The agency had staggered employee arrivals earlier in the day as it worked to address the issue. The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said. “The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said later Tuesday afternoon that the NSA outage was the result of the agency applying a software patch to address major software vulnerabilities that were discovered last month. “The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected,” Clayton said on Fox Business. “That is that is what has happened at the NSA today.” The vulnerabilities Clayton were referring to are in PHP, a programming language that powers about 70% of the world’s websites. The NSA itself urged organizations to apply software patches. The flaws in PHP could allow hackers to break into websites and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords. Clayton said there is no sign that any of the recent tech outages, including that affecting the NSA, were the result of a cyberattack. A current and a former US official said an outage at NSANet would not impact the agency’s ability to communicate urgent intelligence to President Donald Trump while he is traveling in Asia on Air Force One. Both sources described multiple redundancies and backup networks that the government could use to communicate securely with the president who is currently in the Philippines before heading to China tomorrow for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. NSANet is “more of a network of networks, and it’s unlikely that a full outage exists given the many redundancies in place,” a former senior NSA official told CNN. So it is alarming, but likely not crippling.” A voicemail inbox recording for NSA employees on Tuesday morning described the situation as a “code yellow,” the second-highest in a system of three main levels that governs whether NSA employees report for work at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters or not. coreStoryFacts.text: Speaking on Fox Business Tuesday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton directly linked the NSA's classified network outage to urgent software updates following the discovery of critical vulnerabilities in PHP.
Unlike the NSA outage, Friday's FAA nationwide ground stop involved a hardware problem, rather than a software vulnerability.
Routine telecommunications maintenance triggered excessive network traffic that overwhelmed older routers, creating a cascading disruption across much of the air traffic control system.
It is not yet clear whether the banking, airline or technology companies' outages shared the same cause.
"If you go back about 10 days ago, we had what was labeled as PHP, an update to a web interface system," Clayton said.
"And the patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected.
NSA maintains that mission critical information sharing has not been impacted, while it asks personnel to delay nonessential tasks, according to sources.
The NSA said Tuesday the agency had experienced a "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance," adding that its mission/critical capabilities were still fully operational.
The NSA is responsible for collecting and analyzing foreign signals intelligence, identifying and countering cyber threats and protecting U.S. government communications.
The PHP2Shell threat was so serious that the FBI, NSA and CISA issued urgent warnings just under a month ago, on Oct.
21, directing organizations to immediately patch vulnerable systems.
The three agencies also advised those unable to install the fixes to take affected systems offline altogether until they could be secured.

The sweeping IT disruptions that have kept large swaths of the National Security Agency’s workforce at home for the past two days also impacted operations at a critical Georgia facility that supports signals intelligence and cybersecurity operations focused on the Middle East, where the US is currently engaged in a war with Iran, four sources familiar with the matter told CNN.
A highly classified network used by the US National Security Agency (NSA) for internal communications went offline on Tuesday for an unspecified period of time, according to US media reports.

"While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues," an NSA spokesperson said in a statement to the BBC.

Multiple sources told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, that the agency was seeking to avoid having large numbers of employees log on to their computers simultaneously while the network was experiencing problems on Tuesday.
The outage reportedly affected the NSANet network, which is how officials send and receive top secret or classified information.
Chase Bank - the largest banking institution in the US - said a "software bug" in its hardware systems may have affected other banks and that it was not a cyber security incident.

However, network restoration was still underway and had not been completed, according to the report.The agency's multiple layers of redundancy and backup networks were expected to help maintain essential operations while efforts to restore the affected systems continued.The disruption came amid a series of unrelated outages affecting major US technology companies, airlines and financial institutions over the past week.

Artificial intelligence helped uncover a pair of critical security vulnerabilities, triggering a global scramble last month to update software used by much of the internet, including the NSA. The flaws, collectively known as PHP2Shell, affect PHP, which is a programming language used by roughly 70% of websites. The race to patch vulnerable systems may help explain some of the recent technology disruptions. The PHP2Shell threat was so serious that the FBI, NSA and CISA issued urgent warnings just under a month ago, on Oct. 21, directing organizations to immediately patch vulnerable systems. The three agencies also advised those unable to install the fixes to take affected systems offline altogether until they could be secured. Speaking on Fox Business Tuesday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton directly linked the NSA's classified network outage to urgent software updates following the discovery of critical vulnerabilities in PHP. "If you go back about 10 days ago, we had what was labeled as PHP, an update to a web interface system," Clayton said. "And the patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected. That is what has happened at the NSA today." According to two sources familiar with the system, NSA Net as of right now is back up and running. Nonetheless, staggered arrival is continuing as fears persist that the system might not be able to handle everyone signing on at the same time. There is no word yet on how long the agency will continue the staggered arrival schedule, known as "Code Gray." NSA maintains that mission critical information sharing has not been impacted, while it asks personnel to delay nonessential tasks, according to sources. The NSA said Tuesday the agency had experienced a "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance," adding that its mission/critical capabilities were still fully operational. The NSA is responsible for collecting and analyzing foreign signals intelligence, identifying and countering cyber threats and protecting U.S. government communications. The agency has not yet responded to a CBS News request for an update on Wednesday. One U.S. intelligence official described the broader challenge of updating infrastructure that was originally designed for an earlier internet era. The volume and speed of changes can overwhelm aging equipment. The official's assessment reflects a growing concern among intelligence and Homeland Security officials that modern technology is advancing faster than the systems that support it. Speaking about PHP vulnerabilities, Clayton also pointed to the growing role of AI in speeding up both those kinds of discoveries and the pressure to respond. He described PHP as a "legacy vulnerability" that has been successfully patched across systems globally, adding, "This type of identification of vulnerabilities and patching goes on all the time." Unlike the NSA outage, Friday's FAA nationwide ground stop involved a hardware problem, rather than a software vulnerability. Routine telecommunications maintenance triggered excessive network traffic that overwhelmed older routers, creating a cascading disruption across much of the air traffic control system. It is not yet clear whether the banking, airline or technology companies' outages shared the same cause. sources.title: US National Security Agency's classified internal network reportedly goes offline - BBC
passages: A highly classified network used by the US National Security Agency (NSA) for internal communications went offline on Tuesday for an unspecified period of time, according to US media reports.

"While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues," an NSA spokesperson said in a statement to the BBC.

Multiple sources told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, that the agency was seeking to avoid having large numbers of employees log on to their computers simultaneously while the network was experiencing problems on Tuesday.
The outage reportedly affected the NSANet network, which is how officials send and receive top secret or classified information.
Chase Bank - the largest banking institution in the US - said a "software bug" in its hardware systems may have affected other banks and that it was not a cyber security incident.

Last week, a massive Microsoft outage impacted schools, healthcare systems, businesses, courts and governments around the world - including the US and Canada - while a network failure grounded all US flights.

extraction.body: The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter. The NSA closed its campus to most employees on Tuesday night, reverting to essential personnel only as it works to restore the network, according to a voicemail inbox used by NSA employees and a source familiar with the matter. The move to further restrict staffing levels came just hours after the NSA told employees they could return to work as normal. The agency had staggered employee arrivals earlier in the day as it worked to address the issue. The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said. “The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” A source familiar with the matter told CNN that restoration of the network was ongoing but not yet complete. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said later Tuesday afternoon that the NSA outage was the result of the agency applying a software patch to address major software vulnerabilities that were discovered last month. “The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected,” Clayton said on Fox Business. “That is that is what has happened at the NSA today.” The vulnerabilities Clayton were referring to are in PHP, a programming language that powers about 70% of the world’s websites. The NSA itself urged organizations to apply software patches. The flaws in PHP could allow hackers to break into websites and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords. Clayton said there is no sign that any of the recent tech outages, including that affecting the NSA, were the result of a cyberattack. A current and a former US official said an outage at NSANet would not impact the agency’s ability to communicate urgent intelligence to President Donald Trump while he is traveling in Asia on Air Force One. Both sources described multiple redundancies and backup networks that the government could use to communicate securely with the president who is currently in the Philippines before heading to China tomorrow for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. NSANet is “more of a network of networks, and it’s unlikely that a full outage exists given the many redundancies in place,” a former senior NSA official told CNN. So it is alarming, but likely not crippling.” A voicemail inbox recording for NSA employees on Tuesday morning described the situation as a “code yellow,” the second-highest in a system of three main levels that governs whether NSA employees report for work at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters or not. The recording told non-emergency personnel to arrive for work in a staggered manner and for emergency personnel to arrive as usual. The New York Times first reported that detail. Sometime Tuesday evening, the inbox reverted to “code green,” instructing employees to report to work as scheduled. It was not immediately clear whether the outage was resolved. But later Tuesday night, the inbox moved to a “code orange,” closing the campus for most employees until further notice, according to the inbox recording and source familiar with the matter. The outage at America’s most powerful intelligence agency comes on the heels of multiple major tech glitches affecting airlines and other corporations around the country. Meanwhile, a massive outage last week affecting Microsoft products left people around the world unable to access Outlook email and Team meetings. And in recent weeks banks and other services have experienced outages, on Monday thousands of Chase Bank customers reported they had trouble using their online accounts. There is no indication that the NSA, FAA or Microsoft outages were caused by a cyberattack. But they are stark examples of how tech failures can roil markets and potentially threaten national security. extraction.body: Democrats try to prevent quorum, say Thumann lied about not working on media issues. A Senate committee chaired by Ted Cruz (R-Texas) voted today to approve a Federal Communications Commission nominee, despite accusations that the nominee gave false testimony about her work as a legal advisor for FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. Democrats attempted to prevent a quorum by not showing up, but Cruz proceeded with a Republican-only vote. All 15 Republicans on the Senate Commerce Committee voted to approve Trump nominee Danielle Thumann, while the committee’s 13 Democrats were absent. “We’re going to be doing our job today, even if the Democrats refuse to show up to do theirs,” Cruz said at today’s hearing. Nominees are vetted in committees first, and then seek require majority approval from the Senate. Republicans are hoping to get Thumann confirmed before Democrats take Senate control in January. Although the Senate Commerce Committee generally requires one minority member to be present for nomination votes, a spokesperson for Cruz said Senate rules allow the nomination to be advanced for a vote in the entire chamber. A spokesperson for Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), the top Democrat on the committee, said in response that “since 2005, Commerce Committee rules required that a quorum include one member of the minority for official action on bill, resolution, or nomination.” Technically, the committee has operated with no rules during Cruz’s chairmanship because Cruz “failed to pass committee rules” for the current session of Congress, Cantwell’s spokesperson said. “Nevertheless, in practice it has operated in line with rules from the last Congress (and this provision, specifically, since 2005), including that a quorum with a member of the minority party must be present for official action on a nomination or legislation. Until today.” At a hearing last week, Thumann said she never worked with Carr on media-related topics, leading to accusations that she provided false testimony. “I have not worked with the chairman on any media-related issues,” Thumann said after Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) asked, “Do you support Chairman Carr’s illegal campaign to remove Jimmy Kimmel from the nation’s airwaves?” “It appears that Ms. Thumann misled the Committee and offered false testimony, seriously calling into question her judgment and character and impeding the Committee’s work in determining whether she should be seated on the Commission,” Luján wrote in a letter to Cruz yesterday. “While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media-related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount.” The FCC website describes Thumann as senior counsel to Carr on matters before the Wireline Bureau, the Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau, and the Consumer and Governmental Affairs Bureau. Emails obtained in a public records request by the group Protect Democracy show she had some involvement in media-related matters. Thumann provided follow-up responses to senators’ questions this week. She said that her work sometimes includes “reviewing documents or filings in a matter outside of my designated portfolio. However, I did not have any conversations with Paramount, CBS, or Skydance related to the merger.” Thumann has been referred to as Thumann Severs in the nomination process, but she uses the name Thumann. Luján wrote that Thumann “played a role in processing informal complaints related to” alleged news distortion on CBS’s 60 Minutes , and that “she apparently orchestrated the Commission’s response to consumers regarding the Jimmy Kimmel controversy.” However, Thumann was only a recipient of the Kimmel-related emails we found in a search of the messages. The emails do show that Thumann approved language used in a response the FCC gave to complaints about the alleged news distortion in a 60 Minutes interview with Kamala Harris. The response informed people who submitted complaints that they should instead submit comments on an FCC docket that had been set up for the 60 Minutes proceeding. “Hi Kristi, I have confirmed with the Chairman and Erin that we would like for complainants to be encouraged to resubmit their news distortion complaints in the relevant ECFS [Electronic Comment Filing System] proceeding,” Thumann wrote. “Can you please work on some draft language to send to consumers that would advise them on this step (including how to use ECFS)?” Democrats announced yesterday that they would try to prevent a quorum for today’s vote. They objected to adding a third Republican to the committee while a Democratic seat remains empty. “All Democratic members of the Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee object to the majority stacking independent commissions with Republicans and rushing nominees through the Committee process in this lame duck session with no Democratic pairs,” Cantwell said in a statement. Cantwell and other Democrats on the committee sent a letter to Cruz urging him to cancel the vote, while quoting his own words from 2014. “As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the Democratic committee members said. Cruz said today that “Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January. But today is November 18.” Cruz said there is “ample precedent” for advancing nominations in a lame-duck session. Senate Commerce Committee rules state that a quorum for nomination votes requires a “majority of the members, which includes at least one minority member.” But a Cruz spokesperson pointed to certain clauses regarding committee quorums in Senate rules when contacted by Ars today. In the Standing Rules of the Senate , paragraph 7 of rule XXVI says that “no measure or matter or recommendation shall be reported from any committee unless a majority of the committee were physically present,” and does not have any requirement for minority members to be present. Elsewhere, the Senate rules say that when a committee reports a measure to the Senate floor, “no point of order shall lie with respect to that measure” as long as the committee took its action “in conformity with the requirements of paragraph 7 of rule XXVI.” While committees can have different quorum rules, a Cruz spokesperson said this functions as a “cleansing clause” so that “earlier procedural irregularities, such as a violation of a committee rule, cannot be used to invalidate the vote on the Senate floor.” FCC nominations have traditionally been paired with one Republican and one Democrat when there is an empty seat for each party. But Cruz said that’s not a requirement. “There’s nothing that requires the president to nominate in pairs… the law merely says that no more than three of the commissioners may be from the same party,” Cruz said during the Republican-only meeting. The Communications Act prohibits a single party from holding more FCC seats than is necessary to form a majority. It says, “The maximum number of commissioners who may be members of the same political party shall be a number equal to the least number of commissioners which constitutes a majority of the full membership of the Commission.” Republicans would have a 3-1 majority on the FCC if Thumann is confirmed by the Senate. The sole Democrat, Anna Gomez, would have to leave at the end of 2027 if Trump does not nominate her for another term. “There is no mandate for the outgoing majority to rush through a partisan FCC nomination in its final weeks… Ms. Thumann Severs’ nomination should be postponed until the next Congress and paired with Commissioner Gomez’s renomination and the nomination of an additional Democratic commissioner,” Democrats told Cruz in their letter this week. extraction.body: Senate commerce committee Chair Ted Cruz (R-TX) began a meeting Wednesday meant to confirm President Donald Trump’s nominee to the Federal Communications Commission with a lopsided dais. To his right sat all 14 Republican members of the panel, including Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD). Cruz said he’d learned the night before that Democrats intended to boycott the vote, though Democrats say they’d repeatedly raised their concerns about advancing a Republican FCC nominee without a Democratic one. “The administration has shown it’s willing to move Democrats,” Cruz said, pointing to Senate votes scheduled on bipartisan pairs of nominations to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and the Securities and Exchange Commission. And even though the Supreme Court confirmed his power to do so, Cruz said, Trump has not moved to fire any Democrats from the FCC, as he did at the Federal Trade Commission. “This is an ordinary nomination to fill a vacancy previously held by someone in the same party,” Cruz said. But in statements and comments to reporters outside the committee room, Democrats said that the process has been far from normal. Senate committees often vote on nominations to historically independent agencies in bipartisan pairs. Confirming Danielle Thumann Severs, senior counsel to FCC Chair Brendan Carr, to become a commissioner at the agency would put the FCC at four total members — three Republicans and one Democrat, Anna Gomez. Gomez’s term has technically expired, though she can remain on the commission through next year unless she’s replaced. But Democrats fear that by confirming a third Republican to the FCC, Trump might finally fire Gomez, because he’d no longer need her present for a quorum to vote on key actions. Democrats asked for Thumann’s confirmation vote to be withheld until her nomination could be paired with a Democratic nomination. But so far, the president has not offered any Democratic nominees for the commission. Democrats said they made their concerns clear to Cruz, and added, “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In addition to the procedural concerns, Democrats worry about Thumann’s work as an adviser to Carr, and whether she was truthful about the matters she worked on. In a letter asking Cruz to delay her confirmation vote, Sen. At the November 10th hearing where Thumann answered committee members’ questions, she testified that she had “not worked with the Chairman on any media-related issues,” Luján noted in the letter. But documents obtained via a Freedom of Information Act request show that Thumann was “looped in” on various media matters, and “helped draft Skydance’s commitments that facilitated the 2 FCC’s approval of the Skydance-Paramount merger,” Luján wrote. “She also played a role in processing informal complaints related to CBS 60 Minutes alleged news distortion and she apparently orchestrated the Commission’s response to consumers regarding the Jimmy Kimmel controversy.” The FCC did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the matter. Even Cruz admitted concerns with Carr’s handling of Kimmel’s comments in the aftermath of conservative activist Charlie Kirk’s killing. But at Wednesday’s meeting, he said he “emphatically agree[s]” that Thumann had resolved any lingering worries about that. He added that his JAWBONE Act, which the committee previously passed, could directly address First Amendment violations by government agencies of either party. extraction.body: Senate Democrats are urging Senator Ted Cruz to delay a committee vote on President Donald Trump's nominee to the Federal Communications Commission, citing the Texas Republican's own past opposition to confirming controversial nominees during a lame-duck session. All Democratic members of the Senate Commerce Committee, led by Ranking Member Maria Cantwell, asked Cruz to remove FCC nominee Danielle Thumann Severs from Wednesday's markup agenda and postpone consideration until the next Congress, when Democrats will control the Senate. They argued that any Republican FCC nominee should be considered alongside the renomination of Democratic Commissioner Anna Gomez and a Democratic nominee for another vacant commission seat. "We look forward to reporting her out tomorrow and suggest Senate Democrats weigh in with the White House on nominating Democrats to the unfilled spot," committee spokesperson Blair Taylor told Politico . Newsweek has reached out to Cruz's office and Thumann Severs for comment. The confirmation battle could help determine the partisan balance of the FCC, the independent agency that regulates telecommunications, broadcasting and broadband policy. If confirmed, Thumann Severs would join FCC Chairman Brendan Carr and Commissioner Olivia Trusty, giving Republicans a 3-1 advantage over the commission's lone Democrat, Anna Gomez. Critics have argued the move would allow Republicans to further advance Carr's agenda before Democrats take control of the Senate in January. The fight also comes as Democrats and outside advocacy groups raise questions about Thumann Severs' role in matters involving media regulation and broadcast licensing. In a letter dated November 16, Commerce Committee Democrats argued there was "no mandate for the outgoing majority to rush through a partisan FCC nomination in its final weeks" following elections that returned control of Congress to Democrats. They asked Cruz to remove the nomination from Wednesday's executive session and revisit it next year. The lawmakers pointedly quoted language Cruz used in 2014 regarding controversial nominees advanced after an election. "As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees 'should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters,'" the Democrats wrote. "We agree." Their letter argues that , because Democrats will control the Senate and the Commerce Committee next year, any FCC nomination should be handled through a bipar tisan process that also includes the renomination of Gomez and the selection of a replacement for former Democratic Commissioner Geoffrey Starks. Thumann Severs currently serves as senior counsel to FCC Chairman Carr. She previously worked as a legal adviser in his office before taking a government affairs role at telecommunications infrastructure company Crown Castle and later returning to the FCC. Her portfolio has included issues related to broadband deployment, public safety, telecommunications infrastructure, and consumer affairs. Carr has praised her as an experienced communications policy attorney and public servant. The nomination would fill a Republican seat left vacant on the five-member commission. The nomination fight has intensified following allegations from Senator Ben Ray Luján that internal FCC emails conflict with testimony Thumann Severs provided during her confirmation hearing earlier this month. According to Bloomberg , Luján said emails obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests indicate that Thumann Severs was involved in matters related to the Paramount-Skydance merger review, despite her testimony that she had not worked with Carr on media-related issues. The senator has argued the records raise questions about whether her hearing testimony was complete and whether FCC staff played a role in shaping commitments submitted as part of the merger review process. “The letter mischaracterizes the situation and facts entirely. As Danielle’s QFR responses and FOIA at hand make clear, Danielle was not in the ex-parte and never engaged once with the outside parties. Her testimony and QFR responses were truthful, including and specifically referencing working on cross cutting matters like unlawful discrimination," an FCC spokesperson told Newsweek . The Senate Commerce Committee is expected to consider Thumann Severs' nomination Wednesday. While Democrats are pressing for a delay, Republicans currently retain control of the committee and appear poised to move the nomination forward. If approved by the committee, the nomination would advance to the Senate floor before Democrats formally take control of the chamber in January. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gray R. Thomas

extraction.body: Democrats try to prevent quorum, say Thumann lied about not working on media issues. A Senate committee chaired by Ted Cruz (R-Texas) voted today to approve a Federal Communications Commission nominee, despite accusations that the nominee gave false testimony about her work as a legal advisor for FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. Democrats attempted to prevent a quorum by not showing up, but Cruz proceeded with a Republican-only vote. All 15 Republicans on the Senate Commerce Committee voted to approve Trump nominee Danielle Thumann, while the committee’s 13 Democrats were absent. “We’re going to be doing our job today, even if the Democrats refuse to show up to do theirs,” Cruz said at today’s hearing. Nominees are vetted in committees first, and then seek require majority approval from the Senate. Republicans are hoping to get Thumann confirmed before Democrats take Senate control in January. Although the Senate Commerce Committee generally requires one minority member to be present for nomination votes, a spokesperson for Cruz said Senate rules allow the nomination to be advanced for a vote in the entire chamber. A spokesperson for Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), the top Democrat on the committee, said in response that “since 2005, Commerce Committee rules required that a quorum include one member of the minority for official action on bill, resolution, or nomination.” Technically, the committee has operated with no rules during Cruz’s chairmanship because Cruz “failed to pass committee rules” for the current session of Congress, Cantwell’s spokesperson said. “Nevertheless, in practice it has operated in line with rules from the last Congress (and this provision, specifically, since 2005), including that a quorum with a member of the minority party must be present for official action on a nomination or legislation. Until today.” At a hearing last week, Thumann said she never worked with Carr on media-related topics, leading to accusations that she provided false testimony. “I have not worked with the chairman on any media-related issues,” Thumann said after Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) asked, “Do you support Chairman Carr’s illegal campaign to remove Jimmy Kimmel from the nation’s airwaves?” “It appears that Ms. Thumann misled the Committee and offered false testimony, seriously calling into question her judgment and character and impeding the Committee’s work in determining whether she should be seated on the Commission,” Luján wrote in a letter to Cruz yesterday. “While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media-related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount.” The FCC website describes Thumann as senior counsel to Carr on matters before the Wireline Bureau, the Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau, and the Consumer and Governmental Affairs Bureau. Emails obtained in a public records request by the group Protect Democracy show she had some involvement in media-related matters. Thumann provided follow-up responses to senators’ questions this week. She said that her work sometimes includes “reviewing documents or filings in a matter outside of my designated portfolio. However, I did not have any conversations with Paramount, CBS, or Skydance related to the merger.” Thumann has been referred to as Thumann Severs in the nomination process, but she uses the name Thumann. Luján wrote that Thumann “played a role in processing informal complaints related to” alleged news distortion on CBS’s 60 Minutes , and that “she apparently orchestrated the Commission’s response to consumers regarding the Jimmy Kimmel controversy.” However, Thumann was only a recipient of the Kimmel-related emails we found in a search of the messages. The emails do show that Thumann approved language used in a response the FCC gave to complaints about the alleged news distortion in a 60 Minutes interview with Kamala Harris. The response informed people who submitted complaints that they should instead submit comments on an FCC docket that had been set up for the 60 Minutes proceeding. “Hi Kristi, I have confirmed with the Chairman and Erin that we would like for complainants to be encouraged to resubmit their news distortion complaints in the relevant ECFS [Electronic Comment Filing System] proceeding,” Thumann wrote. “Can you please work on some draft language to send to consumers that would advise them on this step (including how to use ECFS)?” Democrats announced yesterday that they would try to prevent a quorum for today’s vote. They objected to adding a third Republican to the committee while a Democratic seat remains empty. “All Democratic members of the Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee object to the majority stacking independent commissions with Republicans and rushing nominees through the Committee process in this lame duck session with no Democratic pairs,” Cantwell said in a statement. Cantwell and other Democrats on the committee sent a letter to Cruz urging him to cancel the vote, while quoting his own words from 2014. “As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the Democratic committee members said. Cruz said today that “Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January. But today is November 18.” Cruz said there is “ample precedent” for advancing nominations in a lame-duck session. Senate Commerce Committee rules state that a quorum for nomination votes requires a “majority of the members, which includes at least one minority member.” But a Cruz spokesperson pointed to certain clauses regarding committee quorums in Senate rules when contacted by Ars today. In the Standing Rules of the Senate , paragraph 7 of rule XXVI says that “no measure or matter or recommendation shall be reported from any committee unless a majority of the committee were physically present,” and does not have any requirement for minority members to be present. Elsewhere, the Senate rules say that when a committee reports a measure to the Senate floor, “no point of order shall lie with respect to that measure” as long as the committee took its action “in conformity with the requirements of paragraph 7 of rule XXVI.” While committees can have different quorum rules, a Cruz spokesperson said this functions as a “cleansing clause” so that “earlier procedural irregularities, such as a violation of a committee rule, cannot be used to invalidate the vote on the Senate floor.” FCC nominations have traditionally been paired with one Republican and one Democrat when there is an empty seat for each party. But Cruz said that’s not a requirement. “There’s nothing that requires the president to nominate in pairs… the law merely says that no more than three of the commissioners may be from the same party,” Cruz said during the Republican-only meeting. The Communications Act prohibits a single party from holding more FCC seats than is necessary to form a majority. It says, “The maximum number of commissioners who may be members of the same political party shall be a number equal to the least number of commissioners which constitutes a majority of the full membership of the Commission.” Republicans would have a 3-1 majority on the FCC if Thumann is confirmed by the Senate. The sole Democrat, Anna Gomez, would have to leave at the end of 2027 if Trump does not nominate her for another term. “There is no mandate for the outgoing majority to rush through a partisan FCC nomination in its final weeks… Ms. Thumann Severs’ nomination should be postponed until the next Congress and paired with Commissioner Gomez’s renomination and the nomination of an additional Democratic commissioner,” Democrats told Cruz in their letter this week. Cantwell and other Democrats on the committee sent a letter to Cruz urging him to cancel the vote, while quoting his own words from 2014. “As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the Democratic committee members said.
Cruz said today that “Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January. But today is November 18.” Cruz said there is “ample precedent” for advancing nominations in a lame-duck session.

Senate Commerce Committee rules state that a quorum for nomination votes requires a “majority of the members, which includes at least one minority member.” But a Cruz spokesperson pointed to certain clauses regarding committee quorums in Senate rules when contacted by Ars today.

In the Standing Rules of the Senate , paragraph 7 of rule XXVI says that “no measure or matter or recommendation shall be reported from any committee unless a majority of the committee were physically present,” and does not have any requirement for minority members to be present. Elsewhere, the Senate rules say that when a committee reports a measure to the Senate floor, “no point of order shall lie with respect to that measure” as long as the committee took its action “in conformity with the requirements of paragraph 7 of rule XXVI.”

While committees can have different quorum rules, a Cruz spokesperson said this functions as a “cleansing clause” so that “earlier procedural irregularities, such as a violation of a committee rule, cannot be used to invalidate the vote on the Senate floor.”
FCC nominations have traditionally been paired with one Republican and one Democrat when there is an empty seat for each party. But Cruz said that’s not a requirement.

“There’s nothing that requires the president to nominate in pairs… the law merely says that no more than three of the commissioners may be from the same party,” Cruz said during the Republican-only meeting.

The Communications Act prohibits a single party from holding more FCC seats than is necessary to form a majority. It says, “The maximum number of commissioners who may be members of the same political party shall be a number equal to the least number of commissioners which constitutes a majority of the full membership of the Commission.”

Republicans would have a 3-1 majority on the FCC if Thumann is confirmed by the Senate. The sole Democrat, Anna Gomez, would have to leave at the end of 2027 if Trump does not nominate her for another term.

“There is no mandate for the outgoing majority to rush through a partisan FCC nomination in its final weeks… Ms. Thumann Severs’ nomination should be postponed until the next Congress and paired with Commissioner Gomez’s renomination and the nomination of an additional Democratic commissioner,” Democrats told Cruz in their letter this week.

To his right sat all 14 Republican members of the panel, including Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD). Cruz said he’d learned the night before that Democrats intended to boycott the vote, though Democrats say they’d repeatedly raised their concerns about advancing a Republican FCC nominee without a Democratic one. “The administration has shown it’s willing to move Democrats,” Cruz said, pointing to Senate votes scheduled on bipartisan pairs of nominations to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and the Securities and Exchange Commission. And even though the Supreme Court confirmed his power to do so, Cruz said, Trump has not moved to fire any Democrats from the FCC, as he did at the Federal Trade Commission. “This is an ordinary nomination to fill a vacancy previously held by someone in the same party,” Cruz said. Gomez’s term has technically expired, though she can remain on the commission through next year unless she’s replaced. But Democrats fear that by confirming a third Republican to the FCC, Trump might finally fire Gomez, because he’d no longer need her present for a quorum to vote on key actions. Democrats asked for Thumann’s confirmation vote to be withheld until her nomination could be paired with a Democratic nomination. At the November 10th hearing where Thumann answered committee members’ questions, she testified that she had “not worked with the Chairman on any media-related issues,” Luján noted in the letter. “The letter mischaracterizes the situation and facts entirely.
As Danielle’s QFR responses and FOIA at hand make clear, Danielle was not in the ex-parte and never engaged once with the outside parties.
Her testimony and QFR responses were truthful, including and specifically referencing working on cross cutting matters like unlawful discrimination," an FCC spokesperson told Newsweek .

extraction.body: Senate Democrats are urging Senator Ted Cruz to delay a committee vote on President Donald Trump's nominee to the Federal Communications Commission, citing the Texas Republican's own past opposition to confirming controversial nominees during a lame-duck session. All Democratic members of the Senate Commerce Committee, led by Ranking Member Maria Cantwell, asked Cruz to remove FCC nominee Danielle Thumann Severs from Wednesday's markup agenda and postpone consideration until the next Congress, when Democrats will control the Senate. They argued that any Republican FCC nominee should be considered alongside the renomination of Democratic Commissioner Anna Gomez and a Democratic nominee for another vacant commission seat. "We look forward to reporting her out tomorrow and suggest Senate Democrats weigh in with the White House on nominating Democrats to the unfilled spot," committee spokesperson Blair Taylor told Politico . Newsweek has reached out to Cruz's office and Thumann Severs for comment. The confirmation battle could help determine the partisan balance of the FCC, the independent agency that regulates telecommunications, broadcasting and broadband policy. If confirmed, Thumann Severs would join FCC Chairman Brendan Carr and Commissioner Olivia Trusty, giving Republicans a 3-1 advantage over the commission's lone Democrat, Anna Gomez. Critics have argued the move would allow Republicans to further advance Carr's agenda before Democrats take control of the Senate in January. The fight also comes as Democrats and outside advocacy groups raise questions about Thumann Severs' role in matters involving media regulation and broadcast licensing. In a letter dated November 16, Commerce Committee Democrats argued there was "no mandate for the outgoing majority to rush through a partisan FCC nomination in its final weeks" following elections that returned control of Congress to Democrats. They asked Cruz to remove the nomination from Wednesday's executive session and revisit it next year. The lawmakers pointedly quoted language Cruz used in 2014 regarding controversial nominees advanced after an election. "As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees 'should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters,'" the Democrats wrote. "We agree." Their letter argues that , because Democrats will control the Senate and the Commerce Committee next year, any FCC nomination should be handled through a bipar tisan process that also includes the renomination of Gomez and the selection of a replacement for former Democratic Commissioner Geoffrey Starks. Thumann Severs currently serves as senior counsel to FCC Chairman Carr. She previously worked as a legal adviser in his office before taking a government affairs role at telecommunications infrastructure company Crown Castle and later returning to the FCC. Her portfolio has included issues related to broadband deployment, public safety, telecommunications infrastructure, and consumer affairs. Carr has praised her as an experienced communications policy attorney and public servant. The nomination would fill a Republican seat left vacant on the five-member commission. The nomination fight has intensified following allegations from Senator Ben Ray Luján that internal FCC emails conflict with testimony Thumann Severs provided during her confirmation hearing earlier this month. According to Bloomberg , Luján said emails obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests indicate that Thumann Severs was involved in matters related to the Paramount-Skydance merger review, despite her testimony that she had not worked with Carr on media-related issues. The senator has argued the records raise questions about whether her hearing testimony was complete and whether FCC staff played a role in shaping commitments submitted as part of the merger review process. “The letter mischaracterizes the situation and facts entirely. As Danielle’s QFR responses and FOIA at hand make clear, Danielle was not in the ex-parte and never engaged once with the outside parties. Her testimony and QFR responses were truthful, including and specifically referencing working on cross cutting matters like unlawful discrimination," an FCC spokesperson told Newsweek . The Senate Commerce Committee is expected to consider Thumann Severs' nomination Wednesday. While Democrats are pressing for a delay, Republicans currently retain control of the committee and appear poised to move the nomination forward. If approved by the committee, the nomination would advance to the Senate floor before Democrats formally take control of the chamber in January. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gray R. Thomas

Although she was one of four nominees that appeared during the nearly two-hour hearing, about three-quarters of the questions were directed to her. Committee Democrats are concerned that a recent Supreme Court decision regarding authority over executive departments could lead President Donald Trump to fire Gomez. They lobbied for Gomez to appear in the same hearing but were denied. Their concerns were echoed by the Committee to Protect Journalists on Wednesday, which called for bipartisan FCC nominees. “Americans trust the Federal Communications Commission to act as an independent, bipartisan agency that upholds the First Amendment,” said José Zamora, CPJ’s regional director for the Americas. “The Senate must ensure the FCC upholds that trust by not allowing a partisan nomination to move forward.” At the hearing on Tuesday, Thumann Severs hesitated to directly address questions from committee Democrats over accusations that Carr has overstepped his authority towards broadcasters’ First Amendment rights. CEO Satya Nadella may be on stage trying to wow investors and customers at his company’s annual Ignite conference , but somewhere in the bowels of a building in Redmond his open source team is likely panicking at what appears to be unauthorized access to an administrator account on Microsoft’s Github organization. The problem package is Microsoft’s agent-framework, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, researchers reported late yesterday and this morning . According to OX Security, version 1.26.1 was reverted to a safe version, but the attacker later uploaded 1.26.2 through Microsoft’s official PyPI publisher account, suggesting that, at least at the time of their report, the credentials hadn’t been locked down. Safe to say, but if you find either version in your environment assume you have some account security work to do. sources.title: Two poisoned releases of Microsoft's agent-framework Python package carried a stealer aimed at Azure and CI credentials - MLQ.ai
passages: Two releases of agent-framework, the official Python package for Microsoft 's Agent Framework for building AI agents, were published to the Python Package Index (PyPI) on Tuesday, Nov.
17, with a credential stealer inside, according to research from Wiz and OX Security [1] [2] .
The package gets about 190,000 downloads a month [2] [3] .

The code collected secrets from environment variables and other running processes, credential files for cloud command-line tools, package registries and source control, and Azure managed identity and Azure DevOps pipeline tokens, then sent them to an outside web service [1] [2] .
Version 1.26.2 extended the theft to GitHub Actions workflows [1] [3] .
Microsoft has not said publicly how an attacker was able to publish to the package.
OX Security, Wiz, Endor Labs and SafeDep each analysed the code [3] .

The malicious releases contained only built packages with no matching source release, and Wiz found no matching releases or malicious code in Microsoft's source repository, which suggests the uploads came from outside the normal release process [1] [3] .
Wiz says the root cause is not confirmed [1] .

Any Python process started in an affected environment ran the payload, so the researchers say every secret on those hosts and build runners should be rotated, including cloud sessions, pipeline tokens, package-registry tokens and git credentials [1] [2] .
They also recommend reviewing Azure sign-in and activity logs for managed identities and federated credentials; Wiz notes stolen tokens may stay valid for up to 24 hours [1] .
This article was produced by MLQ.ai's AI newsroom and checked against primary sources such as company filings, official releases and court documents.

extraction.body: Two releases of agent-framework, the official Python package for Microsoft 's Agent Framework for building AI agents, were published to the Python Package Index (PyPI) on Tuesday, Nov. 17, with a credential stealer inside, according to research from Wiz and OX Security [1] [2] . The package gets about 190,000 downloads a month [2] [3] . Wiz says version 1.26.1 was uploaded at 20:35 UTC and version 1.26.2, a repackaged copy, at about 21:08 UTC; both were unavailable when it checked at 21:30 UTC, so they were live for roughly 55 and 22 minutes [1] . PyPI has quarantined both, and 1.26.0, published on Nov. 12, is the most recent safe version [1] [3] . According to the researchers, the malicious versions ran their code whenever a Python interpreter started in the affected environment, even if an application never imported the package, while still installing the genuine framework so applications kept working [1] [2] [3] . The code collected secrets from environment variables and other running processes, credential files for cloud command-line tools, package registries and source control, and Azure managed identity and Azure DevOps pipeline tokens, then sent them to an outside web service [1] [2] . Version 1.26.2 extended the theft to GitHub Actions workflows [1] [3] . OX Security, Wiz, Endor Labs and SafeDep each analysed the code [3] . The malicious releases contained only built packages with no matching source release, and Wiz found no matching releases or malicious code in Microsoft's source repository, which suggests the uploads came from outside the normal release process [1] [3] . SafeDep identified a PyPI maintainer account created on the day of the attack with publishing rights to the package; its role is unconfirmed [3] . Wiz says the root cause is not confirmed [1] . A maintainer of Agent Framework confirmed in a GitHub discussion that the compromised releases had been removed from PyPI and that an investigation is under way, SecurityWeek reported [3] . Microsoft has not said publicly how an attacker was able to publish to the package. Wiz and OX Security advise teams to search lockfiles, CI logs, virtual environments and container images for 1.26.1 or 1.26.2, remove them and pin to 1.26.0 with hash checking [1] [2] . Any Python process started in an affected environment ran the payload, so the researchers say every secret on those hosts and build runners should be rotated, including cloud sessions, pipeline tokens, package-registry tokens and git credentials [1] [2] . They also recommend reviewing Azure sign-in and activity logs for managed identities and federated credentials; Wiz notes stolen tokens may stay valid for up to 24 hours [1] . For GitHub Actions workflows that installed 1.26.2 with OIDC write permissions, Wiz says to treat those tokens as exposed [1] . The incident lands in a busy week for software supply-chain security: on the same day, OpenJDK and Oracle shipped fixes for the Java4Shell flaw ( our report ). sources.title: Attackers hijack Microsoft’s agent-framework package to steal Azure and CI credentials
passages: Attackers briefly hijacked Microsoft's official Agent Framework package on PyPI and used it to distribute credential-stealing malware capable of harvesting cloud tokens, developer secrets and CI/CD credentials from developer workstations and automated build systems, according to multiple security researchers.

“The package is a credential stealer: it harvests environment secrets, cloud and package-manager credentials, and Azure managed identity tokens, then exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled webhook,” OX Security, one of several security firms that flagged the releases, said in a blog post.
Ox recommended pinning the agent-framework to a verified Microsoft release with hash checking and blocking outbound traffic to webhook.site from build infrastructure.
Microsoft has not said publicly how the attacker got access to publish the package.
OX also advised teams to review Azure sign-in and activity logs for use of managed identities and federated credentials from affected build agents.
In May, Endor Labs detected three trojanized versions of durabletask, Microsoft’s Python SDK for Azure Durable Functions.

extraction.body: Attackers briefly hijacked Microsoft's official Agent Framework package on PyPI and used it to distribute credential-stealing malware capable of harvesting cloud tokens, developer secrets and CI/CD credentials from developer workstations and automated build systems, according to multiple security researchers. Two malicious versions of the package, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, appeared on PyPI on November 17 and stayed live for less than an hour. “The package is a credential stealer: it harvests environment secrets, cloud and package-manager credentials, and Azure managed identity tokens, then exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled webhook,” OX Security, one of several security firms that flagged the releases, said in a blog post. The payload ran automatically every time Python started, even if no code imported the package, OX said. The malicious versions also installed the genuine framework code, so applications kept working, and the compromise was easy to miss. The package has 192,534 monthly downloads, according to the firm. Other security firms, including Aikido Security, Endor Labs, and SafeDep, published similar analyses of the attack. Microsoft has not said publicly how the attacker got access to publish the package. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment. How the stealer worked The stealer collected environment variables with names containing words such as TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, and OPENAI, OX said. These included Azure CLI settings, Git and Docker credentials, npm and pip configuration, Hugging Face tokens, Azure DevOps build agent credentials and application .env files. Inside Azure DevOps pipelines, it requested an identity token that can be exchanged for Azure access, OX said in the blog post. It also requested managed identity tokens for Azure services, including Resource Manager, Microsoft Graph, Key Vault, Storage, Cognitive Services, AI Foundry, and Azure DevOps. Endor Labs said the attack was aimed mainly at automated build systems. “Developer laptops are in scope, but the payload is written for CI runners and Azure workloads,” the firm wrote in its analysis. It sat in a module named _telemetry.py and sent data with a user agent labeled “af-runtime-diagnostics,” OX said. The attacker then uploaded 1.26.2, which used a different file path for the same payload, the firm said. The first version went up at 20:35 UTC and the second at 21:08 UTC, according to Aikido Security. “This attack isn’t just a one-off exfiltration attempt, but a planned, live and coordinated effort to reach as many victims as they can, while still being able to bypass blocks and restrictions,” OX said. OX said the attackers appear to have found a way to hijack the process that builds the package’s wheel files. Endor Labs, in its analysis, said both malicious versions were uploaded as wheel files only, without the source code package that came with the clean release. Microsoft has not confirmed how the breach happened. Any unpinned install during that time pulled in a malicious version, Endor Labs said. AI pipelines in focus OX said the attack shows how attackers are targeting the AI developer ecosystem and the CI pipelines behind it. The stealer’s target list includes OpenAI and Hugging Face tokens and Azure AI Foundry access. It is also not the first time this year that attackers have compromised an official Microsoft Python package. In May, Endor Labs detected three trojanized versions of durabletask, Microsoft’s Python SDK for Azure Durable Functions. What security teams should do Removing the package does not undo the damage. “Removing the package stops future runs, but it doesn’t undo anything that was already sent,” Aikido said. Teams should look for agent_framework_meta.pth and agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py on hosts and build agents, the firm said. Version 1.26.2 used different files, af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py, according to Aikido. If the package ran anywhere, every secret reachable from that host should be treated as compromised, OX said. The firm recommended rotating Azure service principal secrets, personal access tokens, and GitHub, npm, PyPI, NuGet, Docker, Hugging Face, and OpenAI tokens. OX also advised teams to review Azure sign-in and activity logs for use of managed identities and federated credentials from affected build agents. Ox recommended pinning the agent-framework to a verified Microsoft release with hash checking and blocking outbound traffic to webhook.site from build infrastructure.

coreStoryFacts.text: To make matters worse, the package never needs to be imported to do its dirty work – all it takes is a Python interpreter with the package installed to start up – the infected package still pulls the genuine 1.26.0 version of Microsoft’s agent-framework in order to keep itself running and looking legitimate, while in the background it gathers up credentials, encrypts them as a base64-encoded chunk of JSON, and sends them off to a webhook.site address hard coded into the malware.
Microsoft agent-framework for Python boasts nearly 200,000 downloads a month and is used to build and deploy AI agents.

As of those latest releases, it’s also being used to exfiltrate environment variables, credential files, and other secrets for Azure, Git, Docker, Hugging Face, and other sensitive developer services.
The agent-framework GitHub repo is offline as of writing.
It’s been pointed out online that Microsoft’s repo for ONNX Runtime , an AI accelerator, is also offline.
Other Microsoft repos remain available, and neither Microsoft nor security researchers have linked the ONNX repo’s pull to the malware campaign.
“We have made some repositories private while we investigate malicious content,” a Microsoft spokesperson told The Register.
“Our priority is to protect customers and the broader ecosystem.
We are working to review and will take further action as needed.”®

Versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 of agent-framework on PyPI steal Azure, Azure DevOps, and GitHub Actions credentials when Python starts.

Allie Mellen joined Microsoft as Principal Director, Security Research and Threat Intelligence.
Two releases of agent-framework, the official Python package for Microsoft 's Agent Framework for building AI agents, were published to the Python Package Index (PyPI) on Tuesday, Nov.
17, with a credential stealer inside, according to research from Wiz and OX Security [1] [2] .
The package gets about 190,000 downloads a month [2] [3] .

The code collected secrets from environment variables and other running processes, credential files for cloud command-line tools, package registries and source control, and Azure managed identity and Azure DevOps pipeline tokens, then sent them to an outside web service [1] [2] .
Version 1.26.2 extended the theft to GitHub Actions workflows [1] [3] .
Microsoft has not said publicly how an attacker was able to publish to the package.
OX Security, Wiz, Endor Labs and SafeDep each analysed the code [3] .

The malicious releases contained only built packages with no matching source release, and Wiz found no matching releases or malicious code in Microsoft's source repository, which suggests the uploads came from outside the normal release process [1] [3] .
Wiz says the root cause is not confirmed [1] .

Any Python process started in an affected environment ran the payload, so the researchers say every secret on those hosts and build runners should be rotated, including cloud sessions, pipeline tokens, package-registry tokens and git credentials [1] [2] .

Attackers briefly hijacked Microsoft's official Agent Framework package on PyPI and used it to distribute credential-stealing malware capable of harvesting cloud tokens, developer secrets and CI/CD credentials from developer workstations and automated build systems, according to multiple security researchers.

“The package is a credential stealer: it harvests environment secrets, cloud and package-manager credentials, and Azure managed identity tokens, then exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled webhook,” OX Security, one of several security firms that flagged the releases, said in a blog post.
Ox recommended pinning the agent-framework to a verified Microsoft release with hash checking and blocking outbound traffic to webhook.site from build infrastructure.
Microsoft has not said publicly how the attacker got access to publish the package.
OX also advised teams to review Azure sign-in and activity logs for use of managed identities and federated credentials from affected build agents.
In May, Endor Labs detected three trojanized versions of durabletask, Microsoft’s Python SDK for Azure Durable Functions.
These included Azure CLI settings, Git and Docker credentials, npm and pip configuration, Hugging Face tokens, Azure DevOps build agent credentials and application .env files.
OX said the attackers appear to have found a way to hijack the process that builds the package’s wheel files.
It is also not the first time this year that attackers have compromised an official Microsoft Python package.
Teams should look for agent_framework_meta.pth and agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py on hosts and build agents, the firm said.

“Developer laptops are in scope, but the payload is written for CI runners and Azure workloads,” the firm wrote in its analysis.
The firm recommended rotating Azure service principal secrets, personal access tokens, and GitHub, npm, PyPI, NuGet, Docker, Hugging Face, and OpenAI tokens.

The problem package is Microsoft’s agent-framework, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, researchers reported late yesterday and this morning . According to OX Security, version 1.26.1 was reverted to a safe version, but the attacker later uploaded 1.26.2 through Microsoft’s official PyPI publisher account, suggesting that, at least at the time of their report, the credentials hadn’t been locked down. SafeDep identified a PyPI maintainer account created on the day of the attack with publishing rights to the package; its role is unconfirmed [3] . Wiz says the root cause is not confirmed [1] . A maintainer of Agent Framework confirmed in a GitHub discussion that the compromised releases had been removed from PyPI and that an investigation is under way, SecurityWeek reported [3] . For GitHub Actions workflows that installed 1.26.2 with OIDC write permissions, Wiz says to treat those tokens as exposed [1] . extraction.body: Attackers briefly hijacked Microsoft's official Agent Framework package on PyPI and used it to distribute credential-stealing malware capable of harvesting cloud tokens, developer secrets and CI/CD credentials from developer workstations and automated build systems, according to multiple security researchers. Two malicious versions of the package, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, appeared on PyPI on November 17 and stayed live for less than an hour. “The package is a credential stealer: it harvests environment secrets, cloud and package-manager credentials, and Azure managed identity tokens, then exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled webhook,” OX Security, one of several security firms that flagged the releases, said in a blog post. The payload ran automatically every time Python started, even if no code imported the package, OX said. The malicious versions also installed the genuine framework code, so applications kept working, and the compromise was easy to miss. The package has 192,534 monthly downloads, according to the firm. Other security firms, including Aikido Security, Endor Labs, and SafeDep, published similar analyses of the attack. Microsoft has not said publicly how the attacker got access to publish the package. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment. How the stealer worked The stealer collected environment variables with names containing words such as TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, and OPENAI, OX said. These included Azure CLI settings, Git and Docker credentials, npm and pip configuration, Hugging Face tokens, Azure DevOps build agent credentials and application .env files. Inside Azure DevOps pipelines, it requested an identity token that can be exchanged for Azure access, OX said in the blog post. It also requested managed identity tokens for Azure services, including Resource Manager, Microsoft Graph, Key Vault, Storage, Cognitive Services, AI Foundry, and Azure DevOps. Endor Labs said the attack was aimed mainly at automated build systems. “Developer laptops are in scope, but the payload is written for CI runners and Azure workloads,” the firm wrote in its analysis. It sat in a module named _telemetry.py and sent data with a user agent labeled “af-runtime-diagnostics,” OX said. The attacker then uploaded 1.26.2, which used a different file path for the same payload, the firm said. The first version went up at 20:35 UTC and the second at 21:08 UTC, according to Aikido Security. “This attack isn’t just a one-off exfiltration attempt, but a planned, live and coordinated effort to reach as many victims as they can, while still being able to bypass blocks and restrictions,” OX said. OX said the attackers appear to have found a way to hijack the process that builds the package’s wheel files. Endor Labs, in its analysis, said both malicious versions were uploaded as wheel files only, without the source code package that came with the clean release. Microsoft has not confirmed how the breach happened. Any unpinned install during that time pulled in a malicious version, Endor Labs said. AI pipelines in focus OX said the attack shows how attackers are targeting the AI developer ecosystem and the CI pipelines behind it. The stealer’s target list includes OpenAI and Hugging Face tokens and Azure AI Foundry access. It is also not the first time this year that attackers have compromised an official Microsoft Python package. In May, Endor Labs detected three trojanized versions of durabletask, Microsoft’s Python SDK for Azure Durable Functions. What security teams should do Removing the package does not undo the damage. “Removing the package stops future runs, but it doesn’t undo anything that was already sent,” Aikido said. Teams should look for agent_framework_meta.pth and agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py on hosts and build agents, the firm said. Version 1.26.2 used different files, af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py, according to Aikido. If the package ran anywhere, every secret reachable from that host should be treated as compromised, OX said. The firm recommended rotating Azure service principal secrets, personal access tokens, and GitHub, npm, PyPI, NuGet, Docker, Hugging Face, and OpenAI tokens. OX also advised teams to review Azure sign-in and activity logs for use of managed identities and federated credentials from affected build agents. Ox recommended pinning the agent-framework to a verified Microsoft release with hash checking and blocking outbound traffic to webhook.site from build infrastructure.

The figure is way above the analysts' estimates of $125.3 billion, reflecting the company's confidence despite the latest controversy surrounding co-founder Jensen Huang. Last week, Huang decided to step down as CEO after admitting to an extramarital affair with a woman the U.S. intelligence officials believe to be a Chinese spy. The company not only beat the earnings estimate in Q3, but it also expects to perform well in this quarter, anticipating continued demand for its AI chips. sources.title: Anthropic reportedly prices IPO at $83 a share, above projected range
passages: Anthropic has reportedly priced its long-awaited IPO at $83 per share, above its initial range of $70 to $78, signaling strong investor appetite for one of the companies at the center of the AI boom, despite market jitters following the departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, which shook confidence in the industry.

At the IPO price, Anthropic is reportedly valued at $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis, a significant increase from the $965 billion the company reached in May when it raised $65 billion in its last private market round , but below the $2 trillion it was reportedly aiming for several months ago.
Investors that own approximately 1% of the company reportedly include Sequoia and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt.
Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC also holds about a 1% stake in the company, according to a person familiar with the matter.

A group of major tech companies, including AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC Partners, have also agreed to purchase $26 billion worth of non-voting shares through a private placement alongside the IPO.

Anthropic will begin its life as a public company on Thursday, trading on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT.” A strong first day of trading would signal that investors remain optimistic about AI adoption, despite recent volatility in AI-driven stocks.

At the IPO price, Anthropic is reportedly valued at $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis, a significant increase from the $965 billion the company reached in May when it raised $65 billion in its last private market round , but below the $2 trillion it was reportedly aiming for several months ago. Anthropic will begin its life as a public company on Thursday, trading on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT.” A strong first day of trading would signal that investors remain optimistic about AI adoption, despite recent volatility in AI-driven stocks. The company’s performance is expected to set expectations for private AI companies, including Anthropic’s main rival OpenAI, which was last reportedly valued at $1.25 billion but has yet to announce plans for an IPO. Although none of Anthropic’s venture capital investors holds more than a 5% stake in the company, the IPO is a massive windfall for its numerous backers . Investors that own approximately 1% of the company reportedly include Sequoia and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC also holds about a 1% stake in the company, according to a person familiar with the matter. Other backers set to make billions are Iconiq, Menlo Ventures, Coatue, and Sound Ventures, a firm launched by Guy Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, and Spark Ventures, the only VC firm known to hold a board seat at the company. Some of the company’s existing investors, namely Sequoia, Iconiq, Lightspeed, Accel, and Altimeter Capital Management, are so enthusiastic about Anthropic’s future that they were reportedly planning to buy billions of dollars’ worth of the company’s shares in the IPO. Yet the investors’ holdings in Anthropic pale in comparison to those of the Claude maker’s strategic partners , Amazon, which owns nearly 15% of the company, and Google, which holds almost 14%. A group of major tech companies, including AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC Partners, have also agreed to purchase $26 billion worth of non-voting shares through a private placement alongside the IPO. The company’s seven co-founders , including CEO Dario Amodei, each sold nearly 3.4 million shares in the IPO, according to the S-1 filing, bringing in about $282 million for each.
