passages: OAKLAND, Calif. – Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 per share on Wednesday, according to multiple reports, an amount above the expected price range that values the artificial intelligence giant at $1.5 trillion.

Anthropic decided to barrel ahead with the IPO despite jitters among some investors over market volatility, a potential regulatory crackdown by a Democratic-led Congress next year and growing anti-AI sentiment among the public.
Then there's the spectacular downfall of one of the industry's biggest cheerleaders, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , over extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Anthropic's IPO also means its employees can begin to sell their vested stock, a payout that will make many of them millionaires.

The IPO could also give Anthropic enormous resources to accelerate its expansion and potentially add billions of dollars to the fortunes of CEO Dario Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela Amodei.
FILE - Pages from the Anthropic website and the company's logos are displayed on a computer screen in New York on Thursday, Feb.
How that will play out for companies worth potentially trillions of dollars is uncharted territory.
“This is strong appetite for this major AI IPO in Anthropic, and it’s a big win for the tech sector after a white-knuckle time with Nvidia.
The pricing shows strong demand among investors,” said Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co.
Formed in 2021 by former OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company.
But both companies have plenty of other competitors, including Google, startups in the U.S. and China and SpaceX , which has an AI business.
The goal of most companies, above all, is to do well for their owners .
Usually that means making profits and growing the business.

Anthropic says it too will consider its stockholders, but it will balance their interests against another fundamental goal : “the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.”
“Exactly what the flow of that will be, it’s very hard to predict,” Lesser said in an interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday at the Semafor Silicon Valley & The World forum.
Adding to the pressure is the possibility that demand for AI shares could drop or even collapse.
Investors have become anxious about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently.
The trust will not run the day-to-day operations of Anthropic.
But its influence means the company could opt for strategies that may not make the most money for investors.
Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX’s AI division have all lost more money than they’ve made because of the huge costs associated with building AI.
That has fueled growing concerns about a bubble forming in the sector.
Amid those fears, the regulatory environment could also change for Anthropic once the new Congress is in session.
Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a backlash against data centers.
Investors will have less control in Anthropic's unusual structure
IPO offers a way to raise money without going deeper into debt

(AP Photo/Patrick Sison, File) OAKLAND, Calif. – Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 per share on Wednesday, according to multiple reports, an amount above the expected price range that values the artificial intelligence giant at $1.5 trillion. The higher-than-anticipated pricing signals broad investor enthusiasm for AI stocks even amid some uncertainty in the market stemming from the ouster of Nvidia's CEO and worries about an AI bubble. The San Francisco-based maker of the Claude AI tool is set to make its debut Thursday on Wall Street. The company had set a price range of $70 to $78 per share, offering 825 million shares that will begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT.” Anthropic decided to barrel ahead with the IPO despite jitters among some investors over market volatility, a potential regulatory crackdown by a Democratic-led Congress next year and growing anti-AI sentiment among the public. Then there's the spectacular downfall of one of the industry's biggest cheerleaders, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , over extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. “This is strong appetite for this major AI IPO in Anthropic, and it’s a big win for the tech sector after a white-knuckle time with Nvidia. The pricing shows strong demand among investors,” said Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co. The company’s rival, OpenAI , is not planning to go public until next year. IPO offers a way to raise money without going deeper into debt Anthropic already has taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is “substantial.” Adding to the strain, the company is unprofitable, at least under standard accounting rules, suggesting that its resources to pay interest and principal are limited. While the company has ample cash for now , it will likely run through it quickly if it cannot raise more soon, given its outsize spending plans. The company said it has already signed leases and other deals requiring it to spend $900 billion on computing power and infrastructure in the coming years, including $70 billion in the next 12 months. An IPO is essentially a way to raise money, instead of going into further debt. And borrowing has gotten more expensive. That’s partly due to inflation fears and partly due to the sector’s massive cash needs, which have drawn comparisons to the Gilded Age splurge on railroads. Lenders fear that AI companies have taken on too much debt to expand while having no clear path to profitability. Anthropic's IPO also means its employees can begin to sell their vested stock, a payout that will make many of them millionaires. The IPO could also give Anthropic enormous resources to accelerate its expansion and potentially add billions of dollars to the fortunes of CEO Dario Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela Amodei. AI industry faces concerns about data centers, a possible bubble and regulations Formed in 2021 by former OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company. But both companies have plenty of other competitors, including Google, startups in the U.S. and China and SpaceX , which has an AI business. Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX’s AI division have all lost more money than they’ve made because of the huge costs associated with building AI. That has fueled growing concerns about a bubble forming in the sector. Dario Amodei cautioned in September that the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned, AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the internet within months. Amid those fears, the regulatory environment could also change for Anthropic once the new Congress is in session. Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a backlash against data centers. And two big states offering incentives for data centers, Texas and Georgia, just elected Democratic governors vowing to stop new construction. Adding to the pressure is the possibility that demand for AI shares could drop or even collapse. Investors have become anxious about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently. Investors will have less control in Anthropic's unusual structure The goal of most companies, above all, is to do well for their owners . Usually that means making profits and growing the business. Anthropic says it too will consider its stockholders, but it will balance their interests against another fundamental goal : “the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.” Like its rival OpenAI , Anthropic is a public-benefit corporation, a legal designation used by companies that pledge to balance shareholder interests with the public good. How that will play out for companies worth potentially trillions of dollars is uncharted territory. Anthropic has set up a long-term benefit trust that will have the ability to elect or remove a majority of the company’s board of directors. The trust will not run the day-to-day operations of Anthropic. But its influence means the company could opt for strategies that may not make the most money for investors. Market valuation for AI companies is going to be “up and down for many years to come, but more up than down,” said Rich Lesser, the global chair and former CEO of Boston Consulting Group. “Exactly what the flow of that will be, it’s very hard to predict,” Lesser said in an interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday at the Semafor Silicon Valley & The World forum. “There’s no question what Anthropic and OpenAI and Google and a number of the other players in this industry have done is pretty remarkable.” If you need help with the Public File, call (313) 222-0566 At WDIV, we are committed to informing and delighting our audience. Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a backlash against data centers. Anthropic says it too will consider its stockholders, but it will balance their interests against another fundamental goal : “the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.”

Like its rival OpenAI , Anthropic is a public-benefit corporation, a legal designation used by companies that pledge to balance shareholder interests with the public good. How that will play out for companies worth potentially trillions of dollars is uncharted territory.

Anthropic has set up a long-term benefit trust that will have the ability to elect or remove a majority of the company’s board of directors. The trust will not run the day-to-day operations of Anthropic. But its influence means the company could opt for strategies that may not make the most money for investors.
Market valuation for AI companies is going to be “up and down for many years to come, but more up than down,” said Rich Lesser, the global chair and former CEO of Boston Consulting Group.

“Exactly what the flow of that will be, it’s very hard to predict,” Lesser said in an interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday at the Semafor Silicon Valley & The World forum. “There’s no question what Anthropic and OpenAI and Google and a number of the other players in this industry have done is pretty remarkable.”

coreStoryFacts.text: Anthropic has reportedly priced its long-awaited IPO at $83 per share, above its initial range of $70 to $78, signaling strong investor appetite for one of the companies at the center of the AI boom, despite market jitters following the departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, which shook confidence in the industry.

At the IPO price, Anthropic is reportedly valued at $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis, a significant increase from the $965 billion the company reached in May when it raised $65 billion in its last private market round , but below the $2 trillion it was reportedly aiming for several months ago.
Investors that own approximately 1% of the company reportedly include Sequoia and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt.
Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC also holds about a 1% stake in the company, according to a person familiar with the matter.

A group of major tech companies, including AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC Partners, have also agreed to purchase $26 billion worth of non-voting shares through a private placement alongside the IPO.

Anthropic will begin its life as a public company on Thursday, trading on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT.” A strong first day of trading would signal that investors remain optimistic about AI adoption, despite recent volatility in AI-driven stocks.

OAKLAND, Calif. – Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 per share on Wednesday, according to multiple reports, an amount above the expected price range that values the artificial intelligence giant at $1.5 trillion.

Anthropic decided to barrel ahead with the IPO despite jitters among some investors over market volatility, a potential regulatory crackdown by a Democratic-led Congress next year and growing anti-AI sentiment among the public.
Then there's the spectacular downfall of one of the industry's biggest cheerleaders, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , over extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Anthropic's IPO also means its employees can begin to sell their vested stock, a payout that will make many of them millionaires.

The IPO could also give Anthropic enormous resources to accelerate its expansion and potentially add billions of dollars to the fortunes of CEO Dario Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela Amodei.
FILE - Pages from the Anthropic website and the company's logos are displayed on a computer screen in New York on Thursday, Feb.
How that will play out for companies worth potentially trillions of dollars is uncharted territory.
“This is strong appetite for this major AI IPO in Anthropic, and it’s a big win for the tech sector after a white-knuckle time with Nvidia.
The pricing shows strong demand among investors,” said Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co.
Formed in 2021 by former OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company.
But both companies have plenty of other competitors, including Google, startups in the U.S. and China and SpaceX , which has an AI business.
The goal of most companies, above all, is to do well for their owners .
Usually that means making profits and growing the business.

Anthropic says it too will consider its stockholders, but it will balance their interests against another fundamental goal : “the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.”
“Exactly what the flow of that will be, it’s very hard to predict,” Lesser said in an interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday at the Semafor Silicon Valley & The World forum.
Adding to the pressure is the possibility that demand for AI shares could drop or even collapse.
Investors have become anxious about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently.
The trust will not run the day-to-day operations of Anthropic.

Anthropic decided to barrel ahead with the IPO despite jitters among some investors over market volatility, a potential regulatory crackdown by a Democratic-led Congress next year and growing anti-AI sentiment among the public.
Then there's the spectacular downfall of one of the industry's biggest cheerleaders, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , over extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Anthropic's IPO also means its employees can begin to sell their vested stock, a payout that will make many of them millionaires.

Formed in 2021 by former OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company.
But both companies have plenty of other competitors, including Google, startups in the U.S. and China and SpaceX , which has an AI business.
The goal of most companies, above all, is to do well for their owners .
Usually that means making profits and growing the business.

Anthropic says it too will consider its stockholders, but it will balance their interests against another fundamental goal : “the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.”
“Exactly what the flow of that will be, it’s very hard to predict,” Lesser said in an interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday at the Semafor Silicon Valley & The World forum.
Adding to the pressure is the possibility that demand for AI shares could drop or even collapse.
Investors have become anxious about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently.
The trust will not run the day-to-day operations of Anthropic.
But its influence means the company could opt for strategies that may not make the most money for investors.
Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX’s AI division have all lost more money than they’ve made because of the huge costs associated with building AI.
Amid those fears, the regulatory environment could also change for Anthropic once the new Congress is in session.

extraction.body: Anthropic has reportedly priced its long-awaited IPO at $83 per share, above its initial range of $70 to $78, signaling strong investor appetite for one of the companies at the center of the AI boom, despite market jitters following the departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, which shook confidence in the industry. At the IPO price, Anthropic is reportedly valued at $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis, a significant increase from the $965 billion the company reached in May when it raised $65 billion in its last private market round , but below the $2 trillion it was reportedly aiming for several months ago. Anthropic will begin its life as a public company on Thursday, trading on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT.” A strong first day of trading would signal that investors remain optimistic about AI adoption, despite recent volatility in AI-driven stocks. The company’s performance is expected to set expectations for private AI companies, including Anthropic’s main rival OpenAI, which was last reportedly valued at $1.25 billion but has yet to announce plans for an IPO. Although none of Anthropic’s venture capital investors holds more than a 5% stake in the company, the IPO is a massive windfall for its numerous backers . Investors that own approximately 1% of the company reportedly include Sequoia and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC also holds about a 1% stake in the company, according to a person familiar with the matter. Other backers set to make billions are Iconiq, Menlo Ventures, Coatue, and Sound Ventures, a firm launched by Guy Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, and Spark Ventures, the only VC firm known to hold a board seat at the company. Some of the company’s existing investors, namely Sequoia, Iconiq, Lightspeed, Accel, and Altimeter Capital Management, are so enthusiastic about Anthropic’s future that they were reportedly planning to buy billions of dollars’ worth of the company’s shares in the IPO. Yet the investors’ holdings in Anthropic pale in comparison to those of the Claude maker’s strategic partners , Amazon, which owns nearly 15% of the company, and Google, which holds almost 14%. A group of major tech companies, including AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC Partners, have also agreed to purchase $26 billion worth of non-voting shares through a private placement alongside the IPO. The company’s seven co-founders , including CEO Dario Amodei, each sold nearly 3.4 million shares in the IPO, according to the S-1 filing, bringing in about $282 million for each. (AP Photo/Patrick Sison, File) OAKLAND, Calif. – Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 per share on Wednesday, according to multiple reports, an amount above the expected price range that values the artificial intelligence giant at $1.5 trillion. The higher-than-anticipated pricing signals broad investor enthusiasm for AI stocks even amid some uncertainty in the market stemming from the ouster of Nvidia's CEO and worries about an AI bubble. The San Francisco-based maker of the Claude AI tool is set to make its debut Thursday on Wall Street. The company had set a price range of $70 to $78 per share, offering 825 million shares that will begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT.” Anthropic decided to barrel ahead with the IPO despite jitters among some investors over market volatility, a potential regulatory crackdown by a Democratic-led Congress next year and growing anti-AI sentiment among the public. Then there's the spectacular downfall of one of the industry's biggest cheerleaders, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , over extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. “This is strong appetite for this major AI IPO in Anthropic, and it’s a big win for the tech sector after a white-knuckle time with Nvidia. The pricing shows strong demand among investors,” said Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co. The company’s rival, OpenAI , is not planning to go public until next year. IPO offers a way to raise money without going deeper into debt Anthropic already has taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is “substantial.” Adding to the strain, the company is unprofitable, at least under standard accounting rules, suggesting that its resources to pay interest and principal are limited. While the company has ample cash for now , it will likely run through it quickly if it cannot raise more soon, given its outsize spending plans. The company said it has already signed leases and other deals requiring it to spend $900 billion on computing power and infrastructure in the coming years, including $70 billion in the next 12 months. An IPO is essentially a way to raise money, instead of going into further debt. And borrowing has gotten more expensive. That’s partly due to inflation fears and partly due to the sector’s massive cash needs, which have drawn comparisons to the Gilded Age splurge on railroads. Lenders fear that AI companies have taken on too much debt to expand while having no clear path to profitability. Anthropic's IPO also means its employees can begin to sell their vested stock, a payout that will make many of them millionaires. The IPO could also give Anthropic enormous resources to accelerate its expansion and potentially add billions of dollars to the fortunes of CEO Dario Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela Amodei. AI industry faces concerns about data centers, a possible bubble and regulations Formed in 2021 by former OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company. But both companies have plenty of other competitors, including Google, startups in the U.S. and China and SpaceX , which has an AI business. Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX’s AI division have all lost more money than they’ve made because of the huge costs associated with building AI. That has fueled growing concerns about a bubble forming in the sector. Dario Amodei cautioned in September that the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned, AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the internet within months. Amid those fears, the regulatory environment could also change for Anthropic once the new Congress is in session. Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a backlash against data centers. And two big states offering incentives for data centers, Texas and Georgia, just elected Democratic governors vowing to stop new construction. Adding to the pressure is the possibility that demand for AI shares could drop or even collapse. Investors have become anxious about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently. Investors will have less control in Anthropic's unusual structure The goal of most companies, above all, is to do well for their owners . Usually that means making profits and growing the business. Anthropic says it too will consider its stockholders, but it will balance their interests against another fundamental goal : “the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.” Like its rival OpenAI , Anthropic is a public-benefit corporation, a legal designation used by companies that pledge to balance shareholder interests with the public good. How that will play out for companies worth potentially trillions of dollars is uncharted territory. Anthropic has set up a long-term benefit trust that will have the ability to elect or remove a majority of the company’s board of directors. The trust will not run the day-to-day operations of Anthropic. But its influence means the company could opt for strategies that may not make the most money for investors. Market valuation for AI companies is going to be “up and down for many years to come, but more up than down,” said Rich Lesser, the global chair and former CEO of Boston Consulting Group. “Exactly what the flow of that will be, it’s very hard to predict,” Lesser said in an interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday at the Semafor Silicon Valley & The World forum. “There’s no question what Anthropic and OpenAI and Google and a number of the other players in this industry have done is pretty remarkable.” If you need help with the Public File, call (313) 222-0566 At WDIV, we are committed to informing and delighting our audience. OAKLAND, Calif. – Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 per share on Wednesday, according to multiple reports, an amount above the expected price range that values the artificial intelligence giant at $1.5 trillion.
The higher-than-anticipated pricing signals broad investor enthusiasm for AI stocks even amid some uncertainty in the market stemming from the ouster of Nvidia's CEO and worries about an AI bubble.

The San Francisco-based maker of the Claude AI tool is set to make its debut Thursday on Wall Street. The company had set a price range of $70 to $78 per share, offering 825 million shares that will begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT.”

Anthropic decided to barrel ahead with the IPO despite jitters among some investors over market volatility, a potential regulatory crackdown by a Democratic-led Congress next year and growing anti-AI sentiment among the public. Then there's the spectacular downfall of one of the industry's biggest cheerleaders, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , over extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

“This is strong appetite for this major AI IPO in Anthropic, and it’s a big win for the tech sector after a white-knuckle time with Nvidia. The pricing shows strong demand among investors,” said Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co.
The company’s rival, OpenAI , is not planning to go public until next year.
IPO offers a way to raise money without going deeper into debt

Anthropic already has taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is “substantial.” Adding to the strain, the company is unprofitable, at least under standard accounting rules, suggesting that its resources to pay interest and principal are limited.

While the company has ample cash for now , it will likely run through it quickly if it cannot raise more soon, given its outsize spending plans. The company said it has already signed leases and other deals requiring it to spend $900 billion on computing power and infrastructure in the coming years, including $70 billion in the next 12 months.

An IPO is essentially a way to raise money, instead of going into further debt. And borrowing has gotten more expensive. Strong investor interest comes despite questions about Anthropic's ability to sustain rapid growth amid intensifying competition.OpenAI, Anthropic's closest rival, is also reportedly considering a public listing as early as next year.Also Read: Anthropic IPO: AI company's listing on Nasdaq to turn thousands of staff into millionairesAnthropic shares are scheduled to debut on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT.Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are leading the IPO, supported by a 22-bank underwriting syndicate. Both investment banks also led SpaceX's IPO earlier this year.Meanwhile, investors are increasingly wary of the debt-driven expansion of AI infrastructure, as technology firms and data-centre operators take on substantial borrowings to fund chips, power supplies and computing facilities.(Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. extraction.body: Nadella cited his longstanding relationship with interim CEO Colette Kress, who previously worked at Microsoft, and said he remains in contact with Nvidia colleagues. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said he believes Nvidia’s team can continue its work after Jensen Huang left the chief executive role last week, as the chipmaker adjusts to a leadership change. Nadella spoke Wednesday, Nov. 18, at the DealBook Summit. He pointed to his longstanding professional relationship with Colette Kress, who previously worked at Microsoft and now serves as Nvidia’s interim CEO. He added that he remains in contact with the same Nvidia colleagues he knew before Huang left. Nadella said he has confidence in the team’s ability to carry on its work. Nadella also reflected on companies moving beyond founder CEOs. He said founders can build something from nothing, but companies eventually need to succeed under someone else’s leadership. Huang held Nvidia’s CEO position for 33 years. Sonny Jang reports on people and leadership in digital assets for TokenPost. Send corrections or tips to info@tokenpost.com.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said he believes Nvidia’s team can continue its work after Jensen Huang left the chief executive role last week, as the chipmaker adjusts to a leadership change. Nadella spoke Wednesday, Nov. 18, at the DealBook Summit. He pointed to his longstanding professional relationship with Colette Kress, who previously worked at Microsoft and now serves as Nvidia’s interim CEO. He added that he remains in contact with the same Nvidia colleagues he knew before Huang left. Nadella said he has confidence in the team’s ability to carry on its work. Nadella also reflected on companies moving beyond founder CEOs. He said founders can build something from nothing, but companies eventually need to succeed under someone else’s leadership. Scandal-hit Californian chip giant Nvidia said Tuesday it has stopped shipping artificial intelligence chips from its "Hopper" series to China, as scrutiny grows over Beijing's access to powerful US semiconductors. Advanced Nvidia chips are the world's top hardware for training and running AI tools -- making them highly sensitive equipment in the tech race between Washington and Beijing. Lucrative sales of Nvidia chips -- and allegations they are smuggled to China through third countries -- are in the spotlight after former CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman whom some US officials reportedly suspect of spying for Beijing. In the third quarter, "sales of licensed Hopper data centre products to China was $2.4 billion," interim CEO Colette Kress told an earnings call Tuesday. But "our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China." Kress did not give a reason for the decision. Dilin Wu, a research strategist at Pepperstone, told AFP "the timing says quite a lot." "We don't know exactly what prompted the decision to stop shipments, but it certainly looks like Nvidia is trying to draw a clearer line around its China business and reassure regulators that compliance comes first." This year, the Trump administration began allowing limited sales of the flagship "H200" chip from Nvidia's "Hopper" series to China. But US conditions have made it difficult for shipments to be approved, with Beijing also seen as reluctant to buy H200s as its homegrown chip industry gains momentum. Washington still bans the export of Nvidia's even more advanced "Blackwell" and "Rubin" GPUs to China, citing security concerns as advanced AI has military applications. Huang's affair with Alice Huang, a former director of a Singapore-based cloud computing company, has tanked Nvidia's market value. Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen, previously led Megaspeed International -- a company under investigation for allegedly helping Chinese tech firms obtain Nvidia chips in violation of US export controls. As the scandal deepens, the United States moved Monday to close loopholes in those restrictions. Its new rules aim to crack down on both chip smuggling to China and the large gray market of Chinese companies renting computing power from data centres full of high-end Nvidia chips in Southeast Asian countries. Chandy Ye, a dual-qualified Hong Kong solicitor and mainland China lawyer, told AFP that the practical impact of Nvidia's decision to stop Hopper shipments to China would be limited. "Chinese authorities have already been actively steering the domestic tech sector away from procuring H200s since January 2026, meaning the local ecosystem has long been adjusting to this decoupling," she said. "The far more consequential development is the sweeping new interim rule from the US Commerce Department restricting remote access to advanced computing capabilities," which closes a "massive loophole."

Scandal-hit Californian chip giant Nvidia said Tuesday it has stopped shipping artificial intelligence chips from its "Hopper" series to China, as scrutiny grows over Beijing's access to powerful US semiconductors. Advanced Nvidia chips are the world's top hardware for training and running AI tools -- making them highly sensitive equipment in the tech race between Washington and Beijing. Lucrative sales of Nvidia chips -- and allegations they are smuggled to China through third countries -- are in the spotlight after former CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman whom some US officials reportedly suspect of spying for Beijing. In the third quarter, "sales of licensed Hopper data centre products to China was $2.4 billion," interim CEO Colette Kress told an earnings call Tuesday. But "our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China." Kress did not give a reason for the decision. Dilin Wu, a research strategist at Pepperstone, told AFP "the timing says quite a lot." "We don't know exactly what prompted the decision to stop shipments, but it certainly looks like Nvidia is trying to draw a clearer line around its China business and reassure regulators that compliance comes first." This year, the Trump administration began allowing limited sales of the flagship "H200" chip from Nvidia's "Hopper" series to China. But US conditions have made it difficult for shipments to be approved, with Beijing also seen as reluctant to buy H200s as its homegrown chip industry gains momentum. Washington still bans the export of Nvidia's even more advanced "Blackwell" and "Rubin" GPUs to China, citing security concerns as advanced AI has military applications. Huang's affair with Alice Huang, a former director of a Singapore-based cloud computing company, has tanked Nvidia's market value. Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen, previously led Megaspeed International -- a company under investigation for allegedly helping Chinese tech firms obtain Nvidia chips in violation of US export controls. As the scandal deepens, the United States moved Monday to close loopholes in those restrictions. Its new rules aim to crack down on both chip smuggling to China and the large gray market of Chinese companies renting computing power from data centres full of high-end Nvidia chips in Southeast Asian countries. Chandy Ye, a dual-qualified Hong Kong solicitor and mainland China lawyer, told AFP that the practical impact of Nvidia's decision to stop Hopper shipments to China would be limited. "Chinese authorities have already been actively steering the domestic tech sector away from procuring H200s since January 2026, meaning the local ecosystem has long been adjusting to this decoupling," she said. "The far more consequential development is the sweeping new interim rule from the US Commerce Department restricting remote access to advanced computing capabilities," which closes a "massive loophole."

Colette Kress, who replaced Jensen Huang following his resignation last week, said during an earnings call on Tuesday that the US chipmaker sold $2.4 billion worth of licensed Hopper-generation data centre products to China in the quarter ended October 25. But she said there were no current plans for further shipments. "Our guidance does not have any licenced Hopper data centre products included, and we are no longer shipping licenced Hopper data centre products to China," Kress said. She did not explain why Nvidia had stopped shipping the processors or whether the halt would be permanent. The Hopper family includes the H200, a powerful processor used to train and run advanced AI models. TRUMP EASED EXPORT CURBS AFTER XI SUMMIT, HUANG LOBBYING The US introduced export controls on the chips in 2022 and subsequently tightened China's access to them. Following a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping last year, however, US President Donald Trump said he would allow H200 sales to approved Chinese customers. The US eased its licensing policy for the H200 in January, allowing export applications to be reviewed individually subject to security conditions. That decision followed months of lobbying from Huang, who stepped down as he faced allegations he had extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two Nvidia employees. H200 chips are manufactured for Nvidia in Taiwan by TSMC, the world's largest contract chipmaker. And the China export arrangement also imposed a 25% tariff on eligible chips imported into the United States before shipment to China. Washington approved H200 sales to 10 Chinese companies, including Alibaba, Tencent and TikTok owner ByteDance, according to previous Reuters reporting. Beijing has since restricted H200 imports, however, as it seeks to reduce its dependence on US technology even as Chinese companies face growing demand for AI computing power. Reuters reported earlier this month that around 600,000 H200 chips were being stored in Hong Kong awaiting shipment to mainland China after Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports. Several major Chinese internet companies had each obtained about 10,000 H200 chips in recent months, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Nvidia stopped shipping licensed Hopper data center chips to China, even though the U.S. had approved sales of the H200 in January, interim CEO Colette Kress said during an earnings call on Tuesday. Kress said Nvidia sold $2.4 billion worth of licensed Hopper-generation data centre products to China in the quarter ended October 25, but she added, "our guidance does not have any licenced Hopper data centre products included, and we are no longer shipping licenced Hopper data centre products to China,". Kress did not explain why Nvidia halted shipments or whether the pause would be permanent, and the Reuters account linked the decision to doubts about the future of the licensing agreement negotiated by Washington and Beijing.

The Reuters report said the Hopper family includes the H200, a processor used to train and run advanced AI models, and it placed the announcement in Shenzhen on Nov 18. The Verge described the move as Nvidia "isn’t selling any more AI chips to China," while also noting that Kress did not explain why Nvidia was ceasing shipments or clarify whether Nvidia would pursue other business with China in the future.

Kress said Nvidia had stopped shipping Hopper-series AI chips to China despite earlier U.S. approval, and CBS News reported that she did not provide a reason for the decision. The shift came as scrutiny of Nvidia’s China sales intensified after revelations that former CEO and cofounder Jensen Huang had a relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Bloomberg Law News reported that Nvidia was no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China despite winning the U.S. government’s blessing to sell a version of that model to the Asian nation last year.

Reuters said the U.S. eased its licensing policy for the H200 in January, allowing export applications to be reviewed individually subject to security conditions, and it described the earlier export controls introduced in 2022. Reuters also reported that Washington approved H200 sales to 10 Chinese companies, including Alibaba, Tencent, and TikTok owner ByteDance, while Beijing restricted H200 imports as it sought to reduce dependence on U.S. technology.

sources.title: Democrats Invoke Ted Cruz's own words in bid to block FCC nominee vote - Yahoo
passages: Senate Democrats are urging Senator Ted Cruz to delay a committee vote on President Donald Trump's nominee to the Federal Communications Commission, citing the Texas Republican's own past opposition to confirming controversial nominees during a lame-duck session.

All Democratic members of the Senate Commerce Committee, led by Ranking Member Maria Cantwell, asked Cruz to remove FCC nominee Danielle Thumann Severs from Wednesday's markup agenda and postpone consideration until the next Congress, when Democrats will control the Senate.
They argued that any Republican FCC nominee should be considered alongside the renomination of Democratic Commissioner Anna Gomez and a Democratic nominee for another vacant commission seat.

In a letter dated November 16, Commerce Committee Democrats argued there was "no mandate for the outgoing majority to rush through a partisan FCC nomination in its final weeks" following elections that returned control of Congress to Democrats.
The lawmakers pointedly quoted language Cruz used in 2014 regarding controversial nominees advanced after an election.
The confirmation battle could help determine the partisan balance of the FCC, the independent agency that regulates telecommunications, broadcasting and broadband policy.
Thumann Severs currently serves as senior counsel to FCC Chairman Carr.
She previously worked as a legal adviser in his office before taking a government affairs role at telecommunications infrastructure company Crown Castle and later returning to the FCC.
"The letter mischaracterizes the situation and facts entirely.
As Danielle's QFR responses and FOIA at hand make clear, Danielle was not in the ex-parte and never engaged once with the outside parties.
Her testimony and QFR responses were truthful, including and specifically referencing working on cross cutting matters like unlawful discrimination," an FCC spokesperson told Newsweek .

The nomination fight has intensified following allegations from Senator Ben Ray Luján that internal FCC emails conflict with testimony Thumann Severs provided during her confirmation hearing earlier this month.

The senator has argued the records raise questions about whether her hearing testimony was complete and whether FCC staff played a role in shaping commitments submitted as part of the merger review process.
While Democrats are pressing for a delay, Republicans currently retain control of the committee and appear poised to move the nomination forward.

Danielle Thumann Severs was nominated by Donald Trump to fill a vacancy on the commission, which is currently split 2-1 with a Republican majority. Democrats objected that the nomination was not paired with a member of their party, as has been a tradition. Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-WA), the top Democrat on the committee, said in a statement that they “made clear” to the committee’s current chairman Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) that “we had concerns about the nominee” being put forward “and asked that she be pulled from markup.” Related Stories News Emergency Broadcast System Test Still On For Today, Homeland Security Says News Another Day, Another Outage: As CNN Reports On NSA Network Down, News Outlets Seize On Back-To-Back Incidents Of Cyber Chaos She noted that the commission’s sole Democrat, Anna Gomez, “could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times. This is not a problem we have created, but a problem that the White House has to solve.” Watch on Deadline Democrats fear that with Thumann Severs’ confirmation, Trump will fire Gomez, leaving the party with no representation on the commission. If Trump were to fire Gomez now, the FCC would have just two members and would be left without a quorum. Gomez has been an outspoken critic of FCC Chairman Brendan Carr , Trump’s appointee, claiming that he has engaged in a campaign of “censorship and control” to limit the speech of broadcasters and journalists critical of the administration. With only Republican votes, the Senate Commerce Committee reported Thumann Servers’ nomination favorably. “There’s nothing that requires the president to nominate in pairs, and this committee has moved FCC nominees separately in the past,” Cruz said at the markup. “The law merely says that no more than three of the commissioners may be from the same party.” He also noted that Thumann Severs was filling the vacancy of a Republican, Nathan Simington, who resigned last year. Thumann Severs is senior counsel to Carr, with a focus on the agency’s wireline bureau, public safety and homeland security bureau and the consumer and government affairs bureau. One of the Senate Commerce Committee Democrats, Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-NM), called for the vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination to be pulled. Luján wrote in a letter to Cruz on Tuesday, “To be clear, the draft letter that Ms. Thumann reviewed, and apparently partially redlined, was not a letter that the Commission intended to send to Skydance or Paramount. It was a letter that Skydance later submitted to the Commission as its own work, a commitment that helped persuade the Commission that the merger was in the public interest, and that was cited in the Commission’s ultimate order approving the transaction. This means that the Chairman’s office was editing a regulated company’s commitments behind closed doors and then presenting them to the public as company’s own pledges.” An FCC spokesperson said that Luján’s letter “mischaracterizes the situation and facts entirely. As Danielle’s responses and FOIA at hand make clear, Danielle was not in the ex-parte and never engaged once with the outside parties. coreStoryFacts.text: Senate Democrats are urging Senator Ted Cruz to delay a committee vote on President Donald Trump's nominee to the Federal Communications Commission, citing the Texas Republican's own past opposition to confirming controversial nominees during a lame-duck session.

All Democratic members of the Senate Commerce Committee, led by Ranking Member Maria Cantwell, asked Cruz to remove FCC nominee Danielle Thumann Severs from Wednesday's markup agenda and postpone consideration until the next Congress, when Democrats will control the Senate.
They argued that any Republican FCC nominee should be considered alongside the renomination of Democratic Commissioner Anna Gomez and a Democratic nominee for another vacant commission seat.

In a letter dated November 16, Commerce Committee Democrats argued there was "no mandate for the outgoing majority to rush through a partisan FCC nomination in its final weeks" following elections that returned control of Congress to Democrats.
The lawmakers pointedly quoted language Cruz used in 2014 regarding controversial nominees advanced after an election.
The confirmation battle could help determine the partisan balance of the FCC, the independent agency that regulates telecommunications, broadcasting and broadband policy.
Thumann Severs currently serves as senior counsel to FCC Chairman Carr.
She previously worked as a legal adviser in his office before taking a government affairs role at telecommunications infrastructure company Crown Castle and later returning to the FCC.
"The letter mischaracterizes the situation and facts entirely.
As Danielle's QFR responses and FOIA at hand make clear, Danielle was not in the ex-parte and never engaged once with the outside parties.

Nominees are vetted in committees first, and then seek require majority approval from the Senate. Republicans are hoping to get Thumann confirmed before Democrats take Senate control in January. Although the Senate Commerce Committee generally requires one minority member to be present for nomination votes, a spokesperson for Cruz said Senate rules allow the nomination to be advanced for a vote in the entire chamber. A spokesperson for Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), the top Democrat on the committee, said in response that “since 2005, Commerce Committee rules required that a quorum include one member of the minority for official action on bill, resolution, or nomination.” Technically, the committee has operated with no rules during Cruz’s chairmanship because Cruz “failed to pass committee rules” for the current session of Congress, Cantwell’s spokesperson said. “Nevertheless, in practice it has operated in line with rules from the last Congress (and this provision, specifically, since 2005), including that a quorum with a member of the minority party must be present for official action on a nomination or legislation. extraction.body: UPDATED, with FCC comment: Democrats boycotted a Senate Commerce Committee markup on Wednesday in protest of efforts to advance the nomination of a sole Republican to the FCC. Danielle Thumann Severs was nominated by Donald Trump to fill a vacancy on the commission, which is currently split 2-1 with a Republican majority. Democrats objected that the nomination was not paired with a member of their party, as has been a tradition. Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-WA), the top Democrat on the committee, said in a statement that they “made clear” to the committee’s current chairman Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) that “we had concerns about the nominee” being put forward “and asked that she be pulled from markup.” Related Stories News Emergency Broadcast System Test Still On For Today, Homeland Security Says News Another Day, Another Outage: As CNN Reports On NSA Network Down, News Outlets Seize On Back-To-Back Incidents Of Cyber Chaos She noted that the commission’s sole Democrat, Anna Gomez, “could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times. This is not a problem we have created, but a problem that the White House has to solve.” Watch on Deadline Democrats fear that with Thumann Severs’ confirmation, Trump will fire Gomez, leaving the party with no representation on the commission. If Trump were to fire Gomez now, the FCC would have just two members and would be left without a quorum. Gomez has been an outspoken critic of FCC Chairman Brendan Carr , Trump’s appointee, claiming that he has engaged in a campaign of “censorship and control” to limit the speech of broadcasters and journalists critical of the administration. With only Republican votes, the Senate Commerce Committee reported Thumann Servers’ nomination favorably. “There’s nothing that requires the president to nominate in pairs, and this committee has moved FCC nominees separately in the past,” Cruz said at the markup. “The law merely says that no more than three of the commissioners may be from the same party.” He also noted that Thumann Severs was filling the vacancy of a Republican, Nathan Simington, who resigned last year. Thumann Severs is senior counsel to Carr, with a focus on the agency’s wireline bureau, public safety and homeland security bureau and the consumer and government affairs bureau. One of the Senate Commerce Committee Democrats, Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-NM), called for the vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination to be pulled. He cited her testimony that at her confirmation hearing, she said that she had not worked with Carr on “any media related issues.” Yet he said that documents show that she was involved in reviewing the draft of a letter that Skydance intended to submit in its regulatory proceeding to purchase Paramount last year. Luján wrote in a letter to Cruz on Tuesday, “To be clear, the draft letter that Ms. Thumann reviewed, and apparently partially redlined, was not a letter that the Commission intended to send to Skydance or Paramount. It was a letter that Skydance later submitted to the Commission as its own work, a commitment that helped persuade the Commission that the merger was in the public interest, and that was cited in the Commission’s ultimate order approving the transaction. This means that the Chairman’s office was editing a regulated company’s commitments behind closed doors and then presenting them to the public as company’s own pledges.” An FCC spokesperson said that Luján’s letter “mischaracterizes the situation and facts entirely. As Danielle’s responses and FOIA at hand make clear, Danielle was not in the ex-parte and never engaged once with the outside parties. Her testimony and QFR responses were truthful, including and specifically referencing working on cross cutting matters like unlawful discrimination.” Get our Breaking News Alerts and Keep your inbox happy. The activity comes as President Trump threatened Iran’s infrastructure, particularly its bridges and power plants.

Iran's attack targeted products by Rockwell Automation's Allen-Bradley, one of the most widely used industrial automation brands, according to the notice, which was first reported Tuesday by The Times.

The advisory said that cyber actors affiliated with Iran were exploiting "programmable logic controllers across U.S. critical infrastructure." Tehran's targeting campaigns against U.S. organizations "have recently escalated, likely in response to hostilities between Iran and the United States and Israel," the notice added.

The advisory was issued Tuesday jointly by the FBI, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the National Security Agency, the Environmental Protection Agency, the Department of Energy and Cyber Command.

Hall, the EPA's assistant administrator for enforcement and compliance assurance, said in a statement.

"A single breach can disrupt treatment or introduce contaminants, damage equipment, and erode public trust." extraction.body: US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Wednesday that Iran and Iranian-backed actors have targeted critical infrastructure in the United States since the war began in February, even as the Trump administration continues to dismiss suggestions that a series of major technological outages across the country were part of a coordinated cyberattack. In written testimony submitted to the House Homeland Security Committee ahead of a congressional hearing, Mullin described Iranian cyber activity targeting critical American infrastructure, including transportation, healthcare, water, energy, and financial services. “Iranian government and Tehran-backed actors have targeted US critical infrastructure,” Mullin stated in his testimony. According to the secretary, Iranian cyber activity has intensified since the outbreak of the conflict earlier this year. He noted that previous incidents had largely resulted in limited, localized disruptions involving inadequately secured industrial control systems, while warning that vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure could potentially lead to more significant consequences. Mullin’s testimony comes amid growing public concern over a series of unusual technological failures in the United States. In recent days, a major malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s air traffic control system prompted a nationwide ground stop, disrupting thousands of flights. Separately, several major American banks experienced online banking outages , while technical problems also affected the National Security Agency’s highly classified internal communications network. However, Mullin did not suggest that Iran was responsible for any of these incidents, nor did he establish a connection between the Iranian cyber activity described in his testimony and the recent disruptions. Threats from Iran to Americans inside and outside the United States have increased substantially, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told lawmakers on Wednesday. "We remain committed to detecting, deterring, and combating the Iranian lethal plotting outside the United States and inside the United States," Clayton said at a House of Representatives Homeland Security Committee hearing. "These threats have substantially increased. Our women and men abroad, our women and men here in the United States, are under greater threat." The testimony follows an unusual press appearance Tuesday by Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio, who sought to reassure Americans that the disruptions were not part of a coordinated hostile operation. “We are not under systemic attack,” Rubio said. “These events have nothing to do with each other. They’re not interrelated. They’re all separate, and they’re distinct.” Rubio stressed that US authorities had found no evidence linking the incidents to cybercriminals, foreign governments, or other malicious actors. Senior White House officials reinforced that assessment during a separate background briefing, attributing the disruptions to efforts to strengthen and modernize aging technological infrastructure, including software updates and hardware upgrades. One senior administration official said the incidents reflected the challenges of upgrading legacy systems rather than evidence of hostile cyber operations. Nevertheless, Mullin’s testimony highlights a separate and continuing national security concern: Iranian cyber actors have been targeting American infrastructure while the United States remains engaged in a military confrontation with Tehran. For now, the administration maintains that the recent nationwide disruptions were unrelated, with no evidence establishing Iranian involvement in the outages. The distinction remains significant: while the US government acknowledges Iranian cyber threats against critical infrastructure, it has not attributed the latest technological failures to Tehran or to a coordinated cyberattack. extraction.body: U.S. intelligence agencies are "urgently warning" private-sector companies nationwide that Iranian actors are conducting cyber operations targeting critical U.S. infrastructure, a campaign that has already caused disruptions, according to a government notice. The activity comes as President Trump threatened Iran’s infrastructure, particularly its bridges and power plants. Iran's attack targeted products by Rockwell Automation's Allen-Bradley, one of the most widely used industrial automation brands, according to the notice, which was first reported Tuesday by The Times. The advisory said that cyber actors affiliated with Iran were exploiting "programmable logic controllers across U.S. critical infrastructure." Tehran's targeting campaigns against U.S. organizations "have recently escalated, likely in response to hostilities between Iran and the United States and Israel," the notice added. The advisory was issued Tuesday jointly by the FBI, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the National Security Agency, the Environmental Protection Agency, the Department of Energy and Cyber Command. In its own notice, the EPA warned that Iran's cyberattack had already disrupted "commonly used operational technology at drinking water and wastewater systems," and that the federal government is "diligently working to ensure that Americans can rely on clean and safe water." “Cyberattacks on drinking water and wastewater systems directly threaten public health and community resilience," Jeffrey A. Hall, the EPA's assistant administrator for enforcement and compliance assurance, said in a statement. "A single breach can disrupt treatment or introduce contaminants, damage equipment, and erode public trust." Top executives from companies at the core of the nation's ability to function — those leading America's largest energy, water, transportation and communications corporations — had already been taking it upon themselves to increase their vigilance over potential attacks, concerned that Trump's willingness to target Iran's critical infrastructure inadvertently put a mark on their backs. Some fear Iran's ability to conduct cyber operations that could take down transformers or power inverters, if not a wide-scale power system. Others are concerned about threats to brick-and-mortar sites from proxies of Tehran — physical attacks against facilities such as nuclear plants, or power management systems, the crown jewels of the sector. Larger, even more capable actors, particularly Russia and China, may also take advantage of the fog of war to launch strikes themselves. "There remains concern about Iranian cyber capabilities and retaliation if the U.S. carries through on threats to attack their infrastructure," said Ernest Moniz, former U.S. secretary of Energy under President Obama who helped negotiate the 2015 nuclear deal with Iran. "There may already be backdoors, Trojan horses and malware hidden in our infrastructure." "I have to believe that the government cyber experts — or what’s left of them — are working closely and indeed overtime with the power companies and other infrastructure operators on cyber defense and intrusion detection and warning," Moniz added. Iran has demonstrated an ability to penetrate networks tied to critical U.S. infrastructure before. In 2015, Iran-backed hackers accessed data associated with Calpine Corp., one of California's largest power producers, obtaining detailed engineering diagrams and credentials related to power plant systems. Some were labeled “mission critical.” U.S. officials feared at the time that the breach would allow Tehran to initiate blackouts nationwide. Since that time, companies at the center of the U.S. energy and telecommunications sectors have markedly improved their defenses. But Iran's offensive capabilities have improved, as well. Large players in the energy sector are operating with "a watchful eye and an elevated posture right now," said Pedro J. Pizarro, president and chief executive of Edison International, the parent company of Southern California Edison, one of the nation’s largest electric utilities. In 2024, a pair of devastating cyber espionage attacks targeting U.S. critical infrastructure attributed to Chinese hackers, Volt Typhoon and Salt Typhoon, were discovered after avoiding detection for at least three years. The threat of a similarly latent attack — in which malware lies dormant in critical infrastructure systems, waiting for a signal to activate — is a real cause for concern in the sector, despite its best efforts and technological advances, experts and insiders said. "The threat of cyber and physical attacks targeting critical infrastructure is not new," said Jennifer DeCesaro, senior vice president of industry operations at the Edison Electric Institute, "which is why we partner with the government through the Electricity Subsector Coordinating Council to share actionable intelligence and prepare to respond to incidents that could affect our ability to provide electricity safely and reliably.” The ESCC works closely with the National Security Council and its intelligence arms, particularly the intelligence agencies and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA, to coordinate regular briefings on safety standards, best practices and intelligence tips. A spokesperson with CISA, listed as out of office due to the ongoing federal funding hiatus for the Department of Homeland Security, could not be reached for comment. Last summer, announcing a 40% cut to the workforce of her office, Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard eliminated the Cyber Threat Intelligence Integration Center, previously seen as a critical fusion hub of information by private sector partners. Trump has threatened to destroy every bridge and power plant in Iran if it fails to come to an agreement that ends its control over the Strait of Hormuz. Ultimately, corporate executives shoulder much of the burden as the first line of defense for the country's critical infrastructure, roughly 85% of which is owned by private sector companies. Tom Fanning, former chief executive of Southern Co. and now executive committee chair at the Alliance for Critical Infrastructure, said the threat from Iran is “credible.” "I have not seen what I would describe as the existential threat, to take down a wide-ranging power system," Fanning said. Is the United States critical infrastructure prepared to act? I think so." Last month, early on in the war, the Los Angeles Metro transit system was forced to shut down a portion of its network due to a hack. Authorities say it is still unclear who was behind the breach, but a source told The Times that Iran-backed hackers are being investigated as potential culprits. The transportation agency said its security team had “discovered unauthorized activity,” and were making sure its roughly 1,400 servers were secure before bringing them back online. Homeland Security is working with local partners “to address cyber threats to critical infrastructure," an official said. "The reality is that the threats are here and now," Fanning added. "The truth is, the bad guys are already here." Times staff writers Kevin Rector, Richard Winton and Rebecca Ellis, in Los Angeles, contributed to this report.

extraction.body: US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Wednesday that Iran and Iranian-backed actors have targeted critical infrastructure in the United States since the war began in February, even as the Trump administration continues to dismiss suggestions that a series of major technological outages across the country were part of a coordinated cyberattack. In written testimony submitted to the House Homeland Security Committee ahead of a congressional hearing, Mullin described Iranian cyber activity targeting critical American infrastructure, including transportation, healthcare, water, energy, and financial services. “Iranian government and Tehran-backed actors have targeted US critical infrastructure,” Mullin stated in his testimony. According to the secretary, Iranian cyber activity has intensified since the outbreak of the conflict earlier this year. He noted that previous incidents had largely resulted in limited, localized disruptions involving inadequately secured industrial control systems, while warning that vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure could potentially lead to more significant consequences. Mullin’s testimony comes amid growing public concern over a series of unusual technological failures in the United States. In recent days, a major malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s air traffic control system prompted a nationwide ground stop, disrupting thousands of flights. Separately, several major American banks experienced online banking outages , while technical problems also affected the National Security Agency’s highly classified internal communications network. However, Mullin did not suggest that Iran was responsible for any of these incidents, nor did he establish a connection between the Iranian cyber activity described in his testimony and the recent disruptions. Threats from Iran to Americans inside and outside the United States have increased substantially, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told lawmakers on Wednesday. "We remain committed to detecting, deterring, and combating the Iranian lethal plotting outside the United States and inside the United States," Clayton said at a House of Representatives Homeland Security Committee hearing. "These threats have substantially increased. Our women and men abroad, our women and men here in the United States, are under greater threat." The testimony follows an unusual press appearance Tuesday by Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio, who sought to reassure Americans that the disruptions were not part of a coordinated hostile operation. “We are not under systemic attack,” Rubio said. “These events have nothing to do with each other. They’re not interrelated. They’re all separate, and they’re distinct.” Rubio stressed that US authorities had found no evidence linking the incidents to cybercriminals, foreign governments, or other malicious actors. Senior White House officials reinforced that assessment during a separate background briefing, attributing the disruptions to efforts to strengthen and modernize aging technological infrastructure, including software updates and hardware upgrades. One senior administration official said the incidents reflected the challenges of upgrading legacy systems rather than evidence of hostile cyber operations. Nevertheless, Mullin’s testimony highlights a separate and continuing national security concern: Iranian cyber actors have been targeting American infrastructure while the United States remains engaged in a military confrontation with Tehran. For now, the administration maintains that the recent nationwide disruptions were unrelated, with no evidence establishing Iranian involvement in the outages. The distinction remains significant: while the US government acknowledges Iranian cyber threats against critical infrastructure, it has not attributed the latest technological failures to Tehran or to a coordinated cyberattack. In written testimony submitted to the House Homeland Security Committee ahead of a congressional hearing, Mullin described Iranian cyber activity targeting critical American infrastructure, including transportation, healthcare, water, energy, and financial services.
“Iranian government and Tehran-backed actors have targeted US critical infrastructure,” Mullin stated in his testimony.
According to the secretary, Iranian cyber activity has intensified since the outbreak of the conflict earlier this year.

He noted that previous incidents had largely resulted in limited, localized disruptions involving inadequately secured industrial control systems, while warning that vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure could potentially lead to more significant consequences.
Mullin’s testimony comes amid growing public concern over a series of unusual technological failures in the United States.

In recent days, a major malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s air traffic control system prompted a nationwide ground stop, disrupting thousands of flights. Separately, several major American banks experienced online banking outages , while technical problems also affected the National Security Agency’s highly classified internal communications network.

However, Mullin did not suggest that Iran was responsible for any of these incidents, nor did he establish a connection between the Iranian cyber activity described in his testimony and the recent disruptions.
Threats from Iran to Americans inside and outside the United States have increased substantially, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told lawmakers on Wednesday.

"We remain committed to detecting, deterring, and combating the Iranian lethal plotting outside the United States and inside the United States," Clayton said at a House of Representatives Homeland Security Committee hearing.
"These threats have substantially increased. Our women and men abroad, our women and men here in the United States, are under greater threat."

The testimony follows an unusual press appearance Tuesday by Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio, who sought to reassure Americans that the disruptions were not part of a coordinated hostile operation.
“We are not under systemic attack,” Rubio said.
“These events have nothing to do with each other. They’re not interrelated. They’re all separate, and they’re distinct.”
Rubio stressed that US authorities had found no evidence linking the incidents to cybercriminals, foreign governments, or other malicious actors.

Senior White House officials reinforced that assessment during a separate background briefing, attributing the disruptions to efforts to strengthen and modernize aging technological infrastructure, including software updates and hardware upgrades.
One senior administration official said the incidents reflected the challenges of upgrading legacy systems rather than evidence of hostile cyber operations.

Nevertheless, Mullin’s testimony highlights a separate and continuing national security concern: Iranian cyber actors have been targeting American infrastructure while the United States remains engaged in a military confrontation with Tehran.
For now, the administration maintains that the recent nationwide disruptions were unrelated, with no evidence establishing Iranian involvement in the outages.

The distinction remains significant: while the US government acknowledges Iranian cyber threats against critical infrastructure, it has not attributed the latest technological failures to Tehran or to a coordinated cyberattack.

While an AI agent or AI assistant can access an account with a user’s permission and through the use of their login credentials, this often goes against bank policy that requires users to maintain control of their account and not share it with anyone else. One of the fears that executives have is when an AI agent with login access takes unauthorized steps, like spending money or moving funds around without the explicit instructions of the account owner. There have even been situations where an AI agent called the bank directly and took actions independent of direct user command. Even though it wasn’t explicitly told to do that transaction, it considered it a crucial step to accomplish the task assigned to it. One hypothetical example of this is when a user tells an AI agent to purchase an item but gives it a credit card with no available limit. The AI agent could then have accessed the user’s bank account to move some funds from whatever account it sees that has available funds to then effect the transaction, even if the user did not explicitly tell them that they could use the money in that said account. This is just one example where an AI agent’s transaction could go wrong, which is why several U.S. banks are now restricting third-party AI agents from accessing their platforms. Nevertheless, they still recognize that their customers might want to use tools like AI agents to monitor their finances. This is why some institutions have given or are moving towards read-only access for AI agents, which is something that they’ve been doing for years already. The move comes against a background of burgeoning AI agent use, coupled with the risk that agents can and often do act beyond their remit, making mistakes or performing tasks without instruction, often with disastrous results. An unsupervised AI agent recently deleted a TV show's entire edit weeks before broadcast, forcing the program off air. AI agents are notorious for deleting databases and directories, making it a small leap to imagine they cause some havoc with unfettered access to a bank account. Financial institutions have deep experience when it comes to employing new technology while ensuring that their critical infrastructure remains safe — something that AI labs lack , according to a former OpenAI safety employee. Despite that, banks are still concerned about the speed at which AI technology is developing, fearing that the technology’s capabilities might outrun their ability to control it, which is why they’re preparing for worst-case scenarios and even planning for “day after” scenarios after a catastrophic AI event . passages: “As third-party AI tools become more widely available, we want customers to understand the risks associated with sharing banking credentials or authorizing those tools to access their accounts,” a Citi spokesperson told TechCrunch. “We recently updated our Online User Agreement to provide greater clarity about those risks and to reinforce that customers who choose to grant account access to third-party AI agents are responsible for activities conducted through those agents.”
But if AI agents become an important way to interact with financial decisions, banks will fight to control that pathway.
Citi’s terms note that AI agents it provides can be used by customers without worrying about additional liability.

The reaction by banks is part of a broader trend among businesses of all stripes: AI labs promise that their agents will revolutionize the way people engage with a variety of service providers, then the service providers say “hold on a minute.” We’ve seen it in everything from car-hailing to food service , and how these relationships play out will help determine which AI investments pay off.

But financial institutions aren’t thrilled with the unreliable AI actors in their systems, and are telling customers that they won’t be held responsible for reversing an intentional or unintentional transaction made by automated assistants. “As third-party AI tools become more widely available, we want customers to understand the risks associated with sharing banking credentials or authorizing those tools to access their accounts,” a Citi spokesperson told TechCrunch. “We recently updated our Online User Agreement to provide greater clarity about those risks and to reinforce that customers who choose to grant account access to third-party AI agents are responsible for activities conducted through those agents.” JPMorgan and Bank of America , the two largest banks in the country, announced similar policies last month. And PNC, the eighth largest bank, changed its terms today. Citi’s update goes beyond telling customers that they are responsible for anything their agents may do; it also informs them that if the AI tool leaks their credentials or is hacked, the customer will be responsible for anything hackers do with their account. Banking giant Citizens similarly emailed its customers this week, warning that they are also on the hook for anything their AI assistant does, according to an email seen by TechCrunch. sources.title: Apple among the companies facing pressure from US senators over ‘nudify’ apps - 9to5Mac
passages: The Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps.
A trio of US Senators say Apple and Google are failing to effectively detect and remove apps that can be used to generate nonconsensual nude or pornographic imagery.
They also say Meta is continuing to profit off of ads for these so-called nudification apps that “victimize women and girls worldwide”.

Throughout these investigations, Apple has maintained that nudify apps have always been prohibited under its App Review Guidelines, and that it proactively rejects and removes apps that violate its policies, including those flagged through user reports.
Keith Chu, the chief communications adviser and deputy policy director to Wyden, said that clarifying policies is not the same thing as enforcing them.

Apple, of course, is not alone in this challenge, with Google facing similar criticism over their availability on the Play Store, and Meta coming under scrutiny for allowing developers to advertise these apps on Facebook and Instagram, as highlighted in the WIRED report mentioned above.
However, Wyden’s office argues that simply reaffirming, or in Apple’s case, updating these policies, means little if the companies continue to struggle to enforce them.
Apple also warns that apps used primarily for pornographic content or the objectification of real people may be removed from the App Store without notice.

The senators, namely Ron Wyden of Oregon, Ed Markey of Massachusetts, and Ben Luján of New Mexico, claim that in addition to failing to remove these apps, the companies may actually be profiting from their distribution and promotion.
