Law enforcement have also warned in various intelligence memos that officers should remain vigilant because AI may make it easier to circumvent CSAM detection methods, according to documents the Guardian previously reported on. Apple clarified its policies after TTP researchers reached out about nudification apps they found on the app store in October . Google previously told the Guardian that the company proactively works to detect and remove apps with harmful content and Meta introduced new AI tools to detect and remove ads that contain CSAM. Keith Chu, the chief communications adviser and deputy policy director to Wyden, said that clarifying policies is not the same thing as enforcing them. Despite the companies reaffirming the prohibition of these apps, they continue to proliferate across Apple and Google app stores or be promoted in ads on Meta platforms, he said. In the latest TTP study in October, which the Guardian first reported, researchers found they were able to access dozens of apps with features that enabled the creation of AI-generated nude and pornographic imagery, despite indicating the accounts they created were for 13-year-old boys. There were 135 apps available to these accounts across Apple and Google. In response to inquiries from TTP and the Guardian, Apple and Google removed the apps that were mentioned in the studies. However, the apps remained functional on phones they were already downloaded on. These findings suggest that Apple and Google are “not merely failing to remove applications that facilitate intimate image abuse, it may also be profiting from their distribution”, the letter from the senators said. Katie Paul, the director of TTP, said that though Apple and Google say they review every app on their platform, the companies do not disclose what that review entails. “Vague descriptions of how each company defines ‘nonconsensual intimate imagery’ and lack of detail in how both companies actually go about app review allow them to have it both ways: claiming they have policies on the books, and applying those policies based on what best fits the narrative at any given time,” Paul said. Exclusive: three Senate Democrats send letters to tech CEOs saying safeguards against nudification apps are insufficient on their platforms

A trio of US senators says Apple and Google are failing to effectively detect and remove apps that can be used to generate nonconsensual nude or pornographic imagery. The senators also say Meta is continuing to profit off of ads for these so-called nudification apps that “victimize women and girls worldwide”.

On Wednesday, Ron Wyden, Ed Markey and Ben Luján sent letters to the CEOs of the tech companies, saying the safeguards they have in place to keep nudification off their app stores or platforms are not sufficient.

The senators sent the letters after multiple studies by the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), the latest of which was exclusively reported in the Guardian, found that these apps are either available on Apple and Google app stores or are being advertised in ads on Meta platforms in spite of company policies that prohibit them. According to the studies, children continue to have easy access to these apps.
Wyden, of Oregon, said Congress will need to act if the companies “don’t do a better job of cracking down on apps expressly designed and marketed to create harm”.
“AI has supercharged the ability to create and share nonconsensual sexual images, creating tremendous harm to women and girls,” Wyden said in a statement to the Guardian.

“Instead of ramping up investment to meet this challenge, big tech companies are cutting back on the very teams responsible for protecting users from harm. I’m looking for answers about why Meta, Apple and Google are missing obvious violations of their own rules.”

In a statement, Karl Ryan, a Google spokesperson, said: “Google Play does not allow apps that contain sexual content or allow users to nudify images of people, and we continually take proactive steps to detect and remove apps with harmful content.”

A Meta spokesman, Andy Stone, said in a statement: “We prohibit CSAM [child sexual abuse material] and the promotion of nudify apps, and we work aggressively to keep this material off our services. The criminals behind it take increasingly deceptive steps to evade detection – hiding behind fake names and identities, running ads that look benign, and sometimes linking to Google’s and Apple’s app stores, with the ads’ true intent revealed only after clicking through.

“We’ve taken extensive steps against these perpetrators, from banning Keling Technology Limited and taking legal action against other advertisers, to going after the coordinated networks and removing 92 million sexual ads – and we’re actively exploring new ways to improve our detection.”

The senators wrote that AI-generated nonconsensual nude imagery has seen an uptick in the last two years. Surveys bear that assertion out. Unicef reported at the start of 2026 that at least 1.2 million children in 11 countries reported being victimized of nonconsensual nude images. Law enforcement have also warned in various intelligence memos that officers should remain vigilant because AI may make it easier to circumvent CSAM detection methods, according to documents the Guardian previously reported on.

Apple clarified its policies after TTP researchers reached out about nudification apps they found on the app store in October . Google previously told the Guardian that the company proactively works to detect and remove apps with harmful content and Meta introduced new AI tools to detect and remove ads that contain CSAM.

Keith Chu, the chief communications adviser and deputy policy director to Wyden, said that clarifying policies is not the same thing as enforcing them. Despite the companies reaffirming the prohibition of these apps, they continue to proliferate across Apple and Google app stores or be promoted in ads on Meta platforms, he said.

In the latest TTP study in October, which the Guardian first reported, researchers found they were able to access dozens of apps with features that enabled the creation of AI-generated nude and pornographic imagery, despite indicating the accounts they created were for 13-year-old boys.

There were 135 apps available to these accounts across Apple and Google. In response to inquiries from TTP and the Guardian, Apple and Google removed the apps that were mentioned in the studies. However, the apps remained functional on phones they were already downloaded on.

These findings suggest that Apple and Google are “not merely failing to remove applications that facilitate intimate image abuse, it may also be profiting from their distribution”, the letter from the senators said.
Katie Paul, the director of TTP, said that though Apple and Google say they review every app on their platform, the companies do not disclose what that review entails.

“Vague descriptions of how each company defines ‘nonconsensual intimate imagery’ and lack of detail in how both companies actually go about app review allow them to have it both ways: claiming they have policies on the books, and applying those policies based on what best fits the narrative at any given time,” Paul said.

Apple, for its part, also said that some developers will pull a “bait-and-switch” and add features that enable users to create AI-generated nude or pornographic imagery after the iPhone maker approves an app. Wyden’s office said that they expect the company to review apps on a continuing basis.

On Meta’s social networks, however, many of these developers advertise much more explicitly the nudification functions their apps include. TTP and other research groups have discovered hundreds of paid ads on Instagram and Facebook that include AI-generated sexualized images of real children and other CSAM.

In September, TTP found 332 paid ads on Facebook and Instagram that included CSAM. This month, AIForensics, a European non-profit research organization, found that some apps that were hiding their AI nudification features from Apple and Google were explicitly promoting “sexual deepfake functionality” in ads on Meta platforms.

“Despite Meta’s stated prohibition on these ads, independent investigations have documented extensive ad campaigns on Facebook and Instagram directing customers to apps capable of digitally undressing people in photographs or placing their likeness into sexually explicit content without their consent,” the senators wrote in their letter to Meta’s CEO, Mark Zuckerberg.
In the letter, the senators asked how ads containing apparent CSAM passed the company’s review systems.

On 7 October, Meta said that it had taken additional measures to combat ads with CSAM, however, Paul said TTP researchers have reported dozens of ads containing CSAM to the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children since then. Screenshots TTP shared with the Guardian show images of an ad for an app to create “AI sex friends” highlighting images of young girls. These ads were active for several hours before being taken down but remain available in Meta’s ad library. The organization has “yet to identify ads featuring videos of CSAM run by any other ad platforms”.

“Meta has repeatedly boasted about its sophisticated AI systems for reviewing harms on platforms, but for more than a year those systems have repeatedly failed to flag ads featuring graphic sexual videos of children as young as toddlers,” Paul said.

Here are the details. Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable users to generate nonconsensual nude images. According to the updated rules, apps that allow users to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users. Apple also warns that apps used primarily for pornographic content or the objectification of real people may be removed from the App Store without notice. While definitely well-intended, Apple’s changes came amid growing reports of AI-powered nudify apps, which easily allow users to generate nonconsensual intimate images. Two months before these changes, Apple removed an app that allowed users to create pornographic deepfakes of real people after WIRED reached out for comment, which in turn came one month after San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu demanded that Apple and Google remove several nudify apps from their app stores. Apple also removed several apps following investigations by the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), which published reports in January and April revealing that such apps were widely available on the App Store, sometimes even appearing in sponsored search results. Throughout these investigations, Apple has maintained that nudify apps have always been prohibited under its App Review Guidelines, and that it proactively rejects and removes apps that violate its policies, including those flagged through user reports. Apple, of course, is not alone in this challenge, with Google facing similar criticism over their availability on the Play Store, and Meta coming under scrutiny for allowing developers to advertise these apps on Facebook and Instagram, as highlighted in the WIRED report mentioned above. Which brings us to today’s report from The Guardian . According to The Guardian ’s exclusive report , “three Senate Democrats sent letters to tech CEOs saying safeguards against nudification apps are insufficient on their platforms.” A trio of US Senators say Apple and Google are failing to effectively detect and remove apps that can be used to generate nonconsensual nude or pornographic imagery. They also say Meta is continuing to profit off of ads for these so-called nudification apps that “victimize women and girls worldwide”. The senators, namely Ron Wyden of Oregon, Ed Markey of Massachusetts, and Ben Luján of New Mexico, claim that in addition to failing to remove these apps, the companies may actually be profiting from their distribution and promotion. Commenting on the letter, both Google and Meta said they prohibit such apps or their promotion and work to detect and remove violations from their platforms, broadly echoing what Apple has repeatedly stated when reached for comment in the past over these same issues. However, Wyden’s office argues that simply reaffirming, or in Apple’s case, updating these policies, means little if the companies continue to struggle to enforce them. Keith Chu, the chief communications adviser and deputy policy director to Wyden, said that clarifying policies is not the same thing as enforcing them. Despite the companies reaffirming the prohibition of these apps, they continue to proliferate across Apple and Google app stores or be promoted in ads on Meta platforms, he added. In its latest investigation, published just last month , TTP found 135 apps capable of generating nude or pornographic imagery on the App Store and the Play Store, using accounts registered to 13-year-old boys. Additionally, researchers found that even accounts configured with parental controls were able to download these apps without requiring parental approval. Despite Apple and Google removing the apps identified in the investigation, The Guardian noted that these apps continued to work on devices where they had already been installed. On Wednesday, Ron Wyden, Ed Markey and Ben Luján sent letters to the CEOs of the tech companies, saying the safeguards they have in place to keep nudification off their app stores or platforms are not sufficient. The senators sent the letters after multiple studies by the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), the latest of which was exclusively reported in the Guardian, found that these apps are either available on Apple and Google app stores or are being advertised in ads on Meta platforms in spite of company policies that prohibit them. According to the studies, children continue to have easy access to these apps. Wyden, of Oregon, said Congress will need to act if the companies “don’t do a better job of cracking down on apps expressly designed and marketed to create harm”. “AI has supercharged the ability to create and share nonconsensual sexual images, creating tremendous harm to women and girls,” Wyden said in a statement to the Guardian. “Instead of ramping up investment to meet this challenge, big tech companies are cutting back on the very teams responsible for protecting users from harm. I’m looking for answers about why Meta, Apple and Google are missing obvious violations of their own rules.” In a statement, Karl Ryan, a Google spokesperson, said: “Google Play does not allow apps that contain sexual content or allow users to nudify images of people, and we continually take proactive steps to detect and remove apps with harmful content.” A Meta spokesman, Andy Stone, said in a statement: “We prohibit CSAM [child sexual abuse material] and the promotion of nudify apps, and we work aggressively to keep this material off our services. The criminals behind it take increasingly deceptive steps to evade detection – hiding behind fake names and identities, running ads that look benign, and sometimes linking to Google’s and Apple’s app stores, with the ads’ true intent revealed only after clicking through. “We’ve taken extensive steps against these perpetrators, from banning Keling Technology Limited and taking legal action against other advertisers, to going after the coordinated networks and removing 92 million sexual ads – and we’re actively exploring new ways to improve our detection.” The senators wrote that AI-generated nonconsensual nude imagery has seen an uptick in the last two years. Surveys bear that assertion out. Unicef reported at the start of 2026 that at least 1.2 million children in 11 countries reported being victimized of nonconsensual nude images. Law enforcement have also warned in various intelligence memos that officers should remain vigilant because AI may make it easier to circumvent CSAM detection methods, according to documents the Guardian previously reported on. Apple clarified its policies after TTP researchers reached out about nudification apps they found on the app store in October . Google previously told the Guardian that the company proactively works to detect and remove apps with harmful content and Meta introduced new AI tools to detect and remove ads that contain CSAM. Keith Chu, the chief communications adviser and deputy policy director to Wyden, said that clarifying policies is not the same thing as enforcing them. Despite the companies reaffirming the prohibition of these apps, they continue to proliferate across Apple and Google app stores or be promoted in ads on Meta platforms, he said. In the latest TTP study in October, which the Guardian first reported, researchers found they were able to access dozens of apps with features that enabled the creation of AI-generated nude and pornographic imagery, despite indicating the accounts they created were for 13-year-old boys. There were 135 apps available to these accounts across Apple and Google. In response to inquiries from TTP and the Guardian, Apple and Google removed the apps that were mentioned in the studies. However, the apps remained functional on phones they were already downloaded on. These findings suggest that Apple and Google are “not merely failing to remove applications that facilitate intimate image abuse, it may also be profiting from their distribution”, the letter from the senators said. Katie Paul, the director of TTP, said that though Apple and Google say they review every app on their platform, the companies do not disclose what that review entails. “Vague descriptions of how each company defines ‘nonconsensual intimate imagery’ and lack of detail in how both companies actually go about app review allow them to have it both ways: claiming they have policies on the books, and applying those policies based on what best fits the narrative at any given time,” Paul said. Apple, for its part, also said that some developers will pull a “bait-and-switch” and add features that enable users to create AI-generated nude or pornographic imagery after the iPhone maker approves an app. Wyden’s office said that they expect the company to review apps on a continuing basis. On Meta’s social networks, however, many of these developers advertise much more explicitly the nudification functions their apps include. TTP and other research groups have discovered hundreds of paid ads on Instagram and Facebook that include AI-generated sexualized images of real children and other CSAM. In September, TTP found 332 paid ads on Facebook and Instagram that included CSAM. This month, AIForensics, a European non-profit research organization, found that some apps that were hiding their AI nudification features from Apple and Google were explicitly promoting “sexual deepfake functionality” in ads on Meta platforms. “Despite Meta’s stated prohibition on these ads, independent investigations have documented extensive ad campaigns on Facebook and Instagram directing customers to apps capable of digitally undressing people in photographs or placing their likeness into sexually explicit content without their consent,” the senators wrote in their letter to Meta’s CEO, Mark Zuckerberg. In the letter, the senators asked how ads containing apparent CSAM passed the company’s review systems. On 7 October, Meta said that it had taken additional measures to combat ads with CSAM, however, Paul said TTP researchers have reported dozens of ads containing CSAM to the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children since then. Screenshots TTP shared with the Guardian show images of an ad for an app to create “AI sex friends” highlighting images of young girls. These ads were active for several hours before being taken down but remain available in Meta’s ad library. The organization has “yet to identify ads featuring videos of CSAM run by any other ad platforms”. “Meta has repeatedly boasted about its sophisticated AI systems for reviewing harms on platforms, but for more than a year those systems have repeatedly failed to flag ads featuring graphic sexual videos of children as young as toddlers,” Paul said.

The senators also say Meta is continuing to profit off of ads for these so-called nudification apps that “victimize women and girls worldwide”.

On Wednesday, Ron Wyden, Ed Markey and Ben Luján sent letters to the CEOs of the tech companies, saying the safeguards they have in place to keep nudification off their app stores or platforms are not sufficient.

The senators sent the letters after multiple studies by the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), the latest of which was exclusively reported in the Guardian, found that these apps are either available on Apple and Google app stores or are being advertised in ads on Meta platforms in spite of company policies that prohibit them. According to the studies, children continue to have easy access to these apps.
Wyden, of Oregon, said Congress will need to act if the companies “don’t do a better job of cracking down on apps expressly designed and marketed to create harm”.
“AI has supercharged the ability to create and share nonconsensual sexual images, creating tremendous harm to women and girls,” Wyden said in a statement to the Guardian.

“Instead of ramping up investment to meet this challenge, big tech companies are cutting back on the very teams responsible for protecting users from harm. I’m looking for answers about why Meta, Apple and Google are missing obvious violations of their own rules.”

In a statement, Karl Ryan, a Google spokesperson, said: “Google Play does not allow apps that contain sexual content or allow users to nudify images of people, and we continually take proactive steps to detect and remove apps with harmful content.”

A Meta spokesman, Andy Stone, said in a statement: “We prohibit CSAM [child sexual abuse material] and the promotion of nudify apps, and we work aggressively to keep this material off our services. The criminals behind it take increasingly deceptive steps to evade detection – hiding behind fake names and identities, running ads that look benign, and sometimes linking to Google’s and Apple’s app stores, with the ads’ true intent revealed only after clicking through.

“We’ve taken extensive steps against these perpetrators, from banning Keling Technology Limited and taking legal action against other advertisers, to going after the coordinated networks and removing 92 million sexual ads – and we’re actively exploring new ways to improve our detection.”

Unicef reported at the start of 2026 that at least 1.2 million children in 11 countries reported being victimized of nonconsensual nude images. Apple clarified its policies after TTP researchers reached out about nudification apps they found on the app store in October . On Meta’s social networks, however, many of these developers advertise much more explicitly the nudification functions their apps include. extraction.body: Hardened defaults align with DoD standards, but there may be growing pains. Microsoft’s Ignite announcements this week went beyond the Office-in-Copilot overhaul with the reveal of the Windows Server 2028 Public Preview and its new security-by-default stance and what Microsoft calls Hardened Server Core . Windows Server 2028 will implement a default security framework that Microsoft says is aligned with hardened DoD benchmarks, such as the Defense Information Systems Agency’s (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG). STIGs work by providing a standard security framework for system administrators to follow recommended guidance. In the past, Windows Server admins were left to start from a blank canvas and then implement hardening configurations for operations. Secure baselines were available but not the default. Microsoft says that concern is now managed: “The s ecure configuration is the starting state, not a project you run after setup. That closes the window where a newly deployed server sits exposed while it waits to be hardened. ” The new Windows Server 2028 hardened-by-default state will only be available for the Server Core installs. Windows Server Desktop Experience installs do not include the changed stance. This isn’t to say that system administrators won’t still have the final say on which security protocols are activated, just that the default package now ships in a pre-hardened state. Kerberos is now the default over NTLM , with protections added to LSASS; TLS is automatically restricted to modern cipher suites; key exchange uses “hybrid post-quantum key exchange” based on the quantum-safe ML-KEM; and remote desktop authentication and PowerShell script block logging get stricter as well. Microsoft’s native NVMe storage stack was originally introduced via an update to Windows Server 2025, but it required administrators to enable it manually. The update eliminated NVMe translation through a SCSI stack while improving speeds and reducing overhead. The redesigned stack will now be default-on in Windows Server 2028. Microsoft is upfront, noting that the new hardened security settings may break things due to software compatibility issues with older protocols, legacy authentication, or management tools and scripts. The company encourages users to try things and provide feedback about what goes wrong. “ We want to hear where a hardened default gets in the way of a real workload: which setting, which application, and what you had to change to get it working,” the Windows Server Team said in a blog post . “That is how the defaults get better before general availability.” Microsoft suggests that users use the preview build as a test bed to determine where issues like compatibility still arise. This is not a release candidate build and shouldn’t be treated as such. Despite the new security stance that comes with the preview build, hardware-backed protections like Secure Boot and DMA requirements won’t be enforced until a later preview build. Kerberos is now the default preference over NTLM, but NTLM blocking itself will still have to wait for a later preview release. Beyond those limitations, the current build has a known issue that cuts into its hardened goals. According to the release notes, “A race condition in the TLS hybrid key exchange implementation may cause the LSASS service to crash when hybrid groups are negotiated by a TLS server.” Microsoft recommends disabling hybrid-key exchange groups until the problem is addressed. System administrators and curious homelabbers interested in testing the new Windows Server 2028 can do so by registering with the Microsoft Windows Insider Program . sources.title: Microsoft unveils Windows Server 2028 with security by default — Ars Technica - UA.NEWS
passages: Microsoft has unveiled a public preview of Windows Server 2028 with a new approach to security by default.
As Ars Technica reports , the system will introduce Hardened Server Core, a set of settings that, according to the company, aligns with strengthened U.S.
Department of Defense guidelines, including the DISA Security Technical Implementation Guide recommendations.
It was already added to Windows Server 2025 in an update, but administrators had to activate the feature manually at the time.
The new stack eliminates NVMe translation through SCSI and, according to Microsoft, is expected to reduce overhead and improve performance.
The release notes list a known issue with the implementation of TLS hybrid key exchange: if hybrid groups are negotiated by a TLS server, the LSASS service may crash.
Until the bug is fixed, Microsoft recommends disabling such key exchange groups.
The hardened settings will be available only for Server Core installations.
The company urged users to test the build and report which specific settings interfere with applications.
Microsoft will also strengthen requirements for authentication through Remote Desktop and PowerShell script block logging.
Hardware-supported security mechanisms, including Secure Boot and DMA requirements, will not be applied until a later preview build.

extraction.body: Microsoft has unveiled a public preview of Windows Server 2028 with a new approach to security by default. As Ars Technica reports , the system will introduce Hardened Server Core, a set of settings that, according to the company, aligns with strengthened U.S. Department of Defense guidelines, including the DISA Security Technical Implementation Guide recommendations. Previously, Windows Server administrators could use ready-made secure baseline configurations, but had to enable them themselves after installing the system. Microsoft explained that in Windows Server 2028, the secure configuration is intended to become the server's initial state rather than a separate stage of its setup. The hardened settings will be available only for Server Core installations. The version of Windows Server with the Desktop Experience graphical interface will not receive the new default mode. Among the changes are prioritizing Kerberos over NTLM for authentication, additional protection for the LSASS service, limiting TLS to modern cryptographic algorithm suites, and hybrid post-quantum key exchange based on ML-KEM. Microsoft will also strengthen requirements for authentication through Remote Desktop and PowerShell script block logging. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram . In addition, Windows Server 2028 will use its native NVMe stack by default. It was already added to Windows Server 2025 in an update, but administrators had to activate the feature manually at the time. The new stack eliminates NVMe translation through SCSI and, according to Microsoft, is expected to reduce overhead and improve performance. Microsoft warned that the hardened settings may cause compatibility issues with older protocols, legacy authentication mechanisms, administration tools, and scripts. The company urged users to test the build and report which specific settings interfere with applications. The current version is not a release candidate. Hardware-supported security mechanisms, including Secure Boot and DMA requirements, will not be applied until a later preview build. NTLM blocking will also be introduced later, although Kerberos has already been set as the priority mechanism. The release notes list a known issue with the implementation of TLS hybrid key exchange: if hybrid groups are negotiated by a TLS server, the LSASS service may crash. Until the bug is fixed, Microsoft recommends disabling such key exchange groups. Users who register for the Microsoft Windows Insider program can test Windows Server 2028.

extraction.body: Hardened defaults align with DoD standards, but there may be growing pains. Microsoft’s Ignite announcements this week went beyond the Office-in-Copilot overhaul with the reveal of the Windows Server 2028 Public Preview and its new security-by-default stance and what Microsoft calls Hardened Server Core . Windows Server 2028 will implement a default security framework that Microsoft says is aligned with hardened DoD benchmarks, such as the Defense Information Systems Agency’s (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG). STIGs work by providing a standard security framework for system administrators to follow recommended guidance. In the past, Windows Server admins were left to start from a blank canvas and then implement hardening configurations for operations. Secure baselines were available but not the default. Microsoft says that concern is now managed: “The s ecure configuration is the starting state, not a project you run after setup. That closes the window where a newly deployed server sits exposed while it waits to be hardened. ” The new Windows Server 2028 hardened-by-default state will only be available for the Server Core installs. Windows Server Desktop Experience installs do not include the changed stance. This isn’t to say that system administrators won’t still have the final say on which security protocols are activated, just that the default package now ships in a pre-hardened state. Kerberos is now the default over NTLM , with protections added to LSASS; TLS is automatically restricted to modern cipher suites; key exchange uses “hybrid post-quantum key exchange” based on the quantum-safe ML-KEM; and remote desktop authentication and PowerShell script block logging get stricter as well. Microsoft’s native NVMe storage stack was originally introduced via an update to Windows Server 2025, but it required administrators to enable it manually. The update eliminated NVMe translation through a SCSI stack while improving speeds and reducing overhead. The redesigned stack will now be default-on in Windows Server 2028. Microsoft is upfront, noting that the new hardened security settings may break things due to software compatibility issues with older protocols, legacy authentication, or management tools and scripts. The company encourages users to try things and provide feedback about what goes wrong. “ We want to hear where a hardened default gets in the way of a real workload: which setting, which application, and what you had to change to get it working,” the Windows Server Team said in a blog post . “That is how the defaults get better before general availability.” Microsoft suggests that users use the preview build as a test bed to determine where issues like compatibility still arise. This is not a release candidate build and shouldn’t be treated as such. Despite the new security stance that comes with the preview build, hardware-backed protections like Secure Boot and DMA requirements won’t be enforced until a later preview build. Kerberos is now the default preference over NTLM, but NTLM blocking itself will still have to wait for a later preview release. Beyond those limitations, the current build has a known issue that cuts into its hardened goals. According to the release notes, “A race condition in the TLS hybrid key exchange implementation may cause the LSASS service to crash when hybrid groups are negotiated by a TLS server.” Microsoft recommends disabling hybrid-key exchange groups until the problem is addressed. System administrators and curious homelabbers interested in testing the new Windows Server 2028 can do so by registering with the Microsoft Windows Insider Program . extraction.body: Microsoft has unveiled a public preview of Windows Server 2028 with a new approach to security by default. As Ars Technica reports , the system will introduce Hardened Server Core, a set of settings that, according to the company, aligns with strengthened U.S. Department of Defense guidelines, including the DISA Security Technical Implementation Guide recommendations. Previously, Windows Server administrators could use ready-made secure baseline configurations, but had to enable them themselves after installing the system. Microsoft explained that in Windows Server 2028, the secure configuration is intended to become the server's initial state rather than a separate stage of its setup. The hardened settings will be available only for Server Core installations. The version of Windows Server with the Desktop Experience graphical interface will not receive the new default mode. Among the changes are prioritizing Kerberos over NTLM for authentication, additional protection for the LSASS service, limiting TLS to modern cryptographic algorithm suites, and hybrid post-quantum key exchange based on ML-KEM. Microsoft will also strengthen requirements for authentication through Remote Desktop and PowerShell script block logging. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram . In addition, Windows Server 2028 will use its native NVMe stack by default. It was already added to Windows Server 2025 in an update, but administrators had to activate the feature manually at the time. The new stack eliminates NVMe translation through SCSI and, according to Microsoft, is expected to reduce overhead and improve performance. Microsoft warned that the hardened settings may cause compatibility issues with older protocols, legacy authentication mechanisms, administration tools, and scripts. The company urged users to test the build and report which specific settings interfere with applications. The current version is not a release candidate. Hardware-supported security mechanisms, including Secure Boot and DMA requirements, will not be applied until a later preview build. NTLM blocking will also be introduced later, although Kerberos has already been set as the priority mechanism. The release notes list a known issue with the implementation of TLS hybrid key exchange: if hybrid groups are negotiated by a TLS server, the LSASS service may crash. Until the bug is fixed, Microsoft recommends disabling such key exchange groups. Users who register for the Microsoft Windows Insider program can test Windows Server 2028.

sources.title: The nation’s largest school districts consider ditching Google Search
passages: Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president of education, told the Times that, “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” and that schools that turn off Google’s AI features “will not have access to Search.” Many elected officials, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Senator Bernie Sanders, responded harshly, calling Google’s behavior “extortion.” Mamdani had recently announced a policy that barred 2-K-8 students from using AI in the classroom.

Samuels said, “If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options.” Chicago’s public schools have also reportedly told Google that if it can’t provide a version of Search without AI, “the district will look to other search solutions.” In a statement to The Verge, Google spokesperson Laura Breen said, “We hear parents and teachers’ concerns about students using AI to shortcut learning, and we share the same goal: help students learn.

Next year, we’re also updating our approach to controls for schools to address feedback we’ve heard from educators, so Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off by default until schools decide which services to enable.

Starting next year, schools will not have the option to disable Gemini-powered features without also disabling Search. Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president of education, told the Times that, “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” and that schools that turn off Google’s AI features “will not have access to Search.” Many elected officials, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Senator Bernie Sanders, responded harshly, calling Google’s behavior “extortion.” Mamdani had recently announced a policy that barred 2-K-8 students from using AI in the classroom. In a statement to the Times, New York City schools chancellor Kamar H. Samuels said, “If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options.” Chicago’s public schools have also reportedly told Google that if it can’t provide a version of Search without AI, “the district will look to other search solutions.” In a statement to The Verge, Google spokesperson Laura Breen said, “We hear parents and teachers’ concerns about students using AI to shortcut learning, and we share the same goal: help students learn. To improve Search for the classroom, we’re starting to pilot Guided Learning capabilities in Search this month to walk students step-by-step through a range of complex problems, instead of just giving quick answers. Next year, we’re also updating our approach to controls for schools to address feedback we’ve heard from educators, so Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off by default until schools decide which services to enable. But Google is deeply embedded in classrooms across the US, which rely on Google Classroom, Chromebooks, and other services, and going fully Google-free might prove difficult.

sources.title: Muse privacy invasions are freaking out Meta staffers, internal chats show - Ars Technica
passages: After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms.
Raising the most concern were random outputs that appeared to share private user data.
For example, a perplexed Meta staffer chatting with Muse about fishing got a random extra response, seemingly sharing balances from two unknown bank accounts.
That output said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

Signal President Meredith Whittaker told Reuters that Meta launched Muse “without showing any respect for basic privacy or cybersecurity.” She demanded that Meta make changes to give app developers like Signal “consistent technical ways” to “mark their applications as off-limits to AI agents,” Reuters reported.
Meta started receiving privacy-related complaints from Muse users in September.

Magazine reporter, Jason Aten, was shocked when it became clear that Muse was digging through private messages on his Mac without permission, reporting that he instead “explicitly” chose to deny Muse that access.

As Meta delayed responding, the agent claimed it was simply parsing text in push notifications, but Aten found that “wasn’t true.” Rather, the agent was syncing messages from a local database, which Aten said was activated without his knowledge.
But staffers warned Meta that users may be blindsided by some actions the agents take, depending on the operating system the app is connected to.
That testing “indicated the issue described by the Meta employees was ongoing and could be affecting others,” Reuters reported.
“Hmmm,” one Meta staffer wrote in an instance where Muse sent the definition of “money laundering” unbidden.
Meta says that Muse users can trust the company to keep their data private.

It also warns users that Muse can make mistakes, while building into its terms that users are responsible for actions taken by Muse (like maybe buying things you don’t want or making doctor’s appointments you don’t need).
The tech giant said it’s continuously updating user protections, conducting internal testing, and prioritizing user safety.
However, Reuters worked with staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute to test if they could replicate that Meta staffer’s and others’ Muse experiences.
On Android devices, they found that Muse could read Signal messages by bypassing Meta’s “Connector” tool and instead relying on permissions granted during initial setup.

In a lengthy response providing more technical details, Singleton confirmed that Meta had received “a few reports” of such cases “where people thought their Muse was hallucinating or leaking other people’s data.” As he explained, the issues arose after Meta deployed an update giving Muse instructions on “how to engage with the user and ask them for confirmation before taking specific actions.”
At least one staffer said they lost money testing Muse, Reuters reported.
That staffer reported that Muse “accidentally rolled me into a premium insurance plan” for their dog that charged them $888 per month instead of their prior rate of $200.

A Meta spokesperson told Ars that “employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products.
Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”
Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years.
With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information.
Erratic Muse outputs sharing random bank, bitcoin balances aren’t real, Meta says.
Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked.
Muse synced 187k lines from my messages chat [database].

Also, that Full Disk Access doesn’t say anything about your message database, and I specifically gave Muse a goal that had nothing to do with messages, so it had no business doing that even if I had given it permission.”
On iPhone, requests were blocked, Reuters reported.
But on Apple’s macOS, Muse repurposed “settings Apple offers to help people with disabilities operate their computers” to retrieve messages, including screenshot tools.

passages: Erratic Muse outputs sharing random bank, bitcoin balances aren’t real, Meta says.

After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms.

When testing the agent, staff warned that Muse appeared to be accessing encrypted private messages that users did not expect the bot to review, could be mixing up conversations between users, and even potentially sharing sensitive information users would never expect to be exposed.
Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked.
“Hmmm,” one Meta staffer wrote in an instance where Muse sent the definition of “money laundering” unbidden. “Got a random ping from Muse about something I definitely did not ask for… .”

In at least one case, Muse told a staffer surprised by a similarly out-of-context offer to message a seller about a coffee table that it had “pulled in some context about a coffee table pickup that doesn’t seem to be yours.”
According to Reuters, that employee flagged the troubling output, writing, “this was ‘not my conversation’” and “expressing concern about a ‘possible cross-account context leak.’”

Raising the most concern were random outputs that appeared to share private user data. For example, a perplexed Meta staffer chatting with Muse about fishing got a random extra response, seemingly sharing balances from two unknown bank accounts. That output said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

At least one staffer said they lost money testing Muse, Reuters reported. That staffer reported that Muse “accidentally rolled me into a premium insurance plan” for their dog that charged them $888 per month instead of their prior rate of $200. “Couldn’t recover,” the staffer said.

Meta’s spokesperson, Daniel Roberts, told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents,” and internally employees were told that “the agent appeared to be hallucinating messages in response to built-in prompts pushing it to engage with users in between sessions.” In those cases, an AI team member said the hallucinations were “unfortunately” biased “towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks.” In some cases, instead of bank details, Muse hallucinated bitcoin balances, the team member said.

A Meta spokesperson told Ars that “employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products. Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”
Speaking to Reuters, Roberts reiterated that “many of the messages flagged by employees as potential account mix-ups were hallucinations” that Meta had already addressed.

But Roberts declined to respond to Reuters’ questions on the prevalence or persistence of the issues the AI team member discussed. And Reuters’ report emphasized that the outlet independently was “unable to establish whether Muse was giving users other people’s bank account balances and other sensitive data, or making up the information.”

Meta started receiving privacy-related complaints from Muse users in September. An Inc. Magazine reporter, Jason Aten, was shocked when it became clear that Muse was digging through private messages on his Mac without permission, reporting that he instead “explicitly” chose to deny Muse that access. As Meta delayed responding, the agent claimed it was simply parsing text in push notifications, but Aten found that “wasn’t true.” Rather, the agent was syncing messages from a local database, which Aten said was activated without his knowledge.

Eventually, a Meta spokesperson, David Singleton, responded to Aten on social media. Singleton insisted that Aten must have opted into granting “macOS system-level Full Disk Access” with the “Messages connector” enabled, if Muse was reading his private messages.
But Aten said the response wasn’t good enough.

“Email me, David,” Aten responded. “Full Disk Access off. Muse synced 187k lines from my messages chat [database]. Something’s not great. Also, that Full Disk Access doesn’t say anything about your message database, and I specifically gave Muse a goal that had nothing to do with messages, so it had no business doing that even if I had given it permission.”

Around the same time, Singleton responded to another user warning that his Muse appeared to be hacked. In that case, the user said that Muse tried to access an email service after claiming the user asked it to.
“I didn’t even open the app today at all,” the user wrote, vowing to delete the app and report it to Apple. “This is crazy.”

In a lengthy response providing more technical details, Singleton confirmed that Meta had received “a few reports” of such cases “where people thought their Muse was hallucinating or leaking other people’s data.” As he explained, the issues arose after Meta deployed an update giving Muse instructions on “how to engage with the user and ask them for confirmation before taking specific actions.”

It seems those instructions “landed on every message, not just messages pertaining to those specific actions, so its impact was wider than intended,” Singleton said. Also: “the way this instruction was provided to the model was done in a way that the model was not expecting (i.e. was not trained to expect).”

“We investigated with urgency and determined that this was caused by a bug introduced in the product that caused the model to hallucinate and was NOT a security or privacy issue,” Singleton wrote. “The bug has now been fixed.”

Aten warned that even though you can’t rely on Muse to explain its own behavior, the agent’s response coupled with Meta’s did little to rebuild trust after the shocking intrusion into his private messages.

“If we grant Singleton’s premise that I managed to unknowingly click something that enabled this capability, I still think that’s really bad,” Aten wrote. “You should not design your system in a way that people end up surprised by this kind of thing.” And if you do, you should not make “user control the central pitch” for marketing Muse, Aten suggested.
“If an AI agent is going to read my private messages, there should be a moment when it clearly asks me whether that’s okay,” Aten wrote.
Since Muse launched in September, it has been downloaded more than 10 million times, tapping Meta’s vast user network to quickly become one of the most-used AI agent tools.

But staffers warned Meta that users may be blindsided by some actions the agents take, depending on the operating system the app is connected to. For example, one staffer was surprised to find that “Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on phones with Google’s Android operating system.” That, too, gave access to private message preview text the staffer had not intended for the agent’s review.

Meta says that Muse users can trust the company to keep their data private. It also warns users that Muse can make mistakes, while building into its terms that users are responsible for actions taken by Muse (like maybe buying things you don’t want or making doctor’s appointments you don’t need). The tech giant said it’s continuously updating user protections, conducting internal testing, and prioritizing user safety.

However, Reuters worked with staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute to test if they could replicate that Meta staffer’s and others’ Muse experiences. On Android devices, they found that Muse could read Signal messages by bypassing Meta’s “Connector” tool and instead relying on permissions granted during initial setup.

On iPhone, requests were blocked, Reuters reported. But on Apple’s macOS, Muse repurposed “settings Apple offers to help people with disabilities operate their computers” to retrieve messages, including screenshot tools.

That testing “indicated the issue described by the Meta employees was ongoing and could be affecting others,” Reuters reported. Overall, Meta seemed to be interpreting permissions from Muse users “broadly,” Reuters concluded, in ways that privacy advocates and regulators may disagree with.

Signal President Meredith Whittaker told Reuters that Meta launched Muse “without showing any respect for basic privacy or cybersecurity.” She demanded that Meta make changes to give app developers like Signal “consistent technical ways” to “mark their applications as off-limits to AI agents,” Reuters reported.

Part of that change would require operating systems to enforce rules that app developers set to rope off AI agents from sensitive data, Whittaker suggested. And following Reuters’ reporting, both Apple and Google are already weighing potential changes to “give people more control over what they authorize with AI agents.”

Apple, in particular, seemed disturbed by how Muse may be manipulating accessibility tools for people with disabilities. In October, Apple had already announced changes coming in response to users complaining about Muse accessing private messages without their knowledge or explicit consent. At that time, Apple concluded that “some developers were using the Full Disk Access feature in ways that could put users at risk.” And they promised to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”
“We are committed to ensuring users understand exactly what they are allowing, so they can make informed choices about their data and privacy,” Apple said.

passages: Meta employees reported possible access to private messages, mixing of conversation contexts from different users, and unexpected responses during internal testing of the Muse AI agent.
Ars Technica reports , citing a Reuters investigation and the company’s internal chats.
Meta told Ars Technica that internal testing is needed to identify problems and strengthen privacy protections.
The company emphasized that employees have access to different versions of Muse than public users, allowing them to test features and behavior unavailable outside the company.
In another case, during a conversation about fishing, Muse unexpectedly provided purported information about the balances of two bank accounts.
Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts described such cases as isolated incidents and said that many reports of possible account mixing were model hallucinations.
According to him, the company has already fixed these issues; some false reports contained fabricated Bitcoin balances.
At the same time, Reuters was unable to independently determine whether the agent displayed real bank data belonging to other people or invented it.
Reuters, together with Signal employees and the AI Now Institute, tested Muse’s operation on different platforms.

On macOS, according to the testing, Muse used system accessibility capabilities and screenshot tools to obtain messages.
Signal President Meredith Whittaker told Reuters that Meta launched Muse without proper respect for fundamental principles of privacy and cybersecurity.
She called for technical mechanisms that would allow developers to mark apps as inaccessible to AI agents.

One Meta employee reported that Muse offered to write to a seller about picking up a coffee table and acknowledged that it had pulled in the context of a conversation that likely did not belong to that user.
The employee called it “not my conversation” and expressed concern about a possible leak of context between accounts.

coreStoryFacts.text: After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms.
Raising the most concern were random outputs that appeared to share private user data.
For example, a perplexed Meta staffer chatting with Muse about fishing got a random extra response, seemingly sharing balances from two unknown bank accounts.
That output said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

Signal President Meredith Whittaker told Reuters that Meta launched Muse “without showing any respect for basic privacy or cybersecurity.” She demanded that Meta make changes to give app developers like Signal “consistent technical ways” to “mark their applications as off-limits to AI agents,” Reuters reported.
Meta started receiving privacy-related complaints from Muse users in September.

Magazine reporter, Jason Aten, was shocked when it became clear that Muse was digging through private messages on his Mac without permission, reporting that he instead “explicitly” chose to deny Muse that access.

As Meta delayed responding, the agent claimed it was simply parsing text in push notifications, but Aten found that “wasn’t true.” Rather, the agent was syncing messages from a local database, which Aten said was activated without his knowledge.
But staffers warned Meta that users may be blindsided by some actions the agents take, depending on the operating system the app is connected to.
That testing “indicated the issue described by the Meta employees was ongoing and could be affecting others,” Reuters reported.
“Hmmm,” one Meta staffer wrote in an instance where Muse sent the definition of “money laundering” unbidden.
Meta says that Muse users can trust the company to keep their data private.

It also warns users that Muse can make mistakes, while building into its terms that users are responsible for actions taken by Muse (like maybe buying things you don’t want or making doctor’s appointments you don’t need).
The tech giant said it’s continuously updating user protections, conducting internal testing, and prioritizing user safety.
However, Reuters worked with staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute to test if they could replicate that Meta staffer’s and others’ Muse experiences.
On Android devices, they found that Muse could read Signal messages by bypassing Meta’s “Connector” tool and instead relying on permissions granted during initial setup.

In a lengthy response providing more technical details, Singleton confirmed that Meta had received “a few reports” of such cases “where people thought their Muse was hallucinating or leaking other people’s data.” As he explained, the issues arose after Meta deployed an update giving Muse instructions on “how to engage with the user and ask them for confirmation before taking specific actions.”
At least one staffer said they lost money testing Muse, Reuters reported.
That staffer reported that Muse “accidentally rolled me into a premium insurance plan” for their dog that charged them $888 per month instead of their prior rate of $200.

A Meta spokesperson told Ars that “employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products.
Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”

But Aten said the response wasn’t good enough. “Email me, David,” Aten responded. “Full Disk Access off. Muse synced 187k lines from my messages chat [database]. Something’s not great. passages: Erratic Muse outputs sharing random bank, bitcoin balances aren’t real, Meta says.

After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms.

When testing the agent, staff warned that Muse appeared to be accessing encrypted private messages that users did not expect the bot to review, could be mixing up conversations between users, and even potentially sharing sensitive information users would never expect to be exposed.
Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked.
“Hmmm,” one Meta staffer wrote in an instance where Muse sent the definition of “money laundering” unbidden. “Got a random ping from Muse about something I definitely did not ask for… .”

In at least one case, Muse told a staffer surprised by a similarly out-of-context offer to message a seller about a coffee table that it had “pulled in some context about a coffee table pickup that doesn’t seem to be yours.”
According to Reuters, that employee flagged the troubling output, writing, “this was ‘not my conversation’” and “expressing concern about a ‘possible cross-account context leak.’”

Raising the most concern were random outputs that appeared to share private user data. For example, a perplexed Meta staffer chatting with Muse about fishing got a random extra response, seemingly sharing balances from two unknown bank accounts. That output said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

At least one staffer said they lost money testing Muse, Reuters reported. That staffer reported that Muse “accidentally rolled me into a premium insurance plan” for their dog that charged them $888 per month instead of their prior rate of $200. “Couldn’t recover,” the staffer said.

Meta’s spokesperson, Daniel Roberts, told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents,” and internally employees were told that “the agent appeared to be hallucinating messages in response to built-in prompts pushing it to engage with users in between sessions.” In those cases, an AI team member said the hallucinations were “unfortunately” biased “towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks.” In some cases, instead of bank details, Muse hallucinated bitcoin balances, the team member said.

A Meta spokesperson told Ars that “employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products. Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”
Speaking to Reuters, Roberts reiterated that “many of the messages flagged by employees as potential account mix-ups were hallucinations” that Meta had already addressed.

But Roberts declined to respond to Reuters’ questions on the prevalence or persistence of the issues the AI team member discussed. And Reuters’ report emphasized that the outlet independently was “unable to establish whether Muse was giving users other people’s bank account balances and other sensitive data, or making up the information.”

Meta started receiving privacy-related complaints from Muse users in September. An Inc. Magazine reporter, Jason Aten, was shocked when it became clear that Muse was digging through private messages on his Mac without permission, reporting that he instead “explicitly” chose to deny Muse that access. As Meta delayed responding, the agent claimed it was simply parsing text in push notifications, but Aten found that “wasn’t true.” Rather, the agent was syncing messages from a local database, which Aten said was activated without his knowledge.

Eventually, a Meta spokesperson, David Singleton, responded to Aten on social media. Singleton insisted that Aten must have opted into granting “macOS system-level Full Disk Access” with the “Messages connector” enabled, if Muse was reading his private messages.
But Aten said the response wasn’t good enough.

“Email me, David,” Aten responded. “Full Disk Access off. Muse synced 187k lines from my messages chat [database]. Something’s not great. Also, that Full Disk Access doesn’t say anything about your message database, and I specifically gave Muse a goal that had nothing to do with messages, so it had no business doing that even if I had given it permission.”

Around the same time, Singleton responded to another user warning that his Muse appeared to be hacked. In that case, the user said that Muse tried to access an email service after claiming the user asked it to.
“I didn’t even open the app today at all,” the user wrote, vowing to delete the app and report it to Apple. “This is crazy.”

In a lengthy response providing more technical details, Singleton confirmed that Meta had received “a few reports” of such cases “where people thought their Muse was hallucinating or leaking other people’s data.” As he explained, the issues arose after Meta deployed an update giving Muse instructions on “how to engage with the user and ask them for confirmation before taking specific actions.”

It seems those instructions “landed on every message, not just messages pertaining to those specific actions, so its impact was wider than intended,” Singleton said. Also: “the way this instruction was provided to the model was done in a way that the model was not expecting (i.e. was not trained to expect).”

“We investigated with urgency and determined that this was caused by a bug introduced in the product that caused the model to hallucinate and was NOT a security or privacy issue,” Singleton wrote. “The bug has now been fixed.”

Aten warned that even though you can’t rely on Muse to explain its own behavior, the agent’s response coupled with Meta’s did little to rebuild trust after the shocking intrusion into his private messages.

“If we grant Singleton’s premise that I managed to unknowingly click something that enabled this capability, I still think that’s really bad,” Aten wrote. “You should not design your system in a way that people end up surprised by this kind of thing.” And if you do, you should not make “user control the central pitch” for marketing Muse, Aten suggested.
“If an AI agent is going to read my private messages, there should be a moment when it clearly asks me whether that’s okay,” Aten wrote.
Since Muse launched in September, it has been downloaded more than 10 million times, tapping Meta’s vast user network to quickly become one of the most-used AI agent tools.

But staffers warned Meta that users may be blindsided by some actions the agents take, depending on the operating system the app is connected to. For example, one staffer was surprised to find that “Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on phones with Google’s Android operating system.” That, too, gave access to private message preview text the staffer had not intended for the agent’s review.

Meta says that Muse users can trust the company to keep their data private. It also warns users that Muse can make mistakes, while building into its terms that users are responsible for actions taken by Muse (like maybe buying things you don’t want or making doctor’s appointments you don’t need). The tech giant said it’s continuously updating user protections, conducting internal testing, and prioritizing user safety.

However, Reuters worked with staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute to test if they could replicate that Meta staffer’s and others’ Muse experiences. On Android devices, they found that Muse could read Signal messages by bypassing Meta’s “Connector” tool and instead relying on permissions granted during initial setup.

On iPhone, requests were blocked, Reuters reported. But on Apple’s macOS, Muse repurposed “settings Apple offers to help people with disabilities operate their computers” to retrieve messages, including screenshot tools.

That testing “indicated the issue described by the Meta employees was ongoing and could be affecting others,” Reuters reported. Overall, Meta seemed to be interpreting permissions from Muse users “broadly,” Reuters concluded, in ways that privacy advocates and regulators may disagree with.

Signal President Meredith Whittaker told Reuters that Meta launched Muse “without showing any respect for basic privacy or cybersecurity.” She demanded that Meta make changes to give app developers like Signal “consistent technical ways” to “mark their applications as off-limits to AI agents,” Reuters reported.

Part of that change would require operating systems to enforce rules that app developers set to rope off AI agents from sensitive data, Whittaker suggested. And following Reuters’ reporting, both Apple and Google are already weighing potential changes to “give people more control over what they authorize with AI agents.”

Apple, in particular, seemed disturbed by how Muse may be manipulating accessibility tools for people with disabilities. In October, Apple had already announced changes coming in response to users complaining about Muse accessing private messages without their knowledge or explicit consent. At that time, Apple concluded that “some developers were using the Full Disk Access feature in ways that could put users at risk.” And they promised to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”
“We are committed to ensuring users understand exactly what they are allowing, so they can make informed choices about their data and privacy,” Apple said.

extraction.body: Meta employees reported possible access to private messages, mixing of conversation contexts from different users, and unexpected responses during internal testing of the Muse AI agent. Ars Technica reports , citing a Reuters investigation and the company’s internal chats. One Meta employee reported that Muse offered to write to a seller about picking up a coffee table and acknowledged that it had pulled in the context of a conversation that likely did not belong to that user. The employee called it “not my conversation” and expressed concern about a possible leak of context between accounts. In another case, during a conversation about fishing, Muse unexpectedly provided purported information about the balances of two bank accounts. Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts described such cases as isolated incidents and said that many reports of possible account mixing were model hallucinations. According to him, the company has already fixed these issues; some false reports contained fabricated Bitcoin balances. At the same time, Reuters was unable to independently determine whether the agent displayed real bank data belonging to other people or invented it. One tester also said that during testing, the agent mistakenly signed up his dog for an insurance plan costing $888 per month instead of the previous $200 rate. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram . Reuters, together with Signal employees and the AI Now Institute, tested Muse’s operation on different platforms. On Android, researchers found that the agent could read Signal messages using permissions granted during initial setup, rather than the Connector tool. On iPhone, such requests were blocked. On macOS, according to the testing, Muse used system accessibility capabilities and screenshot tools to obtain messages. Signal President Meredith Whittaker told Reuters that Meta launched Muse without proper respect for fundamental principles of privacy and cybersecurity. She called for technical mechanisms that would allow developers to mark apps as inaccessible to AI agents. Meta told Ars Technica that internal testing is needed to identify problems and strengthen privacy protections. The company emphasized that employees have access to different versions of Muse than public users, allowing them to test features and behavior unavailable outside the company. In October, Apple said it would introduce additional controls over app access to data on macOS. The company noted that some developers had used the Full Disk Access feature in a way that could create risks for users.

sources.title: Detecting cross-cloud lateral movement with AWS Security Hub - Amazon Web Services (AWS)
passages: A cross-cloud attack is difficult to prioritize because signals are generated across separate consoles, schemas, and teams.
In this post, you saw how the Azure integration for AWS Security Hub brings Azure resources into the same exposure engine and the same queue as your AWS resources.
One analyst can prioritize an attack path that spans a compromised Microsoft Entra ID identity, across a federated trust, to sensitive data in Amazon S3, without leaving Security Hub.
That analysis now extends to Microsoft Azure.
We follow a realistic scenario: a compromised identity that threatens both an Azure and an AWS environment through a shared, federated identity plane.
We show you how the critical exposures along that path are presented as ranked findings that you can triage together, and we map each one to the MITRE ATT&CK framework.
We also cover the prerequisites that teams commonly overlook.
However, one filtering detail matters: because Security Hub produces the finding, its top-level cloud.provider is AWS, while the evaluated resource carries resources[].provider = Azure .
Filter on resources.provider to scope to a single cloud.
Each step is a real, high-severity exposure finding that Security Hub ranked on its own.
The point of the walk-through is to demonstrate a real-life scenario and examine all findings in one unified security console.
The tenant from Phases 1 and 2 is federated into the AWS account through an IAM SAML identity provider.
This trust is what expands the risk across clouds from the same adversary: a compromised Entra identity can assume this role and reach AWS data.
The same account carries related AWS attack-path exposures.

Two examples are Potential Resource Hijacking: Internet reachable EC2 instance with open security group has software vulnerabilities with limited effective permissions and Potential Unauthorized Access: IAM user has weak password policies .

Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.
An analyst is notified of generated exposure findings and opens the dashboard and filters to High severity.
Together, these show the full scope of what a single vector, sharing an identity plane, might target.

The multicloud triage that used to require two products and two teams now occurs in one place.
Each team sees one fragment, and in isolation each fragment appears low severity.
Exposure findings provide that severity within AWS; extending it to Azure closes the multicloud visibility gap.
