Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels. Most organizations run a multicloud estate, and so do the attackers targeting them. An adversary who compromises an identity in one provider follows that identity wherever it leads, including across a federated trust into a second cloud service provider. The signals enumerating this scenario are rarely missing; the problem is that they live in separate consoles, in different schemas, owned by different teams. No one has visibility into the whole picture, so no one can decide what to fix first. AWS Security Hub addresses prioritization and triage with exposure findings. Security Hub correlates reachability, blast radius, vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and effective permissions, providing a strong correlation layer with an attack-path visualization, providing the context needed to generate risks from findings. That analysis now extends to Microsoft Azure. Security Hub records and analyzes your Azure resources with the same correlation engine used for Amazon Web Services (AWS) resources. The resulting details and meta-data land in the same console, ranked in the same queue, providing holistic, multicloud visibility into your security risks. In this blog post, you learn how to configure the Azure integration for Security Hub and use exposure findings to prioritize attack paths across both clouds from one console. We follow a realistic scenario: a compromised identity that threatens both an Azure and an AWS environment through a shared, federated identity plane. We show you how the critical exposures along that path are presented as ranked findings that you can triage together, and we map each one to the MITRE ATT&CK framework. We also cover the prerequisites that teams commonly overlook. Each team sees one fragment, and in isolation each fragment appears low severity. You see the risk only when you correlate all of it together and discover the same identity plane ties the attack path together. Exposure findings provide that severity within AWS; extending it to Azure closes the multicloud visibility gap. You create the Azure connector in the AWS Management Console for Security Hub. It authenticates to your Entra ID tenant through an application registration, records and evaluates your Azure resource configurations, and streams Microsoft Defender for Cloud alerts and Entra ID audit logs through an Azure Event Hubs namespace. Your Azure resources then flow into the same correlation engine that analyzes signals from AWS Security Hub Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) , Amazon Inspector , Amazon Macie , and Amazon GuardDuty . That engine produces two kinds of findings: Both use the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF) and appear in the same console as your AWS findings. However, one filtering detail matters: because Security Hub produces the finding, its top-level cloud.provider is AWS, while the evaluated resource carries resources[].provider = Azure . Filter on resources.provider to scope to a single cloud. The following steps detail how to connect your Azure environment to Security Hub v2: Registering the Azure application, establishing federated identity credentials, and assigning the roles required for AWS to evaluate your Azure resources. The first step in this configuration is to create the Azure connector in Security Hub. The connector establishes trust with your Azure tenant and defines which subscriptions and regions Security Hub v2 will evaluate. Include the global region scope. Controls that evaluate Entra ID and Microsoft Graph resources require it, and those identity exposures are central to this scenario. If you also create an Amazon Inspector or Security Hub CSPM connector for the same tenant, keep its subscriptions and regions consistent with this one. Health status alone doesn’t tell you whether recording is flowing. Confirm both. AWS CLI command 2: Retrieve exposure findings for Azure resources To add vulnerability findings for Azure virtual machines (VMs), function apps, or container registry images, create an Amazon Inspector connector for the same tenant. VM scanning requires each target VM to have a system-assigned managed identity, which you can enforce with an Azure Policy. Figure 1 shows a correctly configured Azure integration inside Security Hub, with vulnerability management and posture management deployed. Figure 1: Successful configuration of the Azure integration with Security Hub See the AWS documentation for the prerequisites for Microsoft Azure . In this example, the organization has one identity plane across two clouds, comprising a Microsoft Entra ID tenant with a federated trust into an AWS account. An adversary who compromises the right Entra identity gains an initial foothold in Azure and a path into AWS, because both clouds trust the same identity plane. The following sections trace that path. Each step is a real, high-severity exposure finding that Security Hub ranked on its own. The point of the walk-through is to demonstrate a real-life scenario and examine all findings in one unified security console. ATT&CK: Phishing (T1566), Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts (T1078.004) The path begins with an Entra identity that is both over-privileged and unprotected. You’ll find this in the Security Hub console under Exposures , where Security Hub raises it as an identity exposure finding and maps the attack path stemming from it: Potential Unauthorized Access: Azure RBAC user with administrative access has MFA disabled (high). It correlates the user, the role assignment that grants administrative access, and the organization. The tenant’s authorization policies let an attacker broaden that foothold, and Security Hub CSPM reports each policy as a failed control (high): Microsoft Entra ID authorization policies should prohibit default users from registering applications…should restrict user consent for applications , and Azure authorization policies should restrict guest invitations to admin roles only . Each finding expands what a single compromised, non-privileged identity can do without an administrator. ATT&CK: Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190), Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts (T1078.004) The tenant contains an internet-reachable VM whose network security group allows inbound from any address, and whose attached identity holds administrative rights over the subscription. Security Hub surfaces this under Exposures , correlating reachability and effective permissions into one finding that shows why it matters: anyone reaching the VM inherits admin control of the subscription.: Potential Initial Access: Potentially internet reachable Azure virtual machine with open network security group has administrative access (high). It correlates the VM, the role assignment, the network security group, and the public IP address. The finding’s analysis reads like an attack path. The resource “may be reachable from the public internet,” “overly permissive network security group (NSG) rules allow unintended inbound access,” and “the Owner or Contributor role grants extensive permissions… enabling a threat actor to escalate privileges.” Security Hub evaluates this from configuration and network-path modeling, so it surfaces whether or not the VM is running. Figure 2 shows the correlated attack path for that virtual machine. The tenant from Phases 1 and 2 is federated into the AWS account through an IAM SAML identity provider. As shown in Figure 2, a role trusts that provider and grants read access to every bucket in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) . This trust is what expands the risk across clouds from the same adversary: a compromised Entra identity can assume this role and reach AWS data. This one hop lives in IAM rather than in Security Hub. Security Hub doesn’t not raise a finding for a role that trusts your own federated identity provider. Confirming it is a normal investigative pivot: the role trusts a SAML identity provider that represents your Entra tenant, the same tenant whose exposures you triaged when you added Amazon Inspector in Step 4. Figure 3: The federated trust that links the two clouds through a shared identity plane Potential Sensitive Data Destruction: S3 bucket has sensitive data and versioning disabled and Object Lock disabled and MFA delete disabled (high). A Macie finding, The S3 object contains personal information , is a contributing signal, and the control S3 general purpose buckets should be encrypted at rest with AWS KMS keys fails alongside it. The same account carries related AWS attack-path exposures. Two examples are Potential Resource Hijacking: Internet reachable EC2 instance with open security group has software vulnerabilities with limited effective permissions and Potential Unauthorized Access: IAM user has weak password policies . In the exposure queue, these sit next to the Azure findings, ranked by the same severity model. Here is the operational benefit. An analyst is notified of generated exposure findings and opens the dashboard and filters to High severity. In one prioritized list, without switching tools or opening a ticket for another team, they see the Azure admin identity without MFA, the internet-reachable Azure VM with subscription-admin rights, and the AWS sensitive data exposure. Together, these show the full scope of what a single vector, sharing an identity plane, might target. The analyst confirms the connecting federation with one pivot into IAM. The multicloud triage that used to require two products and two teams now occurs in one place. Figure 4 shows that single ranked queue. The following table traces each phase of the attack path to its MITRE ATT&CK techniques, the cloud where it plays out, and the ranked Security Hub exposure that surfaces it — following the pivot from Azure into AWS across the shared identity plane. passages: Cortex XDR and Prisma Cloud provide protection from the lateral movement techniques discussed here.
If you think you might have been impacted or have an urgent matter, get in touch with the Unit 42 Incident Response team.
Let's examine lateral movement technique 2, where an attacker abused the EC2 Instance Connect service to access EC2 instances.

The agentless solution provides insights into the attacker's access methods by offering visibility into all executed cloud-level API calls, including actions such as security group modification and SSH key injection.
Employing both agent and agentless solutions is an effective way to detect the hybrid tactics of attackers who combine traditional and cloud-based techniques for lateral movement.
Lateral movement can be achieved by leveraging both cloud APIs and access to compute instances, with access at the cloud level potentially extending to the latter.
However, cloud APIs do still provide additional mechanisms that attackers could abuse, and misconfigurations can open up further opportunities for malicious behavior.
In cloud services, APIs play a pivotal role in communication, as well as in facilitating lateral movement.
This visibility proved crucial in understanding how the attacker performed lateral movement and pivoted to other environments.
Defenders should be aware of the options available to improve their cloud security posture.

extraction.body: In this post, we examine lateral movement techniques, showcasing some that we have observed in the wild within cloud environments. Lateral movement can be achieved by leveraging both cloud APIs and access to compute instances, with access at the cloud level potentially extending to the latter. We explore cloud lateral movement techniques in all three major cloud providers: Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google Cloud Platform (GCP) and Microsoft Azure, highlighting their differences compared to similar techniques in on-premises environments. Attackers often use different lateral movement techniques to gain access to sensitive data within an organization's network. Lateral movement techniques can certainly be part of attackers’ approach to on-premises environments, and many of the scenarios we discuss could have similarities to situations on-premises. Here, we focus on lateral movement techniques as we specifically observe them used in cloud environments, with the aim of helping defenders better prepare to improve their cloud security posture. In cloud environments, attackers operate at two levels: the host or instance, and the cloud infrastructure. This approach allows them to seamlessly combine traditional lateral movement techniques with cloud-specific methods. Cloud providers offer measures like network segmentation and granular IAM management to limit lateral movement, along with centralized logging to detect this movement. However, cloud APIs do still provide additional mechanisms that attackers could abuse, and misconfigurations can open up further opportunities for malicious behavior. This article will show how both agent and agentless solutions come together to protect against lateral movement, with each contributing unique strengths. This can help defenders understand why combining both solutions ensures comprehensive coverage in the cloud. Cortex XDR and Prisma Cloud provide protection from the lateral movement techniques discussed here. If you think you might have been impacted or have an urgent matter, get in touch with the Unit 42 Incident Response team. Exploring lateral movement in the cloud versus on-premises reveals a marked difference. Each environment has its challenges for defenders. In cloud environments, overly permissive access policies and misconfigured resources can expand opportunities for threat actors to abuse cloud features. These opportunities introduce a different set of lateral movement techniques. When combined with powerful API access within the cloud, this could potentially result in gaining access to compute instances running within the environment. In cloud services, APIs play a pivotal role in communication, as well as in facilitating lateral movement. When attackers are equipped with the right cloud permissions, which are typically write access, they can directly interact with cloud services by executing API calls. In such cases, the barrier between access within the cloud and access to compute instances may not be particularly strong, which enables attackers to create or modify cloud resources, effectively streamlining lateral movement. The scalability of cloud environments – allowing on-demand resource provisioning – simplifies this process, as attackers can effortlessly create new compute instances to expand their operations and take control over existing ones. In one case, an attacker gained access to a cloud environment and attempted to pivot between Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) instances. The attacker first attempted to access an EC2 instance using traditional lateral movement techniques, such as exploiting default open ports and abusing existing SSH keys. When these methods proved unsuccessful, the attacker then shifted to use cloud-specific lateral movement techniques. Because the attacker was equipped with relatively powerful IAM credentials, they were able to take another approach to gain access to data within the instance. This approach would not give access to the runtime environment present on the target instance (including data in memory and data available in the instance's cloud metadata service, such as IAM credentials). However, it would allow access to the data stored on the disk of the target instance. In a different scenario, an attacker with compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials used the AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress API to add an inbound SSH rule to security groups. As a result, instances that were previously protected from internet access by the security group became reachable, including from attacker-controlled IP addresses. Modifying the security groups rules allowed classic network lateral movement, showcasing the simplicity of configuring network resources in the cloud compared to on-premises environments. Following this, the powerful IAM permissions the attacker gained allowed them to use the EC2 Instance Connect service (which manages SSH keys on a machine). They were able to temporarily push a public SSH key by using the SendSSHPublicKey API as shown in Figure 3. This allowed the attacker to connect to an EC2 instance, granting them access to the instance’s data. This serves as an example of how cloud providers have their own mechanisms for accessing compute instances alongside the operating system’s native authentication and authorization technologies. However, there are typically connections between the two. Within the EC2 instance, the attacker discovered additional cleartext credentials saved to disk, notably a private SSH key and AWS access tokens. With these access credentials, the attacker pivoted to additional EC2 instances. Using SSH and cloud tokens for lateral movement demonstrates the combination of both traditional and cloud lateral movement techniques employed by the attacker. Eventually, utilizing these credentials led to the attacker pivoting to other development environments. Figure 4 provides a flow chart for this chain of events. The equivalent lateral movement technique also exists in GCP due to misconfiguration. Compute Engine instances can be configured to store their SSH keys in the instance metadata, as long as the OS Login service is not used. Regardless of the authentication and authorization technologies typically used for managed compute instances, defenders should assume that these are not strong barriers. Attackers with powerful cloud credentials could still gain access to compute instances within the cloud environment. Detecting the activities in this article requires correlating data from both agent and agentless solutions that provide a comprehensive view into cloud environments. Attackers who are able to access hosts often have sufficient privileges to disable local security controls and security agents running on the host. Thus, it is important to be alert to when relevant log streams from hosts stop as a possible indicator of compromise. Let's examine lateral movement technique 2, where an attacker abused the EC2 Instance Connect service to access EC2 instances. The agentless solution provides insights into the attacker's access methods by offering visibility into all executed cloud-level API calls, including actions such as security group modification and SSH key injection. An alert for this in an AWS panel is shown below in Figure 15. The Prisma Cloud Resource Query Language (RQL) query shown below in Figure 16 could also be used to identify suspicious SSH operations taken by a malicious actor. Simultaneously, if a Cortex XDR agent is installed on an EC2 instance that offers host-level visibility, it reveals the attacker's efforts to search for credentials and sensitive files. This visibility proved crucial in understanding how the attacker performed lateral movement and pivoted to other environments. It is more effective to secure cloud environments with both agent and agentless solutions. Agents are great for having full visibility and control over specific instances, with the caveat that agents can often be disabled by attackers. On the other hand, agentless solutions provide cloud-level visibility. Moreover, properly configured cloud logging environments cannot easily be modified or disabled by attackers, providing a critical backstop for defenders. Combining both solutions provides the best of both worlds in terms of securing cloud environments. Attackers with sufficient privileges at the cloud API level can take advantage of the characteristics of cloud environments for lateral movement using cloud APIs. Cloud APIs often enable attackers to pivot through compute instances with relative ease compared to traditional lateral movement in typical on-premises environments. However, on-premises environments, especially virtualized environments with the equivalent power available to an attacker with access to the virtualization layer, have plenty of risks of this type as well. For some of the scenarios described, there may be detections and remediations available from CSPs or other sources. Defenders should be aware of the options available to improve their cloud security posture. Since misconfigurations and similar issues can often weaken organizations’ cloud security, defenders should pay particular attention to using best practices recommended by your CSP, and also to ensuring that your configuration matches your security needs. Employing both agent and agentless solutions is an effective way to detect the hybrid tactics of attackers who combine traditional and cloud-based techniques for lateral movement. The cloud lateral movement techniques illustrated in this article highlight the importance of having a comprehensive security approach to effectively address the challenges inherent in cloud environments. coreStoryFacts.text: A cross-cloud attack is difficult to prioritize because signals are generated across separate consoles, schemas, and teams.
In this post, you saw how the Azure integration for AWS Security Hub brings Azure resources into the same exposure engine and the same queue as your AWS resources.
One analyst can prioritize an attack path that spans a compromised Microsoft Entra ID identity, across a federated trust, to sensitive data in Amazon S3, without leaving Security Hub.
That analysis now extends to Microsoft Azure.
We follow a realistic scenario: a compromised identity that threatens both an Azure and an AWS environment through a shared, federated identity plane.
We show you how the critical exposures along that path are presented as ranked findings that you can triage together, and we map each one to the MITRE ATT&CK framework.
We also cover the prerequisites that teams commonly overlook.
However, one filtering detail matters: because Security Hub produces the finding, its top-level cloud.provider is AWS, while the evaluated resource carries resources[].provider = Azure .
Filter on resources.provider to scope to a single cloud.
Each step is a real, high-severity exposure finding that Security Hub ranked on its own.
The point of the walk-through is to demonstrate a real-life scenario and examine all findings in one unified security console.
The tenant from Phases 1 and 2 is federated into the AWS account through an IAM SAML identity provider.
This trust is what expands the risk across clouds from the same adversary: a compromised Entra identity can assume this role and reach AWS data.
The same account carries related AWS attack-path exposures.

Two examples are Potential Resource Hijacking: Internet reachable EC2 instance with open security group has software vulnerabilities with limited effective permissions and Potential Unauthorized Access: IAM user has weak password policies .
From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs.
Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.
An analyst is notified of generated exposure findings and opens the dashboard and filters to High severity.
Together, these show the full scope of what a single vector, sharing an identity plane, might target.
The analyst confirms the connecting federation with one pivot into IAM.
The multicloud triage that used to require two products and two teams now occurs in one place.
Cortex XDR and Prisma Cloud provide protection from the lateral movement techniques discussed here.
If you think you might have been impacted or have an urgent matter, get in touch with the Unit 42 Incident Response team.

extraction.body: In this post, we examine lateral movement techniques, showcasing some that we have observed in the wild within cloud environments. Lateral movement can be achieved by leveraging both cloud APIs and access to compute instances, with access at the cloud level potentially extending to the latter. We explore cloud lateral movement techniques in all three major cloud providers: Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google Cloud Platform (GCP) and Microsoft Azure, highlighting their differences compared to similar techniques in on-premises environments. Attackers often use different lateral movement techniques to gain access to sensitive data within an organization's network. Lateral movement techniques can certainly be part of attackers’ approach to on-premises environments, and many of the scenarios we discuss could have similarities to situations on-premises. Here, we focus on lateral movement techniques as we specifically observe them used in cloud environments, with the aim of helping defenders better prepare to improve their cloud security posture. In cloud environments, attackers operate at two levels: the host or instance, and the cloud infrastructure. This approach allows them to seamlessly combine traditional lateral movement techniques with cloud-specific methods. Cloud providers offer measures like network segmentation and granular IAM management to limit lateral movement, along with centralized logging to detect this movement. However, cloud APIs do still provide additional mechanisms that attackers could abuse, and misconfigurations can open up further opportunities for malicious behavior. This article will show how both agent and agentless solutions come together to protect against lateral movement, with each contributing unique strengths. This can help defenders understand why combining both solutions ensures comprehensive coverage in the cloud. Cortex XDR and Prisma Cloud provide protection from the lateral movement techniques discussed here. If you think you might have been impacted or have an urgent matter, get in touch with the Unit 42 Incident Response team. Exploring lateral movement in the cloud versus on-premises reveals a marked difference. Each environment has its challenges for defenders. In cloud environments, overly permissive access policies and misconfigured resources can expand opportunities for threat actors to abuse cloud features. These opportunities introduce a different set of lateral movement techniques. When combined with powerful API access within the cloud, this could potentially result in gaining access to compute instances running within the environment. In cloud services, APIs play a pivotal role in communication, as well as in facilitating lateral movement. When attackers are equipped with the right cloud permissions, which are typically write access, they can directly interact with cloud services by executing API calls. In such cases, the barrier between access within the cloud and access to compute instances may not be particularly strong, which enables attackers to create or modify cloud resources, effectively streamlining lateral movement. The scalability of cloud environments – allowing on-demand resource provisioning – simplifies this process, as attackers can effortlessly create new compute instances to expand their operations and take control over existing ones. In one case, an attacker gained access to a cloud environment and attempted to pivot between Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) instances. The attacker first attempted to access an EC2 instance using traditional lateral movement techniques, such as exploiting default open ports and abusing existing SSH keys. When these methods proved unsuccessful, the attacker then shifted to use cloud-specific lateral movement techniques. Because the attacker was equipped with relatively powerful IAM credentials, they were able to take another approach to gain access to data within the instance. This approach would not give access to the runtime environment present on the target instance (including data in memory and data available in the instance's cloud metadata service, such as IAM credentials). However, it would allow access to the data stored on the disk of the target instance. In a different scenario, an attacker with compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials used the AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress API to add an inbound SSH rule to security groups. As a result, instances that were previously protected from internet access by the security group became reachable, including from attacker-controlled IP addresses. Modifying the security groups rules allowed classic network lateral movement, showcasing the simplicity of configuring network resources in the cloud compared to on-premises environments. Following this, the powerful IAM permissions the attacker gained allowed them to use the EC2 Instance Connect service (which manages SSH keys on a machine). They were able to temporarily push a public SSH key by using the SendSSHPublicKey API as shown in Figure 3. This allowed the attacker to connect to an EC2 instance, granting them access to the instance’s data. This serves as an example of how cloud providers have their own mechanisms for accessing compute instances alongside the operating system’s native authentication and authorization technologies. However, there are typically connections between the two. Within the EC2 instance, the attacker discovered additional cleartext credentials saved to disk, notably a private SSH key and AWS access tokens. With these access credentials, the attacker pivoted to additional EC2 instances. Using SSH and cloud tokens for lateral movement demonstrates the combination of both traditional and cloud lateral movement techniques employed by the attacker. Eventually, utilizing these credentials led to the attacker pivoting to other development environments. Figure 4 provides a flow chart for this chain of events. The equivalent lateral movement technique also exists in GCP due to misconfiguration. Compute Engine instances can be configured to store their SSH keys in the instance metadata, as long as the OS Login service is not used. Regardless of the authentication and authorization technologies typically used for managed compute instances, defenders should assume that these are not strong barriers. Attackers with powerful cloud credentials could still gain access to compute instances within the cloud environment. Detecting the activities in this article requires correlating data from both agent and agentless solutions that provide a comprehensive view into cloud environments. Attackers who are able to access hosts often have sufficient privileges to disable local security controls and security agents running on the host. Thus, it is important to be alert to when relevant log streams from hosts stop as a possible indicator of compromise. Let's examine lateral movement technique 2, where an attacker abused the EC2 Instance Connect service to access EC2 instances. The agentless solution provides insights into the attacker's access methods by offering visibility into all executed cloud-level API calls, including actions such as security group modification and SSH key injection. A smart lighting technology has been developed that changes how objects appear in color by adjusting only the light shining on them, without repainting the objects or modifying their surfaces. The technology can change the perceived color of specific objects while maintaining natural white illumination in the surrounding space. Visitors will be able to see how the same object appears in different colors at an exhibition to be held at the National Science Museum in November. The color of an object as perceived by the human eye depends on the light illuminating it. Even the same object can appear to have a different color when the incident light changes, as the light reflected from the object and reaching the eye also changes. Based on this principle, the technology makes objects appear in desired colors simply by adjusting the combination of light emitted from the lighting system, without attaching additional devices to the objects or modifying their surfaces. Conventional lighting systems often change the overall color appearance of a space when the color of the illumination is adjusted. Dr. Jeon addressed this limitation by precisely controlling the brightness of multiple LEDs. This approach maintains natural white illumination in the surrounding space while changing the light reflected from a specific object, making only that object's perceived color appear different. To evaluate the technology's performance, Dr. Jeon developed a lighting system using several types of LEDs along with a measurement system. Color-changing experiments were conducted using color cards and Morpho butterflies, which exhibit vivid structural colors. The experiments confirmed that the same object could appear in different colors depending on the combination of illuminating light. In the final system validation, the researchers observed color changes with a CIEDE2000 color difference (ΔE₀₀) value exceeding 90. ΔE₀₀ (CIEDE2000 color difference): A numerical measure of how differently two colors are perceived by the human eye. Higher values indicate greater color differences (ΔE₀₀ ≤ 1: imperceptible color difference; ΔE₀₀ ≥ 10: very noticeable color difference) The developed technology could be applied to exhibitions, interior design, product design, and artworks by creating various color effects simply through lighting changes, without altering the products or exhibits themselves. Its key advantage is the ability to change the perceived colors of objects to suit different spaces and purposes without repainting or replacing them. Dr. Jeon has also collaborated with artist Geunho Park, who works under the name “Chamsae,” to create an artwork titled “Changing Colors with Light” using the newly developed technology. Lighting has evolved from simply illuminating objects to changing their perceived colors. A smart lighting technology has been developed that changes how objects appear in color by adjusting only the light shining on them, without repainting the objects or modifying their surfaces. The technology can change the perceived color of specific objects while maintaining natural white illumination in the surrounding space. Visitors will be able to see how the same object appears in different colors at an exhibition to be held at the National Science Museum in November.

The color of an object as perceived by the human eye depends on the light illuminating it. Even the same object can appear to have a different color when the incident light changes, as the light reflected from the object and reaching the eye also changes. Based on this principle, the technology makes objects appear in desired colors simply by adjusting the combination of light emitted from the lighting system, without attaching additional devices to the objects or modifying their surfaces.

Conventional lighting systems often change the overall color appearance of a space when the color of the illumination is adjusted. Dr. Jeon addressed this limitation by precisely controlling the brightness of multiple LEDs. This approach maintains natural white illumination in the surrounding space while changing the light reflected from a specific object, making only that object's perceived color appear different.

To evaluate the technology's performance, Dr. Jeon developed a lighting system using several types of LEDs along with a measurement system. Color-changing experiments were conducted using color cards and Morpho butterflies, which exhibit vivid structural colors. The experiments confirmed that the same object could appear in different colors depending on the combination of illuminating light. In the final system validation, the researchers observed color changes with a CIEDE2000 color difference (ΔE₀₀) value exceeding 90.

ΔE₀₀ (CIEDE2000 color difference): A numerical measure of how differently two colors are perceived by the human eye. Higher values indicate greater color differences (ΔE₀₀ ≤ 1: imperceptible color difference; ΔE₀₀ ≥ 10: very noticeable color difference)

The developed technology could be applied to exhibitions, interior design, product design, and artworks by creating various color effects simply through lighting changes, without altering the products or exhibits themselves. Its key advantage is the ability to change the perceived colors of objects to suit different spaces and purposes without repainting or replacing them.

Dr. Jeon has also collaborated with artist Geunho Park, who works under the name “Chamsae,” to create an artwork titled “Changing Colors with Light” using the newly developed technology. The artwork will be exhibited at “2026 Artience Daejeon,” held at the Future Technology Hall of the National Science Museum from November 17 to 28, 2026. Visitors will be able to directly observe how the same object appears in different colors depending on the illuminating light.

Dr. Suwan Jeon, Senior Researcher at the Department of Nano Display Research at KIMM, emphasized, “The most distinctive feature of this technology is that it can change the perceived color of an object simply by adjusting the light shining on it, without changing the object itself.” He added, “We expect this technology to open up new possibilities for color expression using light in exhibitions, spatial design, product presentation, and the arts.”

This research was conducted under three KIMM research projects: “Demonstration Research on KIMM Advanced Technologies Based on DX/AI Technologies,” “Development of Freely Controllable Spectral Technology for Customized Spatial Colorization” under the Young Researcher Support Program, and “Design and Manufacturing Technology of Purpose-Oriented Metastructures for Carbon Neutrality.”

The Korea Institute of Machinery and Materials (KIMM) is a non-profit government-funded research institute under the Ministry of Science and ICT. Since its foundation in 1976, KIMM is contributing to economic growth of the nation by performing R&D on key technologies in machinery and materials, conducting reliability test evaluation, and commercializing the developed products and technologies.

Lighting has evolved from simply illuminating objects to changing their perceived colors. A smart lighting technology has been developed that changes how objects appear in color by adjusting only the light shining on them, without repainting the objects or modifying their surfaces. The technology can change the perceived color of specific objects while maintaining natural white illumination in the surrounding space. Visitors will be able to see how the same object appears in different colors at an exhibition to be held at the National Science Museum in November.

The color of an object as perceived by the human eye depends on the light illuminating it. Even the same object can appear to have a different color when the incident light changes, as the light reflected from the object and reaching the eye also changes. Based on this principle, the technology makes objects appear in desired colors simply by adjusting the combination of light emitted from the lighting system, without attaching additional devices to the objects or modifying their surfaces.

Conventional lighting systems often change the overall color appearance of a space when the color of the illumination is adjusted. Dr. Jeon addressed this limitation by precisely controlling the brightness of multiple LEDs. This approach maintains natural white illumination in the surrounding space while changing the light reflected from a specific object, making only that object's perceived color appear different.

To evaluate the technology's performance, Dr. Jeon developed a lighting system using several types of LEDs along with a measurement system. Color-changing experiments were conducted using color cards and Morpho butterflies, which exhibit vivid structural colors. The experiments confirmed that the same object could appear in different colors depending on the combination of illuminating light. In the final system validation, the researchers observed color changes with a CIEDE2000 color difference (ΔE₀₀) value exceeding 90.

ΔE₀₀ (CIEDE2000 color difference): A numerical measure of how differently two colors are perceived by the human eye. Higher values indicate greater color differences (ΔE₀₀ ≤ 1: imperceptible color difference; ΔE₀₀ ≥ 10: very noticeable color difference)

The developed technology could be applied to exhibitions, interior design, product design, and artworks by creating various color effects simply through lighting changes, without altering the products or exhibits themselves. Its key advantage is the ability to change the perceived colors of objects to suit different spaces and purposes without repainting or replacing them.

Dr. Jeon has also collaborated with artist Geunho Park, who works under the name “Chamsae,” to create an artwork titled “Changing Colors with Light” using the newly developed technology. The artwork will be exhibited at “2026 Artience Daejeon,” held at the Future Technology Hall of the National Science Museum from November 17 to 28, 2026. Visitors will be able to directly observe how the same object appears in different colors depending on the illuminating light.

Dr. Suwan Jeon, Senior Researcher at the Department of Nano Display Research at KIMM, emphasized, “The most distinctive feature of this technology is that it can change the perceived color of an object simply by adjusting the light shining on it, without changing the object itself.” He added, “We expect this technology to open up new possibilities for color expression using light in exhibitions, spatial design, product presentation, and the arts.”

This research was conducted under three KIMM research projects: “Demonstration Research on KIMM Advanced Technologies Based on DX/AI Technologies,” “Development of Freely Controllable Spectral Technology for Customized Spatial Colorization” under the Young Researcher Support Program, and “Design and Manufacturing Technology of Purpose-Oriented Metastructures for Carbon Neutrality.”

Visitors will be able to see how the same object appears in different colors at an exhibition to be held at the National Science Museum in Daejeon, South Korea, in November.

Dr. Suwan Jeon, senior researcher at the Department of Nano Display Research of the Nano Convergence Research Division at the Korea Institute of Machinery and Materials, has developed a smart lighting technology for remote color control that changes the perceived color of objects by precisely adjusting light at multiple wavelengths. Jeon established the principles of color control, developed an LED lighting system based on these principles and experimentally verified the resulting color changes.

The color of an object as perceived by the human eye depends on the light illuminating it. Even the same object can appear to have a different color when the incident light changes, as the light reflected from the object and reaching the eye also changes. Based on this principle, the technology makes objects appear in desired colors simply by adjusting the combination of light emitted from the lighting system, without attaching additional devices to the objects or modifying their surfaces.

Conventional lighting systems often change the overall color appearance of a space when the color of the illumination is adjusted. Jeon addressed this limitation by precisely controlling the brightness of multiple LEDs. This approach maintains natural white illumination in the surrounding space while changing the light reflected from a specific object, making only that object's perceived color appear different.

To evaluate the technology's performance, Jeon developed a lighting system using several types of LEDs along with a measurement system. Color-changing experiments were conducted using color cards and Morpho butterflies, which exhibit vivid structural colors. The experiments confirmed that the same object could appear in different colors depending on the combination of illuminating light. In the final system validation, the researchers observed color changes with a CIEDE2000 color difference (ΔE₀₀) value exceeding 90.

The developed technology could be applied to exhibitions, interior design, product design and artworks by creating various color effects simply through lighting changes, without altering the products or exhibits themselves. Its key advantage is the ability to change the perceived colors of objects to suit different spaces and purposes without repainting or replacing them.

Jeon has also collaborated with artist Geunho Park, who works under the name "Chamsae," to create an artwork titled "Changing Colors with Light" using the newly developed technology. The artwork will be exhibited at "2026 Artience Daejeon," held at the Future Technology Hall of the National Science Museum from Nov. 17 to 28, 2026. Visitors will be able to directly observe how the same object appears in different colors depending on the illuminating light.

Jeon, senior researcher at the Department of Nano Display Research at KIMM, emphasized, "The most distinctive feature of this technology is that it can change the perceived color of an object simply by adjusting the light shining on it, without changing the object itself. We expect this technology to open up new possibilities for color expression using light in exhibitions, spatial design, product presentation and the arts."

passages: As liquidity continues to evaporate from cryptocurrency markets, Bitcoin is testing a long-term technical benchmark that has historically helped investors identify periods of extreme market weakness.

Cryptocurrency markets extended their recent sell-off on Wednesday, November 18, as deteriorating liquidity conditions and weakening risk appetite continued to weigh on digital assets. Bitcoin is once again approaching its recent lows near $62,000, while a rare breach of a long-term technical indicator is drawing considerable attention from investors.

As of early evening, Bitcoin ( BTC -3.22% ) was down 3.84% to $62,386.56, while Ethereum ( ETH -2.83% ) fell 3.80% to $1,753.33 and Solana ( SOL -2.52% ) declined 2.88% to $72.94. Although near-term downside risks remain elevated, historical market cycles suggest that periods of comparable weakness could present compelling opportunities for long-term investors.

Selling pressure intensified on Wednesday as investors awaited further insight into the Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook. With Treasury yields remaining elevated and liquidity continuing to deteriorate across cryptocurrency markets, investors appear increasingly reluctant to take on additional risk. The ongoing unwind of leveraged positions has compounded selling pressure, while subdued spot market demand has made it difficult for cryptocurrencies to sustain meaningful rallies.

Spot Bitcoin and Ethereum ETFs extended their recent losses on Wednesday, reflecting continued weakness in the underlying cryptocurrencies. The iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF ( IBIT -2.16% ) and Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund ( FBTC -2.16% ) both declined 2.16%, while the iShares Ethereum Trust ETF ( ETHA -2.63% ) fell 2.63%.

Despite deteriorating conditions in the cryptocurrency market, one historical indicator offers a potentially encouraging perspective for long-term investors. Following last week's 12% decline, Bitcoin broke below its 200-week moving average, a long-term pricing benchmark that has historically helped identify periods of extreme market weakness. According to CoinDesk, comparable instances in 2015, 2020, and 2022 were followed by positive returns over the subsequent three months. However, Bitcoin experienced further declines before recovering each time.

Before becoming more constructive on the broader cryptocurrency market, investors should look for signs of stabilization. One relatively straightforward way to gauge whether broader market conditions are improving would be to monitor Bitcoin's ability to reclaim and sustain a price above its 200-week moving average.

While historical precedent suggests cryptocurrencies could be approaching attractive long-term valuations, lower prices alone are not necessarily indicative of a market bottom. Until liquidity conditions improve, capital flows stabilize, and major cryptocurrencies demonstrate renewed price strength, the risk of further declines across the digital asset market remains elevated.

Bitcoin fell toward $63,000 Wednesday, extending a six-week retreat just as AI developer Anthropic prepared to price one of Wall Street's biggest initial public offerings. The timing has revived an attractive theory: investors are selling crypto to buy AI shares. Right now Bitcoin is about to touch $62,000, down 3.8% on today's session. Anthropic expects to price shares Wednesday at an indicated $70 to $78, ahead of Thursday's Nasdaq debut under ANT, potentially valuing the company at $1.4 trillion, according to its IPO prospectus. Kraken chief economist Thomas Perfumo told MarketWatch the IPO "could also be drawing capital out of risk assets" as investors position for the sale. That's a theory Binance founder Changpeng Zhao shared, flagging the listing as one possible factor in Bitcoin's decline in an X post Sunday. There is a tempting precedent. Bitcoin fell 19% in the 50 days before SpaceX listed in June and 23% in the equivalent period before Anthropic. But the comparison misses an important difference: AI stocks rallied before SpaceX; this time they have been falling alongside crypto. "This time, the sell-off has been led by the AI trade itself," Block Scholes research analyst Thahbib Rahman wrote in comments shared with Decrypt . Over the prior 50 days, Nvidia fell 32% and the Nasdaq dropped 11%, unlike their gains ahead of SpaceX's IPO. Bitcoin's 30-day correlation with Nvidia rose from 0.20 to 0.56, while its correlation with gold fell from 0.63 to 0.39. "Liquidity is ebbing and flowing out of crypto and equities together once more," Rahman wrote. Bitcoin's daily chart looks weak without any IPO theory. The relative strength index reads 21.8, well below the 30 threshold commonly associated with oversold markets, while an average directional index of 38.7 indicates a strong trend—in this case, downward. The 50-day exponential moving average is also below its 200-day counterpart, a bearish configuration associated with the so-called death cross. The pattern historically signals deteriorating momentum and the possibility of further losses, although it is a lagging indicator and does not necessarily predict where prices will go next. The immediate floor is around $62,000, close to Sunday's low. Glassnode data show buyers absorbed 66,000 BTC between $62,000 and $66,000 during heavy selling, but stablecoin supply has shrunk 4.2% over 90 days. Below $62,000, the next psychological level is $60,000; resistance sits near $65,500, $69,300 and $73,700. More tangible selling pressure has already been recorded. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs lost $239.9 million Tuesday, including $209.5 million from BlackRock's IBIT. Nearly $2 billion in leveraged crypto bets were liquidated during the weekend rout, amplifying losses as exchanges forcibly closed positions. sources.title: Anthropic to go public at $83 per share, jaw-dropping $1.5 trillion valuation: reports - New York Post
passages: AI giant Anthropic reportedly priced its hotly anticipated IPO Wednesday at a higher-than-expected $83 a share — bringing a jaw-dropping valuation of $1.5 trillion and showing strong Wall Street appetite for artificial intelligence despite recent jitters.
The initial public offering is now set to raise $68 billion.
Factoring in $26 billion in private placement, Anthropic’s offering of over $94 billion is set to blow past SpaceX’s $86 billion back in June, Bloomberg noted.

“In regards to the Dario essay humanity fears – many investors view that as background noise relative to how important Anthropic is because there are risks, but the opportunity and the growth with Anthropic way outweigh the risks for many investors,” Dan Ives, partner and analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co., told The Post.
Anthropic will look to defy an increasingly volatile stock market that has grown anxious in recent months about the AI trade, though the company has said its IPO is generating robust investor demand.
Jensen Huang’s recent shock resignation as CEO of Nvidia — one of the companies at the heart of the AI boom — sent many tech stocks plummeting earlier this month.
Meanwhile, Anthropic has gotten into a string of high-profile spats – most notably with Pete Hegseth’s Defense Department – over the use of its tools.
Still, Elon Musk’s rocket-and-telecom conglomerate is poised to hold onto its June record for largest IPO valuation ever — about $1.8 trillion.
Still, the at-times bizarre behavior of Anthropic’s employees – including top executives – seems likely to remain under heavy scrutiny as the world seeks to understand who’s behind the company.
Anthropic has been fighting to convince the Trump administration it isn’t “woke” while coming under criticism for its ties to the cult-like “Effective Altruism” movement .
Wall Street is counting on massive growth for Anthropic.

AI giant Anthropic reportedly priced its hotly anticipated IPO Wednesday at a higher-than-expected $83 a share — bringing a jaw-dropping valuation of $1.5 trillion and showing strong Wall Street appetite for artificial intelligence despite recent jitters. The pricing, reported by multiple outlets, beat expectations in the $70-$78 range. The initial public offering is now set to raise $68 billion. Factoring in $26 billion in private placement, Anthropic’s offering of over $94 billion is set to blow past SpaceX’s $86 billion back in June, Bloomberg noted. Still, Elon Musk’s rocket-and-telecom conglomerate is poised to hold onto its June record for largest IPO valuation ever — about $1.8 trillion. With trading under the ticker symbol “ANT” set to begin Thursday on the Nasdaq, the Anthropic listing could put to rest some of Wall Street’s concerns about the AI sector, which critics view as a bubble that’s poised to pop in spite of recent years’ breathtaking technological advances. Bankers previously said the Anthropic listing is close to seven times oversubscribed, making for an IPO that will extend its fundraising lead over arch-rival OpenAI while enhancing the personal fortunes of Anthropic’s co-founders. The San Francisco-based company, led by the quirky AI guru Dario Amodei, has been the subject of immense hype and controversy – raking in mountains of cash while sparking safety concerns. Amodei himself has been at the forefront of fears sweeping Silicon Valley and Washington, putting out statements and essays warning about the power of his company’s AI systems. Meanwhile, Anthropic has gotten into a string of high-profile spats – most notably with Pete Hegseth’s Defense Department – over the use of its tools. Amodei’s dire predictions include the potential for humans to lose control of AI, with dire consequences, or for power over the tech to become too concentrated. “If an extraordinarily powerful AI is used by one person or company to impress their worldview onto everyone else, the results could be extremely dystopian,” he opined in September. Many investors appear to be betting the doomsday predictions are so much sound and fury, signifying nothing. “In regards to the Dario essay humanity fears – many investors view that as background noise relative to how important Anthropic is because there are risks, but the opportunity and the growth with Anthropic way outweigh the risks for many investors,” Dan Ives, partner and analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co., told The Post. “It’s a white knuckle period and it’s a vote of confidence that Anthropic could have a successful IPO with the black cloud around Nvidia, Jensen and the AI trade,” he added. Still, the at-times bizarre behavior of Anthropic’s employees – including top executives – seems likely to remain under heavy scrutiny as the world seeks to understand who’s behind the company. Anthropic has been fighting to convince the Trump administration it isn’t “woke” while coming under criticism for its ties to the cult-like “Effective Altruism” movement . Amodei’s sister, who serves as president of the AI giant, has been subject to scrutiny for her apparent odd-ball fascination with anthropomorphizing stuffed animals, including using them to help solve business issues. Anthropic will look to defy an increasingly volatile stock market that has grown anxious in recent months about the AI trade, though the company has said its IPO is generating robust investor demand. Jensen Huang’s recent shock resignation as CEO of Nvidia — one of the companies at the heart of the AI boom — sent many tech stocks plummeting earlier this month. But Amodei and his six fellow co-founders are sitting pretty. Each is poised to sell about $250 million in shares while holding onto stakes valued at at least $18 billion apiece, according to reports. Wall Street is counting on massive growth for Anthropic. Some investment bank projections put its revenue at $52 billion to $53 billion in 2026, rising to $135 billion to $137 billion in 2027 and approximately $270 billion to $280 billion in 2028, Reuters recently reported . Analysts at Goldman Sachs say annual revenue could be $685 billion in four years , according to Bloomberg.

AI giant Anthropic reportedly priced its hotly anticipated IPO Wednesday at a higher-than-expected $83 a share — bringing a jaw-dropping valuation of $1.5 trillion and showing strong Wall Street appetite for artificial intelligence despite recent jitters. The pricing, reported by multiple outlets, beat expectations in the $70-$78 range. The initial public offering is now set to raise $68 billion. Factoring in $26 billion in private placement, Anthropic’s offering of over $94 billion is set to blow past SpaceX’s $86 billion back in June, Bloomberg noted. Still, Elon Musk’s rocket-and-telecom conglomerate is poised to hold onto its June record for largest IPO valuation ever — about $1.8 trillion. With trading under the ticker symbol “ANT” set to begin Thursday on the Nasdaq, the Anthropic listing could put to rest some of Wall Street’s concerns about the AI sector, which critics view as a bubble that’s poised to pop in spite of recent years’ breathtaking technological advances. Bankers previously said the Anthropic listing is close to seven times oversubscribed, making for an IPO that will extend its fundraising lead over arch-rival OpenAI while enhancing the personal fortunes of Anthropic’s co-founders. The San Francisco-based company, led by the quirky AI guru Dario Amodei, has been the subject of immense hype and controversy – raking in mountains of cash while sparking safety concerns. Amodei himself has been at the forefront of fears sweeping Silicon Valley and Washington, putting out statements and essays warning about the power of his company’s AI systems. Meanwhile, Anthropic has gotten into a string of high-profile spats – most notably with Pete Hegseth’s Defense Department – over the use of its tools. Amodei’s dire predictions include the potential for humans to lose control of AI, with dire consequences, or for power over the tech to become too concentrated. “If an extraordinarily powerful AI is used by one person or company to impress their worldview onto everyone else, the results could be extremely dystopian,” he opined in September. Many investors appear to be betting the doomsday predictions are so much sound and fury, signifying nothing. “In regards to the Dario essay humanity fears – many investors view that as background noise relative to how important Anthropic is because there are risks, but the opportunity and the growth with Anthropic way outweigh the risks for many investors,” Dan Ives, partner and analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co., told The Post. “It’s a white knuckle period and it’s a vote of confidence that Anthropic could have a successful IPO with the black cloud around Nvidia, Jensen and the AI trade,” he added. Still, the at-times bizarre behavior of Anthropic’s employees – including top executives – seems likely to remain under heavy scrutiny as the world seeks to understand who’s behind the company. Anthropic has been fighting to convince the Trump administration it isn’t “woke” while coming under criticism for its ties to the cult-like “Effective Altruism” movement . Amodei’s sister, who serves as president of the AI giant, has been subject to scrutiny for her apparent odd-ball fascination with anthropomorphizing stuffed animals, including using them to help solve business issues. Anthropic will look to defy an increasingly volatile stock market that has grown anxious in recent months about the AI trade, though the company has said its IPO is generating robust investor demand. Jensen Huang’s recent shock resignation as CEO of Nvidia — one of the companies at the heart of the AI boom — sent many tech stocks plummeting earlier this month. But Amodei and his six fellow co-founders are sitting pretty. Each is poised to sell about $250 million in shares while holding onto stakes valued at at least $18 billion apiece, according to reports. Wall Street is counting on massive growth for Anthropic. Some investment bank projections put its revenue at $52 billion to $53 billion in 2026, rising to $135 billion to $137 billion in 2027 and approximately $270 billion to $280 billion in 2028, Reuters recently reported . Analysts at Goldman Sachs say annual revenue could be $685 billion in four years , according to Bloomberg.

extraction.body: Regional conflicts, a sidelined US administration, and a rising China are complicating global action on climate change. It’s been a tough couple of years for global climate cooperation. US President Donald Trump withdrew the United States from the 2015 Paris Agreement (again) and signaled in January of this year an intent to withdraw from the broader 1992 United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). International efforts to implement and deepen these climate change agreements have struggled amid renewed geopolitical rivalry and resource demands. Meanwhile, global temperatures have continued to rise. The aspirational goal of limiting global temperature increases to 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels is now out of reach , with the threshold likely to be eclipsed on a permanent basis in the next few years—much earlier than anticipated. Manifestations of a warming planet are all around us, from glacier floods in Nepal to wildfires across Europe . It is under these circumstances that some 60,000 diplomats, community leaders, business executives, researchers, and journalists are meeting for the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference, or Conference of the Parties (COP), in Antalya, Turkey. COP31 has an unusual structure. Turkey is hosting but the negotiations are being led by Australia, as both countries wanted to get in on the action: Turkey to showcase its long-term climate ambitions and Australia to highlight regional vulnerabilities of Pacific Island countries. It remains to be seen whether there will be (m)any advances at the summit. Most of the architecture of the Paris Agreement has already been negotiated. And because we are now in the business end of implementation, it’s not clear there is a lot to be delivered through these meetings—though an effort to encourage countries to electrify more of their economy ( 35 percent by 2035 ) might be one breakthrough target. Countries have also already submitted the third round of Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), so-called pledges of what climate actions they intend to take in the next five years. Last year was the year updated NDCs were supposed to be made, though the wider political environment meant that most countries that submitted plans displayed limited ambition. Still, as in previous COPs, there will be significant clamors for new resources to support developing countries with funds for clean energy transitions, adaptation to climate and impacts, and “loss and damage” compensation. With the United States on the sidelines and other governments facing significant challenges in mobilizing foreign assistance, this meeting may not be ripe for big breakthroughs on finance. Still, there is an opportunity to tie climate finance to a renewed push for debt relief. Climate campaigners have not made that a big call to action yet, but they should. Twenty-six years ago, an international coalition successfully mobilized under Jubilee 2000 and campaigned for international financial institutions and wealthy nations to relieve the debts of the world’s poorest countries so they could spend more on education, public health, and other key investments. Ultimately, more than $100 billion in debt was canceled through the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) and Multilateral Debt Relief Initiative (MDRI) frameworks. Now, developing countries, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, are experiencing a new debt crisis, in which they are diverting essential funds for development needs to pay off old loans plus interest to foreign creditors. External debts of developing countries now total some $9.4 trillion. Though domestic mismanagement is partly to blame in some cases, there are other external drivers, including lost years during the COVID-19 pandemic; rising costs of food, fuel, and fertilizers amid the Ukraine and Iran wars; and the higher burden of climate impacts. Poorer countries also tend to face higher borrowing costs than wealthy countries. What’s different today is that China has emerged as a major lender, complicating multilateral debt relief efforts. While expanding other climate finance commitments might be tricky, debt for nature swaps have long been around, offering some debt relief in exchange for committing freed-up resources to conservation projects. New debt-for-climate loan forgiveness might free countries up to make further key investments in resilience and clean energy, with initiatives that include China likely proving more successful. At COP27 in 2022, parties agreed to create the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) to assist developing countries affected by climate impacts. About $822 million has been pledged to the fund and $450 million paid in, with requests from developing countries totaling more than $2.8 billion and one estimate putting developing countries' needs at $400 billion a year. The fund has been slow to capitalize fully and pay out, with petitioning countries often getting a small percentage of what is needed. Following the August 26 flood that killed nearly 1,500 people, Nepal was awarded a mere $20 million by the fund —less than 1 percent of what it will need to cover the damages. There will likely be some pressure at COP31 for donors to meet their pledges and an insistence that the funds be distributed more quickly. At COP29, the international community agreed to scale up its commitment to mobilize $300 billion a year in climate finance by 2035 under the New Collective Quantified Goal on Climate Finance (NCQG) , increasing the previous commitment of $100 billion a year. Those pledges include both public and private money and are distributed as bilateral aid through a variety of channels, including multilateral initiatives like the Green Climate Fund and through private actors. With about $140 billion mobilized in 2024 , we can expect some pressure from developing countries for donors to speed up their contributions and distribute more of them as grants, rather than loans. Progress on climate change has been slow, with many false starts and setbacks. Efforts though have helped blunt the expected warming, which was once thought likely to increase more than 4 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels by the end of the 21st century. Because of technological change and efforts at previous COPs, we are now on track for a rise of 2.8 degrees Celsius , which is still hugely worrisome but a significant improvement. More recently, China’s immense overcapacity in manufacturing has led to declining costs of clean technologies, including solar panels, batteries, and electric vehicles. We are now seeing rapid adoption of these technologies from Pakistan to Cuba, making the prospect of a clean energy transition more attractive and feasible. And while China’s industrial capacity poses real problems for developed countries’ manufacturing industries, it has been a boon for developing countries trying to navigate fuel disruptions and high prices in the wake of the Iran war. China’s own climate trajectory is uncertain, especially given its immense coal reserves and its responsibility for more than 30 percent of global emissions . Yet, with massive installations of renewables, recent reports suggest China’s emissions fell by 3.1 percent in the third quarter of 2026 after a wider two-year plateau in emissions. Thus, in some respects (and despite the lack of progress in global negotiations), we could be poised for greater decarbonization in the years to come. Last year, Trump’s moves against climate action and global coordination cast a pall over the proceedings. The international community put on a brave face and soldiered on with the negotiations, held in the Amazonian town of Belém, Brazil, where perhaps the most significant achievement was the launch of a new financing model for rainforest conservation known as the Tropical Forests Forever Facility (TFFF). The global trust fund has been a modest success, with nearly $8 billion pledged as of October. While there was a conversation about an explicit commitment to phasing out fossil fuels, the largely consensus-based meetings with fossil fuel producers in attendance made it impossible to reach an agreement. However, in May, a conference in Santa Marta, Colombia, attracted nearly 60 first movers who were most interested in making a more explicit commitment to fossil fuel phaseout. This was intended to be the first of a longer-running process, with a second meeting already planned. It was not the first time a “coalition of the willing” has come together. Since COP23 in 2017, the Powering Past Coal Alliance has been championing a coal phaseout through a network of national and subnational governments and other partners. And at COP26 in 2021, more than 100 countries joined the United States and European Union in pledging to reduce methane emissions . To be more broadly successful, however, climate negotiations require favorable circumstances, with leaders in power who are committed to taking action to address the problem. In 2015, that was true for both the United States and China. But save for a brief respite during the Biden administration, the United States has been on the sidelines or worse in the climate arena since 2016. This year’s meeting in Antalya may thus not yield much. Still, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s reelection in Brazil and the Democratic Party’s sweep in the 2026 US midterm elections suggest the politics may again become more favorable—at least to parts of the climate agenda. This may make future COPs more important, though the real action is what is happening on clean energy and resilience in countries around the world. Last year was the year updated NDCs were supposed to be made, though the wider political environment meant that most countries that submitted plans displayed limited ambition.

Still, as in previous COPs, there will be significant clamors for new resources to support developing countries with funds for clean energy transitions, adaptation to climate and impacts, and “loss and damage” compensation.

With the United States on the sidelines and other governments facing significant challenges in mobilizing foreign assistance, this meeting may not be ripe for big breakthroughs on finance. Still, there is an opportunity to tie climate finance to a renewed push for debt relief. Climate campaigners have not made that a big call to action yet, but they should.

Twenty-six years ago, an international coalition successfully mobilized under Jubilee 2000 and campaigned for international financial institutions and wealthy nations to relieve the debts of the world’s poorest countries so they could spend more on education, public health, and other key investments. Ultimately, more than $100 billion in debt was canceled through the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) and Multilateral Debt Relief Initiative (MDRI) frameworks.

External debts of developing countries now total some $9.4 trillion. Though domestic mismanagement is partly to blame in some cases, there are other external drivers, including lost years during the COVID-19 pandemic; rising costs of food, fuel, and fertilizers amid the Ukraine and Iran wars; and the higher burden of climate impacts. Poorer countries also tend to face higher borrowing costs than wealthy countries.

What’s different today is that China has emerged as a major lender, complicating multilateral debt relief efforts. While expanding other climate finance commitments might be tricky, debt for nature swaps have long been around, offering some debt relief in exchange for committing freed-up resources to conservation projects. New debt-for-climate loan forgiveness might free countries up to make further key investments in resilience and clean energy, with initiatives that include China likely proving more successful.

At COP27 in 2022, parties agreed to create the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) to assist developing countries affected by climate impacts. About $822 million has been pledged to the fund and $450 million paid in, with requests from developing countries totaling more than $2.8 billion and one estimate putting developing countries' needs at $400 billion a year. The fund has been slow to capitalize fully and pay out, with petitioning countries often getting a small percentage of what is needed. Following the August 26 flood that killed nearly 1,500 people, Nepal was awarded a mere $20 million by the fund —less than 1 percent of what it will need to cover the damages. There will likely be some pressure at COP31 for donors to meet their pledges and an insistence that the funds be distributed more quickly.

At COP29, the international community agreed to scale up its commitment to mobilize $300 billion a year in climate finance by 2035 under the New Collective Quantified Goal on Climate Finance (NCQG) , increasing the previous commitment of $100 billion a year. Those pledges include both public and private money and are distributed as bilateral aid through a variety of channels, including multilateral initiatives like the Green Climate Fund and through private actors. With about $140 billion mobilized in 2024 , we can expect some pressure from developing countries for donors to speed up their contributions and distribute more of them as grants, rather than loans.

Progress on climate change has been slow, with many false starts and setbacks. Efforts though have helped blunt the expected warming, which was once thought likely to increase more than 4 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels by the end of the 21st century. Because of technological change and efforts at previous COPs, we are now on track for a rise of 2.8 degrees Celsius , which is still hugely worrisome but a significant improvement.

More recently, China’s immense overcapacity in manufacturing has led to declining costs of clean technologies, including solar panels, batteries, and electric vehicles. We are now seeing rapid adoption of these technologies from Pakistan to Cuba, making the prospect of a clean energy transition more attractive and feasible. And while China’s industrial capacity poses real problems for developed countries’ manufacturing industries, it has been a boon for developing countries trying to navigate fuel disruptions and high prices in the wake of the Iran war.

China’s own climate trajectory is uncertain, especially given its immense coal reserves and its responsibility for more than 30 percent of global emissions . Yet, with massive installations of renewables, recent reports suggest China’s emissions fell by 3.1 percent in the third quarter of 2026 after a wider two-year plateau in emissions. The international community put on a brave face and soldiered on with the negotiations, held in the Amazonian town of Belém, Brazil, where perhaps the most significant achievement was the launch of a new financing model for rainforest conservation known as the Tropical Forests Forever Facility (TFFF). The global trust fund has been a modest success, with nearly $8 billion pledged as of October.

While there was a conversation about an explicit commitment to phasing out fossil fuels, the largely consensus-based meetings with fossil fuel producers in attendance made it impossible to reach an agreement. However, in May, a conference in Santa Marta, Colombia, attracted nearly 60 first movers who were most interested in making a more explicit commitment to fossil fuel phaseout. This was intended to be the first of a longer-running process, with a second meeting already planned.

In 2015, that was true for both the United States and China. But save for a brief respite during the Biden administration, the United States has been on the sidelines or worse in the climate arena since 2016.

This year’s meeting in Antalya may thus not yield much. Still, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s reelection in Brazil and the Democratic Party’s sweep in the 2026 US midterm elections suggest the politics may again become more favorable—at least to parts of the climate agenda. This may make future COPs more important, though the real action is what is happening on clean energy and resilience in countries around the world.

At COP29, the international community agreed to scale up its commitment to mobilize $300 billion a year in climate finance by 2035 under the New Collective Quantified Goal on Climate Finance (NCQG) , increasing the previous commitment of $100 billion a year.

Those pledges include both public and private money and are distributed as bilateral aid through a variety of channels, including multilateral initiatives like the Green Climate Fund and through private actors.
With about $140 billion mobilized in 2024 , we can expect some pressure from developing countries for donors to speed up their contributions and distribute more of them as grants, rather than loans.
It’s been a tough couple of years for global climate cooperation.
China’s own climate trajectory is uncertain, especially given its immense coal reserves and its responsibility for more than 30 percent of global emissions .
Regional conflicts, a sidelined US administration, and a rising China are complicating global action on climate change.
Still, there is an opportunity to tie climate finance to a renewed push for debt relief.
Last year, Trump’s moves against climate action and global coordination cast a pall over the proceedings.

extraction.body: Google’s search engine has long offered an incognito mode for all those search queries you don’t want logged or associated with your account. Now, Google’s AI Mode in Search is getting a similar feature. In a blog post , the company announced a new feature that brings “temporary threads” to AI Mode, where the conversations you have won’t be resurfaced later in areas like your search history or recommendations. Many leading AI chatbots already offer the option for temporary chats, Google Gemini included. However, there was not yet an option to have a temporary chat when you’re searching Google and are dropped into its conversational interface, known as AI Mode. Google says that users won’t have to adjust their settings to take advantage of the new option. Instead, they’ll be able to click a temporary threads icon in the upper right corner of AI Mode to engage in a temporary chat. This essentially works the same as a temporary chat would in the stand-alone Gemini chatbot. The option could be convenient to use at those times when you start digging deeper into a particular topic via AI Mode and realize that you don’t want the discussion to become a part of your search history because of its personal nature. Once the temporary thread is started, the session becomes detached from your account, Google says. This means that the responses the AI provides won’t be informed by past preferences, nor will they impact future personalization. That could also be useful for those times when you want to learn about something as more of a one-off, but don’t want Google to start to think of the topic as one of your main interests. When you close out of the thread, you will return to searching as usual. The company says the option to engage in temporary chats in AI Mode is rolling out globally on desktop and mobile across all supported languages.
